# Participant disclosure, cli.sgit.ai

> This site is written by the team that builds the sgit CLI, about its own tool. What that means for how to read it.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/about/participant.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# Participant disclosure

This site is published by the sgit project and written by the team that builds the sgit CLI, people and the agents working with them, about their own tool. Read it as a participant's account.

What that changes, and what is done about it:

- **The command reference is generated, not written.** It is the CLI's account of its own parser, so it cannot be flattering; it can only be out of date, and it names the release it came from.
- **The research articles are published as written**, including the ones that report the tool's own bugs (a pull that discarded uncommitted edits, branches that did not work, paths silently rewritten) and the reviews that corrected the team's designs.
- **The limits are on their own page**: [Limitations](../docs/limitations.md), moved here from sgit.ai with the rest.
- **sgit is beta.** It has no compliance certification of any kind.

Corrections are welcome, and are published above the mistake: [the corrections file](../admin/corrections.md).

# The team, cli.sgit.ai

> Who writes on cli.sgit.ai, as files: one person, the build agent that runs this repository, and the CLI team's agents whose research is published here.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/about/team.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# The team

Who writes on this site, and under which name. An article says who wrote it in its byline; this page is where each name points.

| Name | Who | What they write here |
|---|---|---|
| **Dinis Cruz** | the person: sgit's author, and the editor of this site | the briefs, in full; articles written up from his voice memos and messages, in his voice and under his name, by an agent. The editorial responsibility for everything on the site is his. [About him](https://sgit.ai/about/) |
| **cli.build** | the build agent of this repository, a Claude Code session working from Dinis's briefs | the site itself, the release history, and articles in its own voice about what it delivered, with the commits to check them against |
| **the sgit-ai CLI team** | the agents that work in the CLI repository (Claude Code sessions), for Dinis | the research documents, written in the CLI repository and published here as written |

## The rules the names follow

These are the rules of [Every site its own articles](https://send.sgit.ai/articles/every-site-its-own-articles.html):

- **Never one claimed as the other.** An agent's work is not described as Dinis's, nor the reverse. *We* is used only where both did the thing.
- **No model names in the text.** An article names its author; this page says what kind of agent that is.
- **The editorial responsibility is the person's,** whoever wrote the words.

## Not yet here

Roles as files with the rules each enforces, and a board of work, as the estate's [guidance](https://sgit.ai/docs/guidance/repositories.html) asks. Recorded in [the reality file](../admin/reality.md).

# Corrections to the brief

The brief is [published as given](../briefs/index.md). Where it was wrong, unclear or overtaken, the finding goes here, dated, newest first, and the brief stays as it was.

## 2026-10-20, the second brief, while building v0.2.0

8. **"send.sk.ai" is send.sgit.ai**, and its articles guidance is [Every site its own articles](https://send.sgit.ai/articles/every-site-its-own-articles.html). "The main official repo" is read as SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI, as in the first brief.
9. **The recent research was not on `dev`.** The six documents of 16 and 20 October were on the CLI's working branch `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq` at `5473571`, not yet merged; they were published from there, and every page from them names the branch.
10. **"Research documents that should now be articles" were two different things.** Five of the six were drafts written as newsroom articles; one was a coverage map. The drafts became articles; the map, and every earlier research document, went to a new research area. [Research is not an article](../articles/research-is-not-an-article.md) gives the reasoning.
11. **Correction 5 below is overtaken.** v0.1.0 published 23 research documents as articles. In v0.2.0, 21 of them moved to `/research/` and their old addresses send the reader on; the two that were newsroom drafts stayed as articles, converted to the newsroom's format.

## 2026-10-20, while building v0.1.0

1. **The names in the transcript are transcription errors.** "cli.sketo.ai" is `cli.sgit.ai` (the repository's README says so); "Escrip. AI" and "sk.ai" are `sgit.ai`; "the Skit" is sgit. Read throughout as such.
2. **"The API website for the CLI" is read as the CLI's documentation, with the HTTP API in it.** The brief goes on to describe a documentation site, so the site is that; the HTTP API pages moved here too, because the CLI is a client of that API and nothing else documents it as a whole.
3. **"Move" cannot be finished from this repository.** The pages are copied here and marked as moved, but sgit.ai still serves them and does not point here. Until sgit.ai's team adds links and redirects, both copies exist, and the one here is maintained from now on. The request is on [What moved](../admin/moved.md).
4. **"The most technical and the most detailed" needed a line drawn.** Drawn at: pages about the command-line tool, its keys, its protocol and its operation moved; pages about vaults as a platform (vault apps, `_page.json`, the browser bridge, publishing) stayed, since they are about the vault rather than the CLI. Twenty-seven pages moved.
5. **"The articles in the CLI repository" were not articles yet.** Two are article drafts for the newsroom; the rest are research notes, designs, reviews, measurements and fix write-ups for Dinis. Twenty-three of the October documents, those that take one topic as far as it goes, are published as articles, with a *kind* that says which of these each is. Replies to other teams and per-commit review responses were left in the CLI repository.
6. **The guidance "at sgit.ai for how to set up these websites" is two pages.** [Every sgit repository](https://sgit.ai/docs/guidance/repositories.html) and the vault guidance. The sibling sites (pki.sgit.ai, sgit.ai itself) supplied the pipeline. Where this site does not yet meet the guidance (the review folder, roles and a board, a release script that checks the live site), it is said on [the engineering page](../admin/index.md) and in [the reality file](../admin/reality.md).
7. **One difference from the sibling sites, chosen on purpose.** pki.sgit.ai's pages are hand-written HTML with the chrome injected; here every page is generated from markdown, because most of this site's content arrives as markdown (sgit.ai's twins, the CLI repository's documents, the CLI's own reference) and converting it by hand would be the drift the guidance warns about.

# Engineering, cli.sgit.ai

> How cli.sgit.ai is built, checked and released: one content folder, one generator, one gate, one version, deployed from dev by GitHub Pages; and how it measures against the estate's guidance for every sgit repository.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/admin/index.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# Engineering: how this site is built and released

One folder of content, one generator, one gate, one version number. Deployed to https://cli.sgit.ai by GitHub Pages on every push to `dev`, the same pipeline as [sgit.ai](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website) and [pki.sgit.ai](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__PKI).

## The shape

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `admin/content/<path>.md` | the source of the page at `<path>.html`: flat front matter, then markdown |
| `admin/content/articles/<slug>.md` | one article in the newsroom's format; adding the file publishes it ([the contract](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Cli/blob/dev/admin/content/articles/README.md)) |
| `admin/content/research/<slug>.md` | one research document from the CLI repository, as written, with its topics |
| `admin/content/research/topics/<id>.md` | one research topic: the question, where it stands, and the `!topic` list of its documents and articles |
| `admin/content/reference/sgit-cli-reference.json` | the output of `sgit help all --format json`; the command reference is generated from it |
| `REALITY.md`, `BRIEF-CORRECTIONS.md` | at the repository root, published as [Reality](../admin/reality.md) and [Corrections](../admin/corrections.md) |
| `admin/build/build.py` | the generator: pages, markdown twins, nav and footer, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`, sitemap, `assets/version.js` |
| `admin/build/md.py` | the markdown renderer, from pki.sgit.ai and newsroom.sgit.ai; escapes everything, so content cannot carry HTML |
| `admin/build/validate.js` | the gate |
| `admin/build/import_sgit_ai.py` | moves pages from sgit.ai, from their markdown twins ([what moved](../admin/moved.md)) |
| `admin/build/import_cli_research.py` | publishes documents from the CLI repository in the research area |
| `admin/build/make_figures.py` | draws the v0.2.0 articles' lead figures as SVG |
| `admin/build/render_figures.mjs`, `admin/build/figures/` | renders the drawn figures (one HTML page each) to webp, and every mermaid diagram in the content to SVG, with Playwright; run by hand, its output committed, so CI needs no browser |
| `admin/build/version.txt` | the site version, the one place it is written |
| `assets/themes/themes.css`, `assets/themes/themes.js` | the five themes of newsroom.sgit.ai (Newsprint, Night, Paper, Blueprint, Ember): every colour token in every theme, and the picker in the nav. The choice is kept in this browser only (`cli.theme` in local storage); with none chosen, a system set to dark gets Night. Print is always Newsprint |
| `.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml` | validate, tag, deploy |

Every generated file is listed in `admin/build/generated.json`, and the build deletes a listed file it no longer produces, so removing a content file removes its page and its twin.

## Releasing

1. Bump `admin/build/version.txt` and add a row to `admin/content/admin/versions.md` with one sentence on what changed and why. **Every release is a minor: the last number goes up by one** (v0.2.1, v0.2.2, v0.2.3). The middle number moves only when Dinis Cruz says so; this rule is his, from 20 October 2026. The tag job accepts exactly the next minor or a deliberate step of the middle number.
2. If a figure or a diagram changed, `node admin/build/render_figures.mjs`; then `python3 admin/build/build.py`
3. `node admin/build/validate.js`
4. `git commit -am "site vX.Y.Z: ..." && git push origin dev`. The `site vX.Y.Z:` prefix is load-bearing: the tag job finds the release commit by it and refuses a release whose newest prefix disagrees with `version.txt`.
5. Check that https://cli.sgit.ai/assets/version.js serves the new version. A clean push is not a release.

## The gate

`node admin/build/validate.js` fails the build on any of these, in CI on every push and pull request, before anything is tagged or deployed:

| Check | Why |
|---|---|
| The build is current (`build.py --check`) | a page edited by hand, or content committed without building, ships something the source does not say |
| The version agrees: `version.txt`, `assets/version.js`, `llms.txt`, one row in the release history | the badge on every page reads `version.js`; a release without its row has no record |
| Every internal link and asset resolves | an orphaned or misspelled link is a page nobody can reach |
| Every page has a canonical link on the CNAME host, and a markdown twin, and is in `llms.txt` | pages agents cannot read, or that claim to live elsewhere |
| No page is an orphan: every page is linked from another page | a page nothing links to is unpublished in practice |
| The leak tripwire: vault-key shapes, private-key markers, cloud and provider key prefixes, across every file | this site discusses keys constantly; it must never contain one |
| Every article is in the newsroom's format: its front matter, a summary of 220 to 360 words, In short, limits and sources, a lead figure that exists, no em-dash | the format is what lets the newsroom import an article unchanged ([the guidance](https://send.sgit.ai/articles/every-site-its-own-articles.html)) |
| A page left at a moved address points at a page that exists | the 21 research documents that were under /articles/ in v0.1 |
| The themes: no literal colour in `site.css` outside its `:root`, every token in all five themes, the picker offers exactly those five, every page loads them | a theme with a hole inherits Newsprint's value silently and ships half-applied, which is how a dark theme gets one light panel nobody can explain (the newsroom's rule) |
| Advisory, not failing: em-dashes in prose on this site's own pages | the estate's writing rule; pages moved or published verbatim, and research, keep their authors' punctuation |

## Against the estate's guidance

[Every sgit repository](https://sgit.ai/docs/guidance/repositories.html) lists what each repository carries. Where this one stands at v0.2.0:

| The guidance asks for | Here |
|---|---|
| The brief, published in full | [yes](../briefs/index.md), with the initial prompt |
| A reality file and a corrections file | [yes](../admin/reality.md), [yes](../admin/corrections.md) |
| One version, up on every push, shown on every page | yes: `version.txt`, the badge, the [release history](../admin/versions.md) |
| A gate that fails the build | yes, above |
| Machine-readable twins and `llms.txt` | yes, generated from the same source |
| Licences and a participant disclosure | yes: Apache-2.0 for code, CC BY 4.0 for content, [the disclosure](../about/participant.md) |
| Nav and footer injected at build | yes, from one definition in `build.py` |
| A credentials tier that is never committed | `.local/` is gitignored; nothing in this repository needs a secret to build |
| The review folder (`review/`) | **not yet**, recorded in [the reality file](../admin/reality.md) |
| Roles and a board, as files | **in part**: [the team](../about/team.md) names who writes; roles as files and a board are not yet here |
| A release script that verifies the live site | **not yet**: step 5 above is by hand |

# What moved from sgit.ai

On 20 October 2026 the CLI's most technical pages moved here from sgit.ai, as [the brief](../briefs/index.md) asks: the CLI now has a set of use cases of its own, and sgit.ai is the umbrella for the project and its commercial side. Each page kept its path, so `sgit.ai/docs/quickstart.html` is now `cli.sgit.ai/docs/quickstart.html`, and a redirect on sgit.ai is one rule.

The pages were taken from sgit.ai's markdown twins, which are generated from the same source as its HTML, at sgit.ai site v0.7.87, by `admin/build/import_sgit_ai.py`. The text is unchanged. Links to a page that moved now stay on this site; links to anything else go back to sgit.ai.

## What stayed on sgit.ai, and why

- **Vaults as a platform**: vault apps, `_page.json`, the browser bridge, sub-vaults, static hosting, publishing a vault, and the guidance for working on one. They are about the vault, not the command line.
- **The project**: why it exists, use cases, case studies, the published vaults, comparisons, the newsroom, partnerships.
- **The docs hub and the agent-contact protocol**, which serve the whole network.

## What sgit.ai still has to do

This site cannot change sgit.ai. Until sgit.ai's team acts, both copies exist, and **the copy here is the one maintained from now on**. The request to them, as recorded in [the corrections file](../admin/corrections.md):

1. Point each moved page at its new address: a link at the top, then a redirect.
2. Point sgit.ai's docs hub and `llms.txt` at cli.sgit.ai for the CLI.
3. Add cli.sgit.ai to the network directory (`admin/content/sites/cli.md`, the Cartographer's file).

The rule, from the SG/Send repository's Librarian: a feature that is not in this file does not exist, and nobody may say a thing works because a brief describes it. Kept current by whoever ships.

# Append lanes, cli.sgit.ai

> The six append endpoints) the write-only vault-to-vault message transport. Four separated capabilities, the blind write response, server-assigned sortable filenames, idempotent mark-processed, and the limits.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/api/append-lanes.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Moved from <https://sgit.ai/api/append-lanes.html> (sgit.ai v0.7.87) on 2026-10-20.*

---
# Append lanes

A write-only channel attached to a vault, gated by a token the writer holds and nothing else. This is the transport behind [vault-to-vault messaging](../docs/vault-messaging.md) and behind [`sg.append`](https://sgit.ai/docs/vault/sg-bridge.html) in the browser bridge, and it is deliberately generic: the same primitive carries messages, logs, signals, control messages and state flows.

**Naming.** This API was called **inbox** before v0.32.7. Every `/api/vault/inbox/*` URL is gone, and `purge` takes `folder:"pending"` or `"processed"`, the old `"inbox"` value returns **400**. If you are reading older material, translate.

**Checked in use, 26 September 2026.** Two agent teams ran two-way, signed messaging over these lanes on 25 and 26 September, and wrote down every place where this page differed from what the server did. [Their write-up](../docs/append-lane-messaging.md) is published on this site. The table below, and the sections marked *checked 26 September*, are corrected from it.

## The six endpoints

All **POST**, all under `/api/vault/append/`.

| Path | Gate | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `configure/{vault_id}` | `x-sgraph-vault-write-key`**and** the SG/Send access token (401 without it) | Registers `append_anchors`, hashes of accepted senders, and `enum_key_hash`. **It replaces the anchor list**: to add a sender, send every existing anchor plus the new one, or the existing lanes silently stop accepting writes |
| `write/{vault_id}` | `append_token`**in the body** | Appends a payload. **Account-less**: no access token required |
| `list/{vault_id}` | `x-sgraph-vault-enum-key` | Paginated listing, optionally with inline content. Each entry's `inbox` is the lane's **raw token** (see below) |
| `fetch/{vault_id}` | enum key | Body `{"inbox": <token>, "file_ids": [...]}`: the lane must be named. **Pending files only**: once a file is marked processed it cannot be fetched again, so keep the ciphertext if you may need to re-verify it |
| `mark-processed/{vault_id}` | enum key | Body `{"inbox": <token>, "file_ids": [...]}`. Moves pending → processed. Idempotent |
| `purge/{vault_id}` | `x-sgraph-vault-write-key` and the SG/Send access token (401 without it; checked 29 September) | Body `{"inbox": <token>, "folder": "pending" | "processed"}`. Deletes |

## Where the routes are, and what a failure looks like checked 26 September

- **The routes are on `https://dev.send.sgraph.ai` only.** `send.sgraph.ai` has no append routes today.
- **A bad key or an unknown token returns 404 with an HTML page**, not a 403 with JSON. A missing field returns a JSON 400. When a call 404s, check the key before the path.
- **Getting the write key.** It is derived from the vault key: `Vault__Crypto().derive_keys_from_vault_key(vault_key)['write_key']`. The parser strips the `sgit_private_vault_` prefix first; deriving from the raw string gives a different key, and every call 404s.

## The payload, exactly checked 26 September

`sgit pki encrypt` writes the `.enc` file as base64 text of a JSON envelope. The `payload` sent to `write` is base64 of that file's bytes, so the envelope is **encoded twice**:

```
payload  = base64(open("msg.eml.enc", "rb").read())        # sending
envelope = json.loads(b64decode(b64decode(content)))       # draining
```

A sender that encodes only once is rejected by a strict drainer. The recommendation to the sgit team is a single encoding, since the `.enc` text is already valid base64; until that changes, this is the format.

## Why the gates are split this way

Four capabilities, and the split is the whole design:

| Capability | Holder | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|---|
| `append_token` | the sender | write | list, fetch, read anything |
| `enum_key` | the vault owner | list, fetch, mark-processed | write, purge |
| `write_key` | the vault owner | configure, purge | none |
| private key | the vault owner | **decrypt** | *never sent to the server* |

A sender can put something into your vault and learn nothing at all, not the contents, not the volume, not whether anyone else writes there. The server stores `SHA-256` of the first three capabilities and compares hashes; the fourth it never sees.

## Four contracts worth relying on

- **The write response is blind.** `/write` returns exactly `{"ok": true}`, no file ID, no count, no metadata. This is a security property, not an oversight: a returned ID would leak lane state to a party who is only allowed to write.
- **Filenames are server-assigned** as `{epoch_ms:013d}_{24-hex}.enc`. Being chronologically sortable is what makes cursor pagination stable, pass the last file ID you saw as `after_file_id`.
- **Metadata-only listing is free.** `include_content: false` reads **zero** payloads. Poll with it, then fetch on demand; polling with content is the common way to hit the 3 MB ceiling for no reason.
- **mark-processed is idempotent.** An already-moved file comes back in `missing` rather than as an error, so retrying a batch after a timeout is safe.

## From a vault app: one verb crosses vaults, five do not

This is the constraint to understand before designing anything that spans two vaults, and it was undocumented until the SG/API team's review of 6 September 2026 (quoted here CC BY 4.0). The bridge builds **one** client bound to the **currently open vault**, with the enum key derived from that vault's read key. So:

| Verb | Which vault it acts on | Bridge permission |
|---|---|---|
| `write` | **Any**: it takes an explicit `vault_id` and posts with no headers at all | `append.write` |
| `list` | Always the open vault. There is no way to address a remote vault with these from an app | `append.list` |
| `fetch` | `append.read`, **not**`append.fetch` |
| `markProcessed` | `append.markProcessed` |
| `purge` | `append.purge` |
| `configure` | `append.configure` |

All six are plain booleans, **default-deny**, not path-scoped. The asymmetry is deliberate rather than a gap: listing a remote lane needs the recipient's enum key, and shipping that inside a published app *"would give every visitor read access to the whole lane."*

**Two things that are *not* gates on `append`, despite appearances.** There is **no read-only check** anywhere in the append handler, `sg.app.writable` is irrelevant to it, and a read-key session can write to a lane given the grant. And the CSP is not an append rule: the frame ships `connect-src blob: data:`, so a *direct* `fetch` to these endpoints is blocked unless the app declares `permissions.network: true`, which reopens all egress and is the worse choice. Use the bridge. See [the build brief](https://sgit.ai/docs/briefs/vault-telemetry-append-lanes.html), which had both of these wrong until the review corrected it.

## The `inbox` field is the lane id, and today it is the token

A `list` response labels each entry with an `inbox` value. That value is the storage folder name, and the folder is named by the **raw append token**, byte for byte, while `config.append_anchors` stores `sha256(token)`. So the design hashes the token in config and then writes the plaintext token into the object key.

The disclosure is bounded: `list` is gated by the enum key, so it reaches only the vault owner, who already holds every credential in play; and the token is a **write-only lane address**, closer to an email address than a password. The residual risk is storage rather than API, the raw token becomes an object key, so it lands in access logs, inventory reports and backups, *"surfaces with a very different audience from the enum-key holder."* The team intends to fold the folder name to `sha256(token)`, which is a breaking change needing a migration. **Documented here now so that nobody has to discover it from a debrief.**

Lanes live at `bare/append/{token}/pending/` and `…/processed/`, **outside the version-controlled commit tree**: appends never touch a branch and never conflict with a push.

## Several senders on one vault

Register several `append_anchors` and each sender writes into their own lane, distinguished by their token. A listing can be scoped to one lane, so one correspondent flooding you does not bury another, and revoking one sender is removing one anchor, with no effect on the rest.

## Limits and codes

| Limit | Value | On breach |
|---|---|---|
| Payload per write | 5 MB | 413 |
| Pending files per token | 1000 | 507 |
| File IDs per batch | 100 | 400 |
| Inline content when listing | 3 MB cumulative | 413 |
| Page size | 50 default, 200 max | clamped silently |

The `append_token` pattern is `^[0-9a-f]{16,128}$`, hex only. A prefixed token returns **400**, not 403; see [errors](../api/errors.md) for why that distinction saves time.

- [Vault messaging](../docs/vault-messaging.md), this API composed with PKI into a worked example
- [Append-lane messaging between agents](../docs/append-lane-messaging.md), the write-up of two-way use on 25 and 26 September: per-session keys, a pinned key registry, ephemeral inboxes, the threat model and the recommendations
- [`sg.append`](https://sgit.ai/docs/vault/sg-bridge.html), the same six operations from a vault app

# Authentication, cli.sgit.ai

> The six authentication headers, what each one gates, and the hash-comparison model: the server stores SHA-256 of every capability key and never holds a raw key or a private key. Includes why vault reads are open by default.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/api/authentication.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Moved from <https://sgit.ai/api/authentication.html> (sgit.ai v0.7.87) on 2026-10-20.*

---
# Authentication

Six headers exist. Which apply depends on the endpoint and on how the server is deployed. None of them is a password, and none of them is stored: the server keeps `SHA-256` hashes and compares.

## The headers

| Header | What it gates |
|---|---|
| `x-sgraph-access-token` | The SGraph account or deployment. In a **single-key self-hosted deployment** this gates *every* route, including reads |
| `x-sgraph-vault-write-key` | Vault write capability: writes, deletes, destroy, and append `configure` / `purge` |
| `x-sgraph-vault-enum-key` | Append lane enumeration: `list`, `fetch`, `mark-processed` |
| `x-vault-read-key` | Read key, for public-vault routing |
| `x-vault-public` | Public-vault routing flag |
| `x-sgraph-transfer-delete-auth` | [Transfer deletion](../api/transfers.md), SG/Send transfers, not vaults. Carries the *secret*, never the hash, and only works if a `delete_auth_hash` was set at create time |

One capability is **not** a header: `append_token` travels in the request body of `/append/write`. That is deliberate, see [append lanes](../api/append-lanes.md).

## The hash-comparison model

The server never stores a capability key. It stores `SHA-256(key)` and, on each request, hashes what you presented and compares. Two consequences worth designing around:

- **A server compromise yields hashes and ciphertext**, not keys and not plaintext. An attacker with the whole database still cannot read a vault.
- **There is no recovery path.** The server cannot email you your key, because it has never had it. Same property as the vault key itself, for the same reason.

## Why reads are open by default

`GET /api/vault/read/{vault_id}/{file_id}` requires no authentication on the shared host, which surprises people. It follows from the encryption model rather than being a gap in it: the bytes are AES-256-GCM ciphertext under a key the server has never seen, and the file IDs are HMAC-derived opaque identifiers that reveal no filename. Serving them to an anonymous caller discloses nothing a reader could use.

It is also the property that makes a [published read key](https://sgit.ai/demos/vaults/index.html) work at all, and what lets vault content sit behind an ordinary CDN. If that trade is wrong for your deployment, run in single-key mode, where the access token gates reads too.

What an unauthenticated reader *can* learn is covered honestly on the [security page](../security/index.md#server-sees): object sizes, timing, and approximate activity volume.

## See also

- [Errors](../api/errors.md), what a 403 means as against a 400
- [Security model](../security/index.md), the crypto these capabilities sit on

# Errors and limits, cli.sgit.ai

> 400, 403, 413 and 507: what each means, why a malformed token returns 400 rather than 403, the input patterns enforced before storage is reached, and every documented ceiling.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/api/errors.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Moved from <https://sgit.ai/api/errors.html> (sgit.ai v0.7.87) on 2026-10-20.*

---
# Errors and limits

Four status codes carry almost all the failures, and telling them apart saves real debugging time, particularly 400 versus 403, which fail for opposite reasons.

## Status codes

| Code | Means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **400** | Invalid input, the value never reached a gate. Malformed token, malformed file ID, batch too large, unknown `folder` value | Fix the *shape* of what you sent. Your credential may be perfectly valid |
| **403** | Gate failure, well-formed input, wrong capability | Fix the *credential*. The request shape was fine |
| **413** | Too large, payload over 5 MB, or an inline-content listing over the 3 MB ceiling | Split the payload, or list without inline content and fetch on demand |
| **507** | Lane full, 1000 pending files for that token | Fetch and `mark-processed`, then `purge` the processed folder |

**The 400 that looks like a 403.** Path and token components are validated by typed primitives *before* they reach storage, which is how path traversal is blocked at the type level. A prefixed token such as `tok_abc…` (or a CLI fingerprint pasted straight in, `sha256:a461…`) fails the hex-only pattern and returns **400**. It reads like a rejected credential; it is a rejected string. Use raw hex.

## Input patterns

| Input | Pattern |
|---|---|
| `append_token` | `^[0-9a-f]{16,128}$`: hex only, no prefix |
| `file_id` (append) | `^\d{13}_[0-9a-f]{24}\.enc$`) server-assigned, so you should be echoing one back |
| `vault_id` | lowercase alphanumeric, 8–24 characters, no hyphens |

## Limits

| Limit | Value | On breach |
|---|---|---|
| Payload per append write | 5 MB | 413 |
| Pending files per append token | 1000 | 507 |
| File IDs per batch (fetch / mark / purge) | 100 | 400 |
| Operations per `/vault/batch` request | 100 | 400 |
| Inline content when listing | 3 MB cumulative | 413 |
| Append list page size | 50 default, 200 max | clamped silently |
| `read-base64` response | ~3.75 MB | use [presigned reads](../api/vault-objects.md) above this |

The page-size clamp is silent: ask for 500 and you get 200 with no warning. Page with `after_file_id` rather than assuming your requested size was honoured.

# The HTTP API, cli.sgit.ai

> The protocol surface behind sgit: base URL, the capability model, and the reference for vault objects, append lanes, authentication headers and error codes. Built from a code-verified audit at v0.33.54, with unresolved endpoints labelled rather than guessed at.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/api/index.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Moved from <https://sgit.ai/api/index.html> (sgit.ai v0.7.87) on 2026-10-20.*

---
# The HTTP API

Everything sgit does, it does over this API. The CLI is a client; so is the browser bridge; so is anything you write. This section is the protocol surface, endpoints, headers, gates, limits and the error codes you will actually hit. **Two families share this host**: [vaults](../api/vault-objects.md), which are versioned trees you clone and push, and [transfers](../api/transfers.md), which are single encrypted handovers.

**Where this came from, and how far to trust it.** This section is built from a code-verified audit supplied by the SG/API team, read out of the route tables and constants at **v0.33.54** rather than recalled. It is *their* verification, not ours: this site has not independently exercised every endpoint. Where their audit and the shipped client disagreed we checked and said so; where something is registered but unconfirmed it is labelled **PROPOSED** and you should not build on it yet. Same rule as the rest of this site, if it is not verified, it says so.

## Base URL

`https://send.sgraph.ai` for the hosted service, or your own host if you [run it yourself](https://sgit.ai/deploy/index.html). All request and response bodies are JSON unless stated otherwise.

## The one idea worth reading first

The server is a **capability-checked ciphertext store**, and every access-control decision it makes is a hash comparison. It stores `SHA-256` of each capability key and checks `H(presented) == stored`. It never holds a raw key, and it never holds a private key at all.

That is what makes the rest of the design possible: a vault ID is an address rather than an account, reads are public by default because the bytes are useless without a key, and a stranger can write to your vault without ever having a credential on the platform.

## The reference

| Page | What is in it |
|---|---|
| [Authentication](../api/authentication.md) | The six headers, what each gates, and the hash-comparison model |
| [Vault objects](../api/vault-objects.md) | The pointer store (read, write, batch, destroy) plus the caching contract and storage layout |
| [Append lanes](../api/append-lanes.md) | The six append endpoints: the vault-to-vault message transport |
| [Transfers](../api/transfers.md) | The other family on this host: one encrypted payload, uploaded once, handed over as a single link, the SGMETA envelope, the three calls, and when to reach for this instead of a vault |
| [Errors and limits](../api/errors.md) | 400, 403, 413, 507, what each actually means, and the ceilings that produce them |

## Four capabilities

Most of the API surface is one of four capability tiers. They are separated so that holding one tells you nothing about the others:

| Capability | Presented as | Grants |
|---|---|---|
| `append_token` | a field in the request body | Write to one append lane. Nothing else, not even listing it |
| `enum_key` | `x-sgraph-vault-enum-key` | List, fetch and mark-processed on append lanes |
| `write_key` | `x-sgraph-vault-write-key` | Write and delete objects; configure and purge lanes |
| private key | *never presented* | Decryption, client-side only |

The fourth row is the point of the design rather than a footnote: the server cannot decrypt anything it stores, so the strongest capability in the system is the one it never sees.

## Where to start

- Sending an encrypted message between two vaults → [Vault messaging](../docs/vault-messaging.md), which composes [append lanes](../api/append-lanes.md) with [PKI](../docs/pki.md).
- Reading or writing files → [Vault objects](../api/vault-objects.md).
- Building a vault app in the browser → the [SG bridge](https://sgit.ai/docs/vault/sg-bridge.html) wraps this API so you never write HTTP.
- Using the CLI instead → [Quickstart](../docs/quickstart.md).

## Open questions we will not guess at

Three items came through the audit unresolved. They are listed rather than documented, because a confident page about an endpoint that does not exist is worse than no page:

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/vault/zip/{vault_id}` | **UNRESOLVED**: registered in the route table, marked PROPOSED in the team’s reality document. Not documented either way until that is reconciled |
| `/join/*` | **UNRESOLVED**: the reality document lists three live endpoints, but the routes are not registered in the deployed app. Not documented |
| Client-side lane addressing | **PROPOSED**: `append_token = H(public key)` is the intended model; no shipped command emits it. See the [addressing note](../docs/vault-messaging.md#addressing) for what to do meanwhile |

# The transfer API, one encrypted handover, one link, cli.sgit.ai

> The other API family on this host: a single encrypted payload uploaded once and shared as one link. The two secrets that must not be confused, the SGMETA envelope that keeps the filename off the server, the three calls, revocation that is opt-in at create time only, and when a transfer beats a vault.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/api/transfers.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Moved from <https://sgit.ai/api/transfers.html> (sgit.ai v0.7.87) on 2026-10-20.*

---
# The transfer API, one encrypted handover, one link

The other half of the API on this host. A **vault** is a versioned encrypted tree you clone, pull and push; a **transfer** is a single encrypted payload uploaded once and handed over as one link. Same server, same zero-knowledge property, different job, and until now this site documented a transfer *header* without documenting a single transfer *endpoint*.

**Provenance.** This page is derived from an integration guide written by the team that owns the SG/Send API, who executed **every request, response, status code and byte layout in it against the production user API on 9 September 2026**. That run is theirs, not ours. We have not re-executed it here, and the date is the one to check it against. Their guide is released under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

## Transfer or vault?

Pick this first; it decides everything after it.

|  | Transfer | [Vault](../api/vault-objects.md) |
|---|---|---|
| **Shape** | One payload, uploaded once | A versioned tree of files |
| **History** | None. There is no second version | Commits, branches, merges |
| **The reader gets** | The whole payload, or nothing | Any single file, without fetching the rest |
| **Lifecycle** | Expires, caps downloads, can be revoked | Lives until you delete it |
| **The credential** | A decryption key in the URL fragment | A [read key](https://sgit.ai/docs/vault/reading-a-vault-file.html), derived one-way |
| **Reach for it when** | An agent finishes a job and hands the result over **once**: a bundle, a report, a dated export | The thing is read repeatedly, browsed, updated, or rendered as an app |

The SG/API team's own guidance, for a workflow that ships one bundle per voice memo, is that the transfer API is *“the simpler and better fit”*. That is the right instinct in general: **a vault is the wrong answer for a handover that happens once.**

## Two secrets that must never be confused

This is the part that goes wrong first, and it goes wrong silently, a leaked access key does not throw.

|  | What it authorises | Where it goes |
|---|---|---|
| **The access key** `x-sgraph-access-token` | *You*, to upload | A request **header**. Never a URL, never a share link, never a log |
| **The decryption key** | *Anyone*, to read | The URL **fragment**: everything after `#`, which no browser sends to the server |

They are unrelated values. The fragment is what makes a share link both shareable and private: the key reaches the recipient's client and never the origin serving the page. The API also accepts `?access_token=` as a query fallback and it works, **do not use it**; query strings land in proxy logs, browser history and workflow execution records.

What the server can see: ciphertext size, a hashed sender IP, a creation timestamp, and the `content_type_hint` you supply. What it cannot see: the filename, the contents, or the key.

## The payload format, two layers, in this order

The filename must not reach the server, so it is wrapped *inside* the plaintext before encryption. Getting the order wrong produces a corrupt download with no name.

**Inner, the SGMETA envelope:**

```
"SGMETA\0"          7 bytes    53 47 4D 45 54 41 00
meta_len            4 bytes    uint32, big-endian
metadata JSON       meta_len   {"filename":"…"}  UTF-8
file bytes          rest       your payload
```

**Outer, AES-256-GCM over that whole buffer:**

```
IV                 12 bytes    random, fresh per upload, prepended
ciphertext + tag   rest        GCM appends its own 16-byte tag
```

- **Key:** 32 random bytes, shared as **base64url, unpadded**: 43 characters.
- **IV:** 12 random bytes, never reused with the same key.
- **Overhead:** the uploaded payload is exactly **28 bytes larger** than the plaintext (12 + 16).

Same primitive as everything else here: AES-256-GCM, done client-side, with the server holding ciphertext under a key it never had. [The security page](../security/index.md) covers why that is the whole product rather than a feature of it.

## The three calls

| Call | Endpoint | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1 · create** | `POST /api/transfers/create` | Returns `transfer_id`. Body carries `file_size_bytes` (the *plaintext* length, display metadata only), `content_type_hint` (stored in the clear, keep it generic), `max_downloads`, `auto_delete`, `expires_at` |
| **2 · upload** | `POST /api/transfers/upload/{id}` | **Raw bytes**: not base64, not multipart. `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` |
| **3 · complete** | `POST /api/transfers/complete/{id}` | Nothing is downloadable until this call lands |

Only those three need the access key. `info` and `download` are **public by design**: the decryption key is the gate, which is exactly why a share link works for someone with no account.

**Two traps in the create body.** `expires_at` is in **milliseconds** since epoch, not seconds; `0` means never. And `max_downloads: 0` means *unlimited*, not zero, once a finite allowance is exhausted, downloads return **410**.

### Build the share link yourself

`complete` returns a `download_url` of `/d/{id}`. **Ignore it**: verified as a 404; it is not a live route. The link to hand out is:

```
https://send.sgraph.ai/en-gb/download/#{transfer_id}/{key_base64url}
```

Omit `/{key}` for a link-only form when the key travels through a second channel. The fragment parser splits on the **first** `/` and truncates at a `|`, so `|` is reserved, base64url never produces one, so following the format above keeps you clear.

## What a receiving agent has to do

This is the payoff, and it is two calls with no account and no browser: `GET /api/transfers/download/{id}` needs no auth, and the key from the fragment does the rest, split the IV off the first 12 bytes, AES-GCM decrypt, check the `SGMETA\0` magic, read the big-endian length, and the filename and payload fall out. For a JSON-only transport such as an MCP tool, `GET /api/transfers/download-base64/{id}` returns the same bytes wrapped in JSON.

**Downloads are counted.** An agent retrying a failed run burns the allowance. For agent-facing links prefer `max_downloads: 0` with a short `expires_at`, time-bounded rather than attempt-bounded, because a retry is not a reader.

## Expiry, caps and revocation

Revocation is opt-in **at create time and only then**: set `delete_auth_hash` to `sha256(secret)` in hex and store the secret beside the transfer id. Without it, deletion is disabled for that transfer forever. To revoke, `DELETE /api/transfers/delete/{id}` carrying the access key and `x-sgraph-transfer-delete-auth: <the secret, not the hash>`, the one header [the authentication page](../api/authentication.md) already listed before this page existed to explain it.

**410 and 404 are both normal end states, not errors to retry:** 410 is gone-as-expected (expired or exhausted), 404 is never-existed-or-deleted.

## Size

| Path | Ceiling | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct upload** | keep the encrypted payload under **~4 MB** | The normal case |
| Multipart / presigned | Larger | Needs the S3 backend, check `GET /api/presigned/capabilities` first |

The ~4 MB figure is a working limit rather than a published one: the Lambda URL caps a request body at 6 MB and the browser client switches to presigned at 5 MB. Text bundles compress far below it; **audio does not**, and is usually the most sensitive part of a bundle as well as the largest.

## Verified behaviour

The SG/API team's run, 9 September 2026, reproduced here as they reported it:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Header `x-sgraph-access-token` | **200** |
| Header `x-sgraph-send-access-token` | **401**: that name does not work |
| No token, or a wrong one | **401** |
| `download` / `info` with no token | **200**: public by design |
| Round trip: wrap → encrypt → create → upload → complete → download → decrypt → unwrap | **Byte-identical** payload recovered, filename intact |
| Download #3 against `max_downloads: 2` | **410** |
| Download of an expired transfer | **410** |
| `DELETE` with wrong / correct delete-auth | **403** / **200**, then **404** |
| `GET /d/{transfer_id}` | **404**: not a route |
| Key length | 32 bytes → 43 base64url characters |
| Encrypted payload overhead | plaintext + 28 bytes |

## The rules worth holding to

1. **Never log or return the decryption key** outside the share link. It is not an identifier, anyone holding it reads the payload. In a workflow engine that means keeping it out of node output that gets persisted.
2. **Never put the access key in a URL.** Header only.
3. **Never reuse an IV.** Twelve fresh random bytes per upload.
4. **Keep the filename inside the envelope.** `content_type_hint` is in the clear; the name is not, and that is the reason the envelope exists.
5. **Always set an expiry.** A link pasted into a chat lives as long as the chat does; the transfer should not.
6. **Bundle for a reader who is an agent**: a `manifest.json` saying what each file is, and an `llms.txt`, cost nothing and are the difference between a payload that can be used and one that has to be opened by a person first.

Adapted with attribution from the SG/API team's integration guide of 9 September 2026 (CC BY 4.0); the workflow-specific half of that document (credential wiring, node shapes, the bundle layout for one product) stays with the product it was written for. # Vault objects, cli.sgit.ai

> The pointer store: read, write, batch, destroy and presigned endpoints, the caching contract that separates immutable content-addressed objects from mutable refs, and the storage layout behind every vault.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/api/vault-objects.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Moved from <https://sgit.ai/api/vault-objects.html> (sgit.ai v0.7.87) on 2026-10-20.*

---
# Vault objects

The pointer store: the ciphertext objects a vault is made of, addressed by opaque identifiers the server cannot interpret. This is what `sgit push` and `sgit pull` are doing underneath.

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Auth | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| PUT | `/api/vault/write/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | access token + write key | Body is raw ciphertext |
| GET | `/api/vault/read/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | none | Raw bytes. [Reads are public by default](../api/authentication.md#reads) on the shared host |
| GET | `/api/vault/read-base64/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | none | Base64 in JSON, MCP-safe. Around 3.75 MB ceiling |
| DELETE | `/api/vault/delete/{vault_id}/{file_id}` | access token + write key |  |
| POST | `/api/vault/batch/{vault_id}` | per operation | Mixed reads and writes, **max 100** per request |
| POST | `/api/vault/list/{vault_id}` | none |  |
| GET | `/api/vault/health/{vault_id}` | none |  |
| GET | `/api/vault/public-info/{vault_id}` | none |  |
| DELETE | `/api/vault/destroy/{vault_id}` | write key | Body `{vault_id, purge?}`. Without `purge` it writes a tombstone that blocks reuse of the ID |

Large blobs go through presigned URLs rather than the request body: `POST /api/vault/presigned/initiate|complete|cancel/{vault_id}` and `GET /api/vault/presigned/read-url/{vault_id}/{file_id}`.

`GET /api/vault/zip/{vault_id}` is registered in the route table but marked PROPOSED upstream. It is deliberately [not documented](../api/index.md#unresolved) until that is reconciled.

## Destroy, and why the tombstone matters

`destroy` without `purge:true` leaves a tombstone that prevents the vault ID being registered again. That is a security property, not bookkeeping: vault IDs are short and a released ID is a squattable namespace. If somebody still holds a read key pointing at that ID, a new vault claiming it would be answering reads meant for the old one. `purge:true` skips the tombstone and frees the ID, use it only when you are sure no credential survives.

## The caching contract

Anyone writing a client needs this, and getting it wrong produces a bug that looks like corruption:

| Object | Response header |
|---|---|
| File ID containing `-imm-`, immutable, content-addressed | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` |
| Refs and indexes, mutable | `Cache-Control: no-store` |

Immutable objects are content-addressed, so their bytes can never change and a year-long cache is safe, which is what lets a vault sit behind a CDN. Mutable refs must never be cached: a stale ref renders a previous commit’s tree from ciphertext that is itself perfectly valid, so nothing errors and the reader simply sees the wrong version of the vault.

**Measured 21 September 2026: the immutable header is not currently being sent.** A GET of an `obj-cas-imm-` object on `/api/vault/read/` returned **no `Cache-Control` header at all**, and the CDN reported a miss. The table above is the contract, not a description of what is served on that path today. Build as though the header may be absent: cache on the id, which is a hash of the ciphertext and therefore cannot be stale, rather than on a header you were sent. That is what the client-side caches in this estate already do, and [why caching ciphertext is the easy case](https://sgit.ai/demos/fractal-graphs/performance.html#caching).

## Storage layout

```
bare/data/obj-cas-imm-{hex}     blobs, trees, commits — content-addressed, immutable
bare/keys/key-rnd-imm-{hex}     PKI public keys — immutable
bare/refs/                      branch refs — mutable
bare/indexes/                   branch index — mutable
bare/append/                    append lanes — managed, outside the commit DAG
```

The prefixes are load-bearing. `obj-cas-imm-` is SHA-256 over the *ciphertext*, which gives deduplication without the server knowing any plaintext, and makes the caching rule above derivable from the ID alone. Append lanes sit outside the commit DAG on purpose, a message arriving does not rewrite your history.

This site is itself served from a vault, so these are the objects behind the page you are reading. The [live-vault case study](https://sgit.ai/case-studies/live-vault-docs.html) shows the fetch sequence.

## See also

- [Append lanes](../api/append-lanes.md), the write-only channel that does not touch the commit tree
- [Errors and limits](../api/errors.md)

# A pack per push: git's packfiles, applied to an encrypted vault, with no server change, cli.sgit.ai

> For three days I have been talking with the CLI team about keeping a vault's objects in zip files, and this is where it landed. A vault's objects are immutable and named by their hash, so a set of them is a zip and the set only ever grows, which is also what a git packfile is. The cost of a vault over the network is the number of requests, not the number of bytes: from a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3. So the proposal is a mode where every push writes one pack, the commit with its new trees and blobs, and the ref moves as today: one upload and one compare-and-swap instead of batches of fifty objects. Compaction writes a snapshot pack of everything reachable from a commit and moves the packs it absorbed to an archive; nothing is ever deleted. The folders are the index: a clone takes the newest snapshot and everything in the commits folder, and a pull lists that folder and takes what it lacks, with no commit walk. Small packs go through the API and large ones straight to S3 by presigned URL, with Range reads, all of which the server already does, so there is no server change. The trial is CLI-only, in a vault of its own, gated by a feature flag and a minimum client, so every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name. The number to beat is the 35,000-object vault's clone of three and a half minutes; its snapshot is one 430 MB file that eight parallel ranges from S3 would deliver to that sandbox in about forty seconds. Nothing here is built yet.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-pack-per-push.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

![A pack per push, in one picture. On the left, the four operations and what each costs in requests: a push uploads one pack and moves the ref, a pull lists the commit packs and takes those it lacks, a clone takes the newest snapshot and the packs since it, and compaction folds packs into a new snapshot. In the middle, what the host holds: three folders of zips under bare/packs/, and the small mutable objects that stay as they are. *A pack per push, in one picture. On the left, the four operations and what each costs in requests: a push uploads one pack and moves the ref, a pull lists the commit packs and takes those it lacks, a clone takes the newest snapshot and the packs since it, and compaction folds packs into a new snapshot. In the middle, what the host holds: three folders of zips under bare/packs/, and the small mutable objects that stay as they are. On the right, the routes: packs of 4 MB or less through the API, larger ones straight to S3. Dashed boxes are proposed; the routes exist today.*


> **Update, 22 October 2026.** Pack mode is built and shipped in sgit-ai 0.24.0 as `sgit init --packs` and `sgit pack import`, with no server change, as this article proposed. The numbers are now measured: the comms vault's history clones in 25 seconds (this article estimated about 40), and a 2,087-object vault in 8.1 seconds against 28.6. They are set beside the expectations [below](#measured). To use it, read [the release notes](../docs/update-to-0-24-0.md) and [the playbook for agents](../docs/pack-mode-for-agents.md). The text below is as published.

## In short {#in-short}

- **A vault's objects are immutable and named by their hash, so a set of them is a zip and the
  set only ever grows.** That is also what a git packfile is.
- **The mode: every push writes one pack.** `bare/packs/commits/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip`,
  the commit with its new trees and blobs. The ref moves as today. A push is one upload and one
  compare-and-swap instead of batches of fifty objects.
- **Compaction is a snapshot pack**: every object reachable from a commit, in one zip, written to
  `snapshots/`; the commit packs it absorbed move to `archive/`. Nothing is ever deleted.
- **The folders are the index.** A clone fetches the newest snapshot and everything in
  `commits/`. A pull lists `commits/` and takes what it lacks. No commit walk, no listing of
  thirty-five thousand objects.
- **Small packs go through the API, large ones straight to S3** by presigned URL, with `Range`
  for partial reads; the server already does both, and listing, and delete. **No server change.**
- **CLI-only, gated, in its own vault.** A pack vault carries a feature flag and a minimum client
  in its branch index, so every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name. The web app
  and the static readers come later, once the numbers are in.
- **The numbers to beat:** the 35k-object vault clones in 3½ minutes through the API today; its
  snapshot is one 430 MB file that a local server delivered in 3 s and that eight parallel ranges
  from S3 would deliver from here in about 40 s.

## Where the cost is today {#cost-today}

Three days of measuring the same vault from the same sandbox gave one answer: the cost of a vault
over the network is the number of requests, not the number of bytes. A 28-byte object costs
0.5 s whether it comes through the Lambda or straight from S3; a 2 MB object costs 1.5 s; eight
objects in parallel reach 12 MB/s together. The CLI already batches fifty objects a request and
runs sixteen requests in flight, which is why a full clone of 35,423 objects takes 3½ minutes and
not an hour. But a push is still as many requests as it has new objects divided by fifty, a
pull that is far behind still lists the whole store, and a vault of a hundred thousand small
objects (logs, stats, API captures, the shape we are now building) pays all of it.

Git met the same wall twenty years ago and answered with the packfile: many objects in one file,
written once, never changed, with an index beside it. Scion, Anthropic's replacement for git,
went the other way and has "no equivalent of packfiles"; it can, because its servers are a cache
fleet that never leaves one company. A vault's server is a bucket. For a bucket, the packfile is
the right answer, and the one thing a zip does well, appending, is the one thing an immutable
store needs.

## The mode {#mode}

Nothing about a vault's content changes. Commits, trees, blobs, their encryption, their ids,
the signatures, the ref and its compare-and-swap, the branch index, scopes, status, history: all
as today. What changes is how objects travel and where the host keeps them.

```
bare/packs/
  commits/    <epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip   one per push: the commit, its new trees, its new blobs
  snapshots/  <epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip   every object reachable from <commit>
  archive/    <epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip   commit packs a snapshot has absorbed; kept
bare/refs/, bare/indexes/, bare/cache/         unchanged: small, mutable, compare-and-swap
```

Two things are in every name because they are free and useful: an epoch, so a plain listing comes
back in time order (the append lane's entries are named the same way), and the size, so a client
knows before it fetches whether to go through the API (under 4 MB) or straight to S3 (over it).

**Push.** Build the pack from the commit's new objects, as `publish --bundles` already builds a
per-commit delta zip: `ZIP_STORED` because ciphertext does not compress, sorted members, fixed
timestamps, so the same commit always gives the same bytes. Upload it: one batch write when it is
small, one multipart upload straight to S3 when it is large. Then move the ref, with the same
compare-and-swap as today. Two or three requests, whatever the commit's size.

```mermaid
%% A push in pack mode: one pack per pushed commit, sent by the route its size picks, then the same compare-and-swap on the ref as today.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client, sgit push
    participant A as SG/Send API
    participant S as S3
    C->>C: build one pack per commit, stored, sorted, deterministic
    alt pack of 4 MB or less
        C->>A: batch write packs/commits/epoch__commit__bytes.zip
    else pack over 4 MB
        C->>A: presigned initiate
        A-->>C: one URL per 10 MB part
        C->>S: PUT the parts
        C->>A: presigned complete
    end
    C->>A: compare-and-swap the ref, as today
    A-->>C: moved, or the branch moved on
    C->>C: record the pack in packs_absorbed.json
```

**Pull.** List `bare/packs/commits/`. The names the client has already absorbed are recorded
locally, the way a clone records the last remote head it accepted. Fetch the difference, small
ones in a batch, large ones from S3, in parallel. Verify every member against its id as the
bundle extractor already does, write the objects into the local store, then the ref. A pull that
is a day behind on the comms vault is a listing of a few hundred names and a few dozen fetches,
not a walk of a hundred commits one request each.

```mermaid
%% A pull in pack mode: one listing, the packs this clone has not absorbed, each verified member by member before anything is written.
flowchart TD
    A[sgit pull] --> B[list bare/packs/commits/]
    B --> C{{absorbed already?}}
    C -- yes, in packs_absorbed.json --> D[skip it]
    C -- no --> E{{size in the name}}
    E -- 4 MB or less --> F[batch read, up to 50 packs a request]
    E -- over 4 MB --> G[presigned read-url, parallel Range GETs]
    F --> H[check the size, then every member's id against its bytes]
    G --> H
    H -- a member fails --> I[refuse it, report it, leave the pack unabsorbed]
    H -- all pass --> J[write the objects to the loose store, record the pack]
    J --> K[then the ref and the merge, as today]
```

**Clone.** List `snapshots/`, take the newest, fetch it (one file, or several parallel ranges of
it). List `commits/`, fetch everything there: by construction that is exactly what the snapshot
does not hold. No walk, no listing of the object store. For the comms vault that is the 430 MB
snapshot and a few packs.

```mermaid
%% A clone in pack mode: the newest snapshot, then every commit pack since it, then a local walk that confirms nothing is missing.
flowchart TD
    A[sgit clone] --> B{{client knows packs?}}
    B -- no, says the branch index --> X[refuse by name: run sgit update]
    B -- yes --> C[list snapshots/ and take the newest by epoch]
    C --> D[fetch it: one GET, or parallel 10 MB Range reads]
    D --> E[list commits/ and fetch every pack there]
    E --> F[verify and extract every member]
    F --> G{{local walk complete?}}
    G -- no --> H[fetch what is missing by the ordinary route, a safety net]
    G -- yes --> I[record the packs, check out as today]
    H --> I
```

**Compaction.** Any writer with the write key can run it, when `commits/` holds more than some
number of packs or more than some fraction of the snapshot's size; the trial will find the
numbers. It writes the snapshot to `snapshots/`, reads it back from the host and checks every
expected id is in its directory (a `Range` read of the tail, no members downloaded), and only then
moves each absorbed pack to `archive/`: an upload there and a delete from `commits/`, in that
order, so a crash between the two leaves a pack in both places, which is harmless. Old snapshots
stay. The archive stays. Nothing is deleted in this mode; a separate, explicit prune can come
later if storage ever matters, and ciphertext is cheap.

```mermaid
%% Compaction: build and upload a snapshot, read its directory back before anything moves, then copy each absorbed pack to archive/ before deleting it from commits/. A crash between the last two steps leaves a pack in both places, which is harmless.
flowchart TD
    T{{time to compact?}} -- no --> Z[nothing to do]
    T -- over 50 packs, or a tenth of the snapshot --> A[build a snapshot of every object reachable from the remote head]
    A --> B[upload it to snapshots/]
    B --> C{{directory read back: all ids there?}}
    C -- no --> Y[abort, everything left as it was]
    C -- yes --> D[upload each absorbed pack to archive/]
    D --> E[then delete it from commits/]
    E --> F[old snapshots and the archive stay]
```

**Reading.** First version: packs are extracted into the loose store on arrival, so every read
path in the CLI is untouched. Second version, if it pays: keep the packs and read objects by
offset through a local index over them, which is git's `.idx`. The first version is enough to
measure everything in this article.

## Why a separate vault, and why it is gated {#gated}

A vault that holds only packs is unreadable to the web app and to every static reader, which
look up loose objects by id. Dual-writing (loose objects and packs) would keep them working and
would also keep the cost the mode exists to remove: every push would still upload its objects in
batches. So the trial is packs-only, in a vault of its own, and the vault says so: the branch
index already carries a format gate (`min_client`, `features`) that 0.19.0 built for 128-bit ids
and required signatures, and a pack vault sets `features: [packs]` and a minimum client. Every
older CLI, the web app and the static readers then refuse it by name ("this vault needs
sgit-ai >= X: run sgit update") instead of seeing an empty vault. Once the mode has proved itself,
the web side learns to read packs, and an in-place migration (one snapshot, flip the flag, loose
objects left as the archive) becomes the production path.

```mermaid
%% The gate: a pack vault says so in its branch index, and every reader that does not know packs refuses it by name instead of seeing an empty vault.
flowchart TD
    I[branch index: features packs, min_client] --> N{{reader}}
    N -- sgit with pack mode --> OK[reads the packs]
    N -- an older sgit --> R1[refused: this vault needs a newer sgit-ai, run sgit update]
    N -- the web app or a static reader --> R2[refused by name]
```

**Importing a vault** is a full clone, the re-encryption `vault move` already does (the read key is
derived from the passphrase and the vault id, so a new vault means new keys and new ids for every
object, walked blobs first, then trees, then commits, history intact), one snapshot pack, the ref,
and the index with the flag. The source vault is untouched. The two then live apart, which for a
trial is what you want.

```mermaid
%% Importing a vault: a full clone, re-encrypted under a new key the way vault move does it, written as one snapshot pack. The source is not touched.
flowchart TD
    S[(source vault)] -- full clone --> L[local clone]
    L -- re-encrypt: blobs, trees, commits --> N[new ids under the new key]
    N --> P[one snapshot pack]
    P --> V[(new pack vault: snapshot, ref, index with the flag)]
```

## What it should cost, and how we will know {#should-cost}

| | Today (API, loose objects) | Pack mode (expected) |
|---|---|---|
| push of one small change | 2 to 4 requests | 2 to 3 requests |
| push of 500 new objects | 10 batch requests + ref | 1 upload + ref |
| pull, 50 pushes behind | up to 50 commit requests, then batches | 1 listing + 50 small fetches in batches |
| cold clone, 35k objects | 21 s listing + 700 batch requests, 3½ min | 1 listing + 1 snapshot (430 MB) + a few packs; ~40 s from this sandbox at 12 MB/s, seconds on a good link |
| a vault of 100k objects of 300 bytes | 2,000 batch requests | one 30 MB snapshot |

![Requests, not bytes. Each row is one operation on a vault: the grey bar is today's request count through the batch route, the orange bar the expected count in pack mode, on the same scale. Pack mode wins on large pushes, far-behind pulls and cold clones. The red row is what the bars hide: a scoped clone of one folder is 3 MB today and would be the whole 430 MB snapshot in pack mode's first version. The pack-mode figures are arithmetic, not measurements.](../articles/images/pk-costs.webp)

*Requests, not bytes. Each row is one operation on a vault: the grey bar is today's request count through the batch route, the orange bar the expected count in pack mode, on the same scale. Pack mode wins on large pushes, far-behind pulls and cold clones. The red row is what the bars hide: a scoped clone of one folder is 3 MB today and would be the whole 430 MB snapshot in pack mode's first version. The pack-mode figures are arithmetic, not measurements.*


The tests, on the CLI side, against the dev server with direct S3: a cold clone of the imported
comms vault, pack mode against the batch route; a push loop of a hundred one-file commits, time
and requests per push; pulls after 10, 100 and 1,000 pushes without compaction, then after it,
to set the trigger; two writers pushing at once, which the ref's compare-and-swap already keeps
straight and the packs never collide on. The numbers go in the article that follows this one.

### Measured, 21 and 22 October {#measured}

The expectations above, against what the built code did on dev, from the same cloud sandbox:

| | Expected | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Cold clone of the comms vault's history (33,000 objects) | ~40 s, 1 listing + 1 snapshot + a few packs | **25 s**: 18 s for one 251 MB snapshot in 4 requests, the rest local (CLI team) |
| Cold clone, a published 2,087-object vault | | **8.1 s** in 4 requests, against 28.6 s as a normal vault on the same server |
| Push of one small change | 2 to 3 requests | **5.8 s**, one commit pack, against 10.5 s as a normal vault |
| Pull, several pushes behind | 1 listing + the packs in batches | 2 listings and one batch; **4.2 s** against 4.8 s, most of it local merge work |
| Snapshot size | 430 MB (uncompressed) | **251 MB**, because blobs are compressed before encryption (2.0× on that history) |
| Scoped clone of one folder | the whole snapshot (the cost the review flagged) | the whole snapshot, as expected; agents' one-folder vaults stay normal for now |

The design held. The cold clone came in under the estimate because compression shrank the snapshot. Pulls gained least, because their time was never the transfer. Before release a second agent reviewed the build in four rounds and found four ways compaction could leave a fresh clone without part of the history; all were fixed with a test each. [Four rounds to no blockers](../articles/pack-mode-four-rounds.md) tells that story.

## Side by side: the files and the steps in each mode {#side-by-side}

*This section is not in the CLI team's draft. It was added on cli.sgit.ai on 21 October 2026 at my request, by the site's build agent, from the CLI's code and the spec.*

![The comms vault in each mode. On the left, today: every object one file in data/, and the steps a push, a pull and a cold clone take. On the right, pack mode: the same objects in zips under packs/, and the same three operations. The keys, the refs, the branch index and the cache are the same files in both, in the same places. Colour marks the kind of each file: teal never changes, orange is shared and moves by compare-and-swap, violet has one writer.](../articles/images/pk-side-by-side.webp)

*The comms vault in each mode. On the left, today: every object one file in data/, and the steps a push, a pull and a cold clone take. On the right, pack mode: the same objects in zips under packs/, and the same three operations. The keys, the refs, the branch index and the cache are the same files in both, in the same places. Colour marks the kind of each file: teal never changes, orange is shared and moves by compare-and-swap, violet has one writer.*


The same layout as text, for a reader without the picture:

```text
today (loose)                              pack mode (proposed)
bare/                                      bare/
  data/obj-cas-imm-...   x 35,423            packs/commits/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip
                                             packs/snapshots/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip
                                             packs/archive/<epoch>__<commit>__<bytes>.zip
  keys/key-rnd-imm-...                       keys/key-rnd-imm-...        unchanged
  refs/ref-pid-muw-...  ref-pid-snw-...      refs/                       unchanged
  indexes/idx-pid-muw-...                    indexes/  + features: [packs]
  cache/  value, pointer                     cache/                      unchanged
```

### Why the two can mix: three kinds of object {#three-kinds}

The reason pack mode is a change of shipping and not a change of format is in the names. Every object a vault stores says in its name what kind it is, and the CLI's code treats the three kinds differently:

| Kind | In the name | Written how | Examples | Pack mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Immutable** | `imm` | once, named by its hash (or at random, for a key); a copy anywhere is as good as the original | `obj-cas-imm-…` blobs, trees, commits; `key-rnd-imm-…` public keys | the objects move into zips; still immutable, still checked against their ids |
| **Mutable, many writers** | `muw` | overwritten only by compare-and-swap: a write names the version it replaces, and loses if another got there first | the named branch's ref, the branch index | unchanged |
| **Mutable, one writer** | `snw` | overwritten by its one owner, no race to lose | a clone branch's ref, the cache | unchanged |

So a vault mixes mutable and immutable files today, and that is why the architecture holds together: almost everything is immutable and can be copied, cached, zipped or archived in any shape, because its name is its content; a handful of small files say where the history is, and only they need a host that can compare-and-swap. Pack mode changes the shape of the first group and leaves the second alone. The same split is what lets a whole vault [travel as one file](../articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.md).

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- Nothing is built; the per-commit and head zips exist in `publish --bundles`, the routes exist,
  the rest is the spec.
- The expected costs above are arithmetic from measured request floors and throughputs, from one
  cloud sandbox.
- The web app and static readers cannot read a pack vault; that is by design for the trial.
- A pack vault still has one writer at a time on the ref, as every vault does; packs themselves
  never conflict, because their names are commit ids.

If you keep a vault with tens of thousands of small objects and would like to be in the trial, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

# A second factor without a server: why an authenticator app's code cannot protect a vault, why a passkey or a security key can, and what the second factor is for an agent, cli.sgit.ai

> With sgit keeping keys sealed and opening them only in memory, the next question I asked was about two-factor authentication. I have Google Authenticator on my phone, LastPass, passkeys, a YubiKey. Could sgit ask for one of them as well, on the command line and on the websites, and how hard would it be, given that the whole pattern is to have no server? Working it through changed the question. Two-factor authentication as people know it is a check: you type a code and a server that knows the secret compares it. Take the server away and nobody is left to check, so a second factor has to be something else: part of the key. The decryption must need bytes that only the second factor can produce. An authenticator app cannot do that. Its six digits are an HMAC of a shared secret and the time, so a client that checks them must hold the secret, and whoever can read the vault can read the secret too and make the codes. Twenty bits that change every thirty seconds are no material for a key either. A passkey can. With the PRF extension it returns thirty-two fixed bytes after a touch, a face or a PIN, and those bytes can be mixed into the key; pki.sgit.ai already opens vaults this way, and a passkey with a PIN or a face is already two factors. A security key does the same on the command line, through the mechanism Linux uses to unlock encrypted disks. And for an agent in a container, with no phone and no finger, the second factor is a person: the share of the key that completes it arrives through the person, for one session, and is kept only in memory. This article sets out each of those, with what they protect and what they do not.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-second-factor-without-a-server.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-24 · published

**Summary:** With sgit keeping keys sealed and opening them only in memory, the next question I asked was about two-factor authentication. I have Google Authenticator on my phone, LastPass, passkeys, a YubiKey. Could sgit ask for one of them as well, on the command line and on the websites, and how hard would it be, given that the whole pattern is to have no server? Working it through changed the question. Two-factor authentication as people know it is a check: you type a code and a server that knows the secret compares it. Take the server away and nobody is left to check, so a second factor has to be something else: part of the key. The decryption must need bytes that only the second factor can produce. An authenticator app cannot do that. Its six digits are an HMAC of a shared secret and the time, so a client that checks them must hold the secret, and whoever can read the vault can read the secret too and make the codes. Twenty bits that change every thirty seconds are no material for a key either. A passkey can. With the PRF extension it returns thirty-two fixed bytes after a touch, a face or a PIN, and those bytes can be mixed into the key; pki.sgit.ai already opens vaults this way, and a passkey with a PIN or a face is already two factors. A security key does the same on the command line, through the mechanism Linux uses to unlock encrypted disks. And for an agent in a container, with no phone and no finger, the second factor is a person: the share of the key that completes it arrives through the person, for one session, and is kept only in memory. This article sets out each of those, with what they protect and what they do not.

![Without a server, a second factor has to be part of the key, not a code someone checks. Four candidates. An authenticator app's code (TOTP, as in Google Authenticator, Authy or LastPass): a code, not a key, because checking it needs the shared secret, and about twenty bits that change every thirty seconds cannot be part of a key. A passkey with the PRF extension: a key, in the browser, already used by pki.sgit.ai, supported by iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager, reported for Windows Hello since early 2026 and mixed in third-party password managers.
