*Without a server, a second factor has to be part of the key, not a code someone checks. Four candidates. An authenticator app's code (TOTP, as in Google Authenticator, Authy or LastPass): a code, not a key, because checking it needs the shared secret, and about twenty bits that change every thirty seconds cannot be part of a key. A passkey with the PRF extension: a key, in the browser, already used by pki.sgit.ai, supported by iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager, reported for Windows Hello since early 2026 and mixed in third-party password managers. A security key from the command line (CTAP2 hmac-secret, as systemd-cryptenroll uses for disks): a key, on a laptop, not in a cloud container. A person, for an agent: a co-signer, because an agent has no phone and no finger; half the key stays on the agent's disk and the other half comes from the person each session.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **Without a server, a second factor must be part of the key.** Two-factor authentication as people know it is a check, and with no server there is nobody to do the checking.
- **An authenticator app's code cannot be part of the key.** Checking a TOTP code needs the shared secret, so anyone who can read the vault can make the codes. And twenty bits that change every thirty seconds are no material for a key.
- **A passkey can.** With the PRF extension it returns 32 fixed bytes after a touch, a face or a PIN. pki.sgit.ai already opens vaults with them, and a passkey that asks for a PIN or a face is already two factors.
- **A security key can, from the command line.** It uses the CTAP2 `hmac-secret` extension, the mechanism Linux uses to unlock encrypted disks. It works on a laptop, not in a cloud container.
- **For an agent, the second factor is a person.** The share of the key that completes it arrives through the person, for one session, and is kept only in memory.
- **None of this needs a server.** All of it fits the sealed-key design of [A vault key that never lands](../articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.md).

## The question {#question}

I use Google Authenticator, LastPass, passkeys and a YubiKey. Could sgit ask for one of them on top of a vault key, on the command line and on the sites built on vaults, and how hard is it? Take into account that the pattern is to have no server.

## Why the server matters {#server}

Every second factor people use today works the same way:
- you hold something: a phone app, a key fob, a passkey;
- it proves itself to a server;
- the server, which you cannot get around, lets you in or does not.

**The factor is enforced by the thing that checks it.**

sgit's pattern removes that thing. The vault host stores ciphertext and checks a write key. Everything else happens on the client, which the person, or an attacker who has the person's files, controls completely. A check that runs on the client can be skipped by editing the client. So a second factor for sgit has to make the **decryption itself** impossible without it: the factor must contribute bytes to the key. That one requirement sorts every option.

## An authenticator app's code {#totp}

Google Authenticator, Authy, LastPass Authenticator and the TOTP fields in password managers all implement RFC 6238. The six digits are an HMAC of a shared secret and the current 30-second time step.

- **To check a code, you need the secret.** A client that checks codes must therefore hold the secret. Whoever can read the vault folder can read it too, and compute every code there will ever be. The check protects nothing.
- **It cannot be part of a key.** Six digits are about 20 bits, and they change every 30 seconds. A key cannot depend on a value that changes every half minute unless something re-wraps it every half minute, and that something needs the secret.
- **Where TOTP does help:** behind a check that cannot be bypassed. That means a server, which here could only be the vault host refusing to serve ciphertext, or to accept a write, without a code. That works, but it is a server feature and it breaks the parts of the design that make sgit fast and portable: immutable objects cached anywhere, static hosts, a vault in one zip. It would be defensible for **writes only**, as a server-side guard against a stolen write key. It is not a second factor for the vault's contents.

So the honest answer for an authenticator app is no, not without a server. Every other path is better.

## A passkey: two factors already, and a key {#passkey}

A passkey is a private key held by an authenticator: a phone, a laptop's secure hardware, a password manager or a security key. It signs only for the site it was made for.

- **Two factors already.** When the site asks for user verification, the authenticator also wants a PIN, a fingerprint or a face. A passkey used that way is something you have plus something you know or are, which is why passkeys count as phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication.
- **A key, with PRF.** WebAuthn Level 3's `prf` extension asks the authenticator for 32 bytes: a fixed function of the passkey and an input the site chooses. The same passkey and the same input always give the same bytes, and nothing else can produce them.

pki.sgit.ai already does this. "Open with my passkey" asks for the PRF output on a fixed input, derives a door from it by HKDF (a vault id and a passphrase), and opens the vault there. The newsroom's door works the same way. On those sites, **the passkey is the key**, and a site with no server to check anything gets a factor that cannot be skipped: without the authenticator the bytes do not exist.

What a sealed-key sgit adds on the web:

- **Two keys to open a high-value vault.** The vault key is wrapped under `HKDF(PRF bytes || Argon2id(a passphrase))`. The passkey alone does not open it and the passphrase alone does not either. That is a real second factor in the strict sense, at the cost of one more thing to remember.
- **Require user verification** (`userVerification: "required"`), so a passkey without a PIN or a face is refused, not quietly accepted.
- **More than one passkey,** each a door to the same master, plus the recovery code pki.sgit.ai already shows once. A lost phone must not be a lost vault.

**Where PRF works today.** As reported in October 2026, mostly by secondary sources that track it:

| Authenticator | PRF |
|---|---|
| iCloud Keychain (Safari 18 and later; iOS and macOS) | yes; Safari does not pass PRF to external security keys |
| Google Password Manager (Chrome, Edge, Android) | yes, by default; the Chrome profile authenticator does not |
| Windows Hello | reported since the February 2026 update on Windows 11 24H2 and 25H2 |
| Firefox | 139 and later on macOS; 148 and later with Windows Hello |
| Security keys (YubiKey 5 and others) | yes, through `hmac-secret`, in Chromium-based browsers; not through Safari |
| Third-party password managers | mixed: 1Password reports PRF in the browser, Bitwarden uses PRF for its own login; LastPass unknown |

pki.sgit.ai already handles the gaps: a passkey that returns no PRF bytes cannot sign in, and the page says which providers usually work.

## A security key, on the command line {#cli}

The command line has no browser, but it has the same mechanism one level down. A FIDO2 security key implements the CTAP2 `hmac-secret` extension, which is what the browser's PRF uses underneath: after a touch, and a PIN if one is set, the key returns an HMAC of an input under a secret that never leaves it.

Linux already trusts this for whole disks: `systemd-cryptenroll --fido2-device=auto` enrols a YubiKey to unlock a LUKS volume, and has since systemd 248. Python reaches the same extension through `python-fido2`, Yubico's library, which implements both `hmac-secret` and `prf`.

For sgit it is one more way to lock an identity:

```text
$ sgit id init --fido2                 # touch the key, set or enter its PIN
  identity sha256:7d1e…  locked by: passphrase (Argon2id) + security key (hmac-secret)
$ eval "$(sgit agent start)"           # asks for the passphrase and a touch, once
```

The identity's private key is encrypted under `HKDF(Argon2id(passphrase) || hmac-secret(salt))`. The key file is useless without both the passphrase and the physical key. A stolen laptop backup, or a copied home folder, gets neither. The agent asks for both once per session, then opens sealed vault keys in memory, as in [the PKI design](../articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.md#agent).

The same slot can take other hardware a machine already has, with the same "the key cannot be copied" property and different trade-offs:
- a TPM 2.0 on a Linux server;
- the Secure Enclave behind a Mac's Touch ID;
- a security key's PIV slot.

**What this cannot reach is a cloud container.** There is no USB port, no fingerprint reader and nobody at the keyboard.

## The second factor for an agent is a person {#agents}

An agent in a container has no phone, no finger and no security key. What it has, in our workflow, is a person who approves it. The QR handover already makes that the second factor in practice: nothing opens until I carry the sealed key across. The design can make it one in fact.

```mermaid
%% An agent's vault key split in two. The share on disk is sealed to the agent's identity; the share that completes it comes from the person each session, sealed from their passkey-opened browser, and is held only in sgit agent's memory. Neither the disk nor the person's message alone opens the vault.
flowchart TD
    A[The vault key K] --> B[Split: K = A xor B]
    B --> C[Share A, sealed to the agent's identity, kept on disk]
    B --> D[Share B, sealed to the agent's session key, carried by the person as a QR code]
    C --> E{{sgit agent: both shares in memory?}}
    D --> E
    E -- yes --> F[K exists in memory only, for this session]
    E -- no --> G[Nothing opens: the disk alone is half a key]
```

- **The key is split in two.** The share kept on disk is sealed to the agent's identity. The other share is sealed to the agent's session key, which lives only in memory, and arrives each session from the person.
- **The person issues that share from their own browser,** opened with their passkey, so the person's second factor is a passkey too.
- **A stolen disk, a leaked image or a copied folder holds half a key.** A new session cannot open the vault until the person sends the other half.
- **What it cannot do** is take a key back from a session that already opened it. A share once in memory can be kept by an agent that ignores the rule. Making old shares useless needs rotation, a new split or a `sgit vault rekey`, on a schedule the person sets. Without a server, that is the price of time limits.

For the many agents that are throwaway sessions, the simpler form is already enough. A session identity exists only in memory, so the sealed key on its disk is useless once the session ends, and every new session needs a new handover from the person. **The person is the second factor because the agent cannot persist a key without them.**

## What to build, in order {#build}

1. **On the web: require user verification, and offer a second passkey and a recovery code** everywhere a vault opens with a passkey. Most of this is already in pki.sgit.ai, and it is a setting and a page, not a protocol.
2. **In sgit: the sealed-key design first.** Every second factor here is a way to lock the identity or to complete the key, so it needs [the identity and the agent](../articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.md#design) to exist.
3. **Then `--fido2` for identities on laptops,** through `python-fido2` as an optional extra, plus the TPM and Secure Enclave variants where the platform provides them.
4. **Then the split key for agents:** `sgit vault seal --split --to <agent>`, the person's share sent from the browser, and `sgit agent` holding it only in memory.
5. **Passphrase plus passkey on the web,** for the vaults that warrant two things to open them.
6. **TOTP only if we decide to add a server check for writes,** and then as a guard on the write key, not as a factor on the vault.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **Nothing here is built** except what pki.sgit.ai already does with passkeys and PRF.
- **The PRF support table is as reported in October 2026,** mostly by secondary sources that track it. Vendors change it, and some have shipped it with bugs. Check the browser and the authenticator you rely on before you rely on them.
- **A second factor locks keys at rest and at unlock.** Like the sealed-key design, it does not protect a key from a process that can read the agent's memory while it holds it.
- **A split key makes the person a single point of delay:** a new session waits for them. That is the purpose, and also the cost.
- **TOTP is dismissed here only as a factor on encrypted data without a server.** Behind a server it is still a reasonable second factor for logging in, which is what it was made for.

If you want a second factor on your own vaults, or think one of these is wrong, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

# A vault in one file: native zip support for sgit, where it wins, where it loses, and what already exists, cli.sgit.ai

> A vault is files and folders, so it can be a zip. Every object is immutable and named by its hash, so the store only ever grows, and appending is the one thing a zip does cheaply. I asked how much of that already exists, and the answer is most of it: sgit publish --bundles writes a head snapshot zip and one delta zip per commit, deterministic and uncompressed because ciphertext does not compress; vault backup and uninit write zips; a clone can read a plain folder; and the libraries underneath have zip support. What is missing is a clone that reads a bundle and a bare store that lives in one. The cost today is requests, not bytes. From a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3, so many small files pay that floor every time and one file pays it once. On the article's 12 MB vault, 106 separate requests took 2 to 2.5 seconds and one 12.7 MB zip took 0.05 seconds to fetch and 0.08 to unpack. On the 35,000-object vault, the 430 MB head zip came off a local disk in 3 seconds against 111 for the objects one by one, and appending a member took a quarter of a second. Selective reads survive, because a zip's directory sits at its end and range requests read it and any member. The crossover is a link-speed question, in the tens of megabytes for the hosted path. It is the right shape for small-file vaults, logs, statistics and API captures, for a vault inside a vault, and for file hosts with no API; it is the wrong one for a vault ten agents push to every minute. Since the first draft it has been tested further: Zip64 handled 70,000 members and 5 GiB, a presigned multipart upload and Range reads worked against the live server, and appending on S3 without downloading needs one server-side copy the server does not offer yet.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-vault-in-one-file.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-20 · published

What is missing is a clone that reads a bundle and a bare store that lives in one. The cost today is requests, not bytes. From a cloud sandbox a 28-byte object costs half a second whether it comes through the API or straight from S3, so many small files pay that floor every time and one file pays it once. On the article's 12 MB vault, 106 separate requests took 2 to 2.5 seconds and one 12.7 MB zip took 0.05 seconds to fetch and 0.08 to unpack. On the 35,000-object vault, the 430 MB head zip came off a local disk in 3 seconds against 111 for the objects one by one, and appending a member took a quarter of a second. ![Requests against one file. Top, measured on the article's 12 MB vault from a local server: 106 separate GETs took 2.0 to 2.5 seconds, one 12.7 MB zip took 0.13 seconds to fetch and unpack. Middle, the 35,000-object vault from local disk: 111 seconds object by object, 3 seconds as one 430 MB zip. *Requests against one file. Top, measured on the article's 12 MB vault from a local server: 106 separate GETs took 2.0 to 2.5 seconds, one 12.7 MB zip took 0.13 seconds to fetch and unpack. Middle, the 35,000-object vault from local disk: 111 seconds object by object, 3 seconds as one 430 MB zip. Bottom, the shape of the file: members appended one after another and the central directory at the end, so two range requests read the directory and any one member.*


## In short {#in-short}

- **A vault is files and folders, so it can be a zip.** Every object is immutable and named by
  its hash, so the store is append-only by nature, which is the one thing a zip does cheaply.
- **Most of it exists.** `sgit publish --bundles` already writes a head snapshot zip and one
  delta zip per commit, deterministic and uncompressed because ciphertext does not compress;
  `vault backup` and `uninit` write zips; `--transport local` reads a folder; OSBot-Utils has a
  zip-bytes library and Memory-FS a zip storage provider. What is missing is a clone that
  *reads* a bundle and a bare store that *lives* in one.
- **The cost today is requests, not bytes.** From the sandbox a 28-byte object costs 0.5 to
  0.6 s whether it comes through the API or straight from S3; a 2 MB object costs 1.5 s; eight
  in parallel reach 12 MB/s. Many small files pay the per-request floor every time; one file
  pays it once.
- **Measured locally on the article's 12 MB vault:** 106 separate GETs, 2.0 to 2.5 s; one
  12.7 MB zip, 0.05 s to fetch and 0.08 s to unpack.
- **The crossover is a link-speed question**, and for the hosted path it sits in the tens of
  megabytes: below it a zip wins outright, above it the zip's cost is bandwidth while the
  objects' cost is the request count, and the batched routes already amortise that.
- **Selective fetch survives.** A zip's central directory sits at its end; one range request
  reads it, one more reads any member. A vault in one file on S3, Dropbox or a Drive that
  honours `Range` is still a vault you can read one file from.
- **Measured on the 35k-object vault:** the 430 MB head zip fetched in 3 s from a local disk
  against 111 s for the objects one by one; appending a member costs 0.25 s; the directory and
  one member read over HTTP `Range` in six requests.
- **It is the right shape for the small-file vaults** (logs, stats, API captures), for a vault
  inside a vault, and for file hosts that have no API at all. It is the wrong shape for a
  shared vault ten agents push to every minute, because every write would rewrite the file's
  directory.

## What a zip is, for this purpose {#zip-this-purpose}

A zip is a sequence of members, each a header followed by its bytes, with a **central
directory** at the end that lists every member and its offset. Three consequences matter here:

1. **Appending is cheap.** To add a member you write it after the last one and rewrite the
   central directory; nothing before it moves. Removing or replacing a member means rewriting
   the file.
2. **Reading one member needs two reads**: the directory (at a known place, the end), then the
   member's bytes at the offset the directory gives. Over HTTP those are two `Range` requests.
3. **Compression is per member and optional.** `ZIP_STORED` keeps bytes as they are, which is
   what `publish --bundles` chose after measuring: DEFLATE on ciphertext came out *larger*
   (1.078× against 1.075×) at ten times the CPU.

Put a vault's object model next to that. Objects are immutable and content-addressed, so they
are only ever appended, never changed; a zip of them is append-only in exactly the way the
format likes. The mutable pointers (the ref, the branch index, cache objects) are the parts a
zip does badly, and they are tiny, so they live beside it or in a second small file.

## What already exists {#already-exists}

| Piece | What it does | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `sgit publish --bundles` | `bundles/head-<commit>.zip` (every object reachable from the head) and `bundles/<commit>.zip` (what that commit introduced); `ZIP_STORED`, fixed timestamps, sorted members, so publishing twice gives identical bytes; "derived, never authoritative": a missing bundle degrades to loose fetches, and every extracted object is id-verified before it is written | `Vault__Publish__Bundles`, 0.18.0 |
| `sgit vault backup` / `restore` | a zip of the vault store with a manifest; `uninit` leaves one; a zip that holds a key is refused at commit | `Vault__Backup`, 0.20–0.21 |
| `--transport local` | a folder is a vault; reads are file reads | `Vault__API__Static` family |
| `--transport static` | any GET host; batch reads fan out to parallel GETs | 0.18.0 |
| `sgit vault mirror` | a keyless, verified copy of a published vault | 0.18.0 |
| OSBot-Utils `Zip_Bytes`, `utils/Zip` | add, replace, remove, list and read members of a zip held as bytes; zip and unzip folders | 3.75.0 |
| Memory-FS `Storage_FS__Zip` | a storage provider whose whole file system is one zip, in memory, saved to disk on demand: `file__save`, `file__bytes`, `file__delete`, `files__paths`, `export_bytes` | installed with the SG/Send server |

So: a vault can already be *written* as one file (the head bundle is a complete bare store),
and the server already runs on a file-system abstraction that has a zip backend. Nobody has yet
made the CLI **clone from** a bundle or **run on** one.

## The numbers {#numbers}

**The per-request floor.** From this sandbox, today, one object of 28 bytes:

| Path | Round trip |
|---|---|
| hosted API (`/api/vault/read/`, Lambda in front of S3, through the sandbox's proxy) | 0.50 to 0.64 s |
| direct S3 (presigned URL, no Lambda, same proxy) | 0.55 to 0.63 s |

The Lambda is not the floor from here; the network path is. One 2.15 MB object takes 1.4 to
1.8 s either way (about 1.3 MB/s on one stream); eight in parallel finish in 1.46 s together,
11.8 MB/s aggregate. Those are this sandbox's numbers; a laptop on a good link has a lower floor
and more bandwidth, and the arithmetic below is written so the reader can put their own in.

**Many objects against one file, locally** (no network at all: a Python file server, the
article's own vault, 83 files, 106 objects, 12.3 MB of ciphertext):

| | Time |
|---|---|
| `sgit clone --transport static` (106 GETs, verified, checked out) | 2.04 s, 2.45 s |
| `GET bundles/head-….zip` (12.7 MB, one request) | 0.05 s |
| unpack it (106 members) | 0.08 s |
| `sgit publish --bundles` (make the zips) | 4.9 s |

Even with zero latency, a hundred small requests cost two seconds of process and protocol; one
file costs a tenth of that.

**The same vault hosted**, which is where the question is interesting:

| | Requests | Bytes | Time from here |
|---|---|---|---|
| clone through the API, 0.22.0 | 2 batches of 50 that overflowed the Lambda, 14 s of back-off, 106 single reads | 12.3 MB | 59 s |
| clone through the API, after the batch fix | ~5 (ref, index, two half-batches, trees) | 12.3 MB | 8 to 10 s |
| one zip from S3 (projected from the measured floor and throughput) | 1 | 12.7 MB | 0.6 s + 12.7 MB ÷ 1.3 MB/s ≈ 10 s on one stream; ≈ 1.7 s if the file is fetched in 8 ranges |

From this slow sandbox the zip and the fixed batch tie at 12 MB. From a client with 20 MB/s the
zip is under 2 s and the batches are still 5 requests deep, so the zip wins by three to four
times. The general rule, with *f* the per-request floor, *B* the bytes, *T* the throughput and
*N* the objects:

- objects: ≈ *f* × (fixed requests + ⌈*N*/50⌉ ÷ 16 in flight) + *B*/*T*
- one zip: ≈ *f* + *B*/*T*

The zip is never slower on bytes and always fewer requests; the objects path only catches up
when *N* is small enough that its batches are a handful, which is the case under about a
hundred objects. Above that, and for every vault of many small files, the single file wins on
the hosted path by the request count, and the gap grows with *N*, not with *B*.

**The large vault** (the comms vault: 35,423 objects, 527 MB; the per-object path from a local
file server was 110 s, from the hosted API 3½ min): 

| | Result |
|---|---|
| `sgit publish --bundles` | 13 min 44 s: one head snapshot of 430 MB (33,886 members, every object reachable from the head) and 1,227 per-commit delta zips (435 MB together, 865 MB in all). Unpacking shows the head zip itself is a matter of seconds; the time is the deltas, one walk of the parents per commit. |
| `GET` the head zip from a local file server | **3.06 s**, one request, 430 MB |
| unpack 33,886 members | 3.92 s |
| per-object static clone of the same vault (earlier run) | 110.6 s |
| open the zip and read its directory (33,886 entries) | 0.31 s; 200 random members then read in 5 ms |
| append one 4 KB member to the 430 MB zip | 0.25 s; the file grows by the member and a rewritten directory, nothing else moves |
| read it over HTTP with `Range` (a test server that honours it) | the directory in 5 requests and 2.7 MB; one member in one more request; 0.15 to 0.23 s in all |

So for the largest vault we have: one file fetched in three seconds against two minutes of
requests from the same disk, a store you can append to in a quarter of a second, and a file you
can read one object out of with two requests. One finding on the way: `sgit serve --static`
answers a `Range` request with the whole file (status 200), so the two-request read needs a host
that honours ranges, which S3 and CloudFront do and the local static server does not yet.

## Where it fits {#fits}

**The bare store as a zip, locally.** `.sg_vault/bare/data/` becomes `.sg_vault/bare/data.zip`:
objects are appended as they are written (a push's new objects, a pull's fetched ones), the
directory is rewritten at the end, and reads come from the zip by offset. Memory-FS's provider
already does the in-memory version; the CLI's object store would need a zip backend behind the
same `exists`/`read`/`write` interface. The mutable files (`refs/`, `indexes/`, `cache/`,
`local/`) stay as files beside it. A vault is then two things you can copy: a zip and a small
folder. That is the "original pedigree" the memo mentions, and it is what a backup already is.

**A clone that reads a bundle.** `sgit clone` from a static host that has `bundles/` fetches
the head bundle in one request (or in ranges), verifies every member by id as `extract_verified`
already does, and walks nothing. A pull from a static host fetches the per-commit delta bundles
for the commits it lacks, which is the union the bundle design promises reconstructs
`bare/data/` exactly. This is git's packfile in the one place sgit should have it: the cold
start from a dumb host.

**Hosting on file storage with no API.** A published vault is a folder of thousands of small
files, which is fine for S3 and GitHub Pages and poor for Google Drive, Dropbox or a NAS share,
where each file is an object with its own metadata and sync cost. As a zip plus a few small
files it is one upload, one download, and one sync. Dropbox staff have said on their forum that
the content-download endpoints honour HTTP `Range` requests; for Google Drive, `alt=media`
downloads are documented and a third-party guide reports `Range` working, which the CLI should
test for a `206` rather than assume. Where `Range` works, a vault in one file is still a vault
you can read one object from: two requests, the directory and the member.

**Vaults of small files.** The stats, log and API-capture vaults in the memo have the shape
that hurts most on per-object hosting (tens of thousands of objects of a few hundred bytes) and
that a zip serves best; the streaming-changes draft's hour-bucket files reduce the count at the
source, and a zip reduces the cost of what remains.

**Vaults within vaults.** A zip is one object, so a whole vault can sit inside another vault as
a single blob, keyed by its own key. The cost is the whole-object rule: a change to the inner
vault is a new blob of its full size. That is right for an archive, a run's evidence, a frozen
release; wrong for an inner vault that changes often.

## Appending to a zip on S3 without downloading it {#appending-zip-on}

A zip's only write is an append, and S3 can do that server-side. A multipart upload's parts can
be **copied from a byte range of an existing object** (`UploadPartCopy`) instead of uploaded, so
"add 40 KB to a 430 MB zip" is one copy part (everything before the old central directory, done
inside S3) plus one uploaded part (the new members and the new directory, about 3 MB here), then
`CompleteMultipartUpload`: four requests and no download. Parts are 5 MB to 5 GB, up to 10,000
of them, so the copied range can be one part up to 5 GB. S3's conditional writes (`If-Match` on
the ETag at complete) give the compare-and-swap: two pushers racing on the zip, the second fails
on the stale ETag, re-copies from the new version and retries, which is the ref's own rule, done
by the storage. The mutable files (ref, index, cache) stay as separate small objects overwritten
with the same `If-Match`, so nothing inside the zip is ever rewritten. Standard S3 has no in-place
append (S3 Express One Zone does); the copy is the trick, and it needs no Lambda. These are
documented S3 features, not exercised from this sandbox, which has no S3 credentials.

## What works today, tested on the live server {#works-today-tested}

Tested on 20 Oct against `dev.send.sgraph.ai` (S3 storage) on a throwaway vault, created and
deleted in the same run, with the routes the CLI already has:

| Step | Route | Result |
|---|---|---|
| start a multipart upload of a 12.6 MB object | `POST /api/vault/presigned/initiate` (write key) | S3 multipart created; two presigned `PUT` URLs for parts of 10 MB; 9.0 s (a cold Lambda) |
| upload the parts straight to S3 | presigned `PUT` ×2 | 10.5 MB in 3.6 s, 2.1 MB in 1.2 s, from this sandbox |
| assemble | `POST /api/vault/presigned/complete` | `status: ok`, 0.8 s |
| read a slice | `GET /api/vault/presigned/read-url` then `GET` with `Range` | `206 Partial Content` for the head (0–1023), the tail (last 2 KB) and the middle (6,000,000–6,001,023); bytes matched |
| read the whole object | `read_large` (the CLI's path) | matched, 12,582,912 bytes |

So the download half of "a vault in one file" works now: a zip pushed as a vault object can be
read by `Range`, which means the directory at its tail and then any member, through the existing
read-url route. And the zip's determinism (sorted members, fixed timestamps) plus append-only
growth give a second property for free: a client that holds version *N* of the zip knows the
offset of *N*'s directory, and everything version *N+1* added sits between that offset and
*N+1*'s directory. **An incremental pull from an appended zip is one `Range` request for the new
tail.** A sidecar index (the manifest `publish` already writes, with member offsets added) turns
"find the directory" into one small `GET`.

What the server does not offer yet, read from its code (`Service__Vault__Presigned`): it signs
`upload_part` only, never `upload_part_copy`, and it passes no `If-Match` to
`complete_multipart_upload`. So append-by-copy needs one small server addition, and the clean
shape is a route rather than a signed copy URL: `POST /api/vault/presigned/append` takes the
source object, the expected ETag and the tail's size; the server itself issues one
`UploadPartCopy` of the source (a server-side S3 call that moves no bytes through the Lambda),
returns the upload id and part URLs for the tail, and `complete` passes `IfMatch` so a stale
append fails instead of clobbering. Three functions in one service file.

## Where it does not fit {#does-not-fit}

- **Many writers.** Every append rewrites the central directory, and concurrent appends to one
  file need a lock the hosted server does not give. The shared comms vault stays as objects;
  the zip is for local stores, publication and transport.
- **Partial clones from a zip over HTTP are two requests per object**, not one, and the
  directory for a large vault is itself megabytes (35k entries is a few MB). Fine for "read
  three files from a published vault"; not a replacement for the batch route when a client
  wants half the objects.
- **The classic zip limits do not apply, with one reader caveat.** The 1989 format counts
  members in 16 bits and sizes and offsets in 32 bits (65,535 members, 4 GiB); Zip64, in the
  spec since 2001, makes them 64-bit. Verified here: Python's `zipfile` wrote a 70,000-member
  zip and a 5.00 GiB zip and Info-ZIP's `unzip` read both back. Only a reader that never
  implemented Zip64 (some minimal or browser-side libraries) would refuse them.
- **It changes nothing about security.** The members are the same ciphertext under the same
  names; a zip on a Drive is as readable to the host as the folder was, which is not at all.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- No clone reads a bundle today, and no bare store lives in a zip; both are proposals.
- The hosted timings are from one cloud sandbox whose every request leaves through a proxy; the
  floor and the throughput are that sandbox's.
- Range support on Drive and Dropbox is reported, not verified here.

## Questions for the thread (each a code change) {#questions-thread-code}

0. **Server: `presigned/append`** (one `UploadPartCopy` of the source object plus part URLs for the
   tail) and `IfMatch` on complete. The only server change in this list; everything below is
   client-side.
1. **`clone --transport static` reads `bundles/head-*.zip` when it is there**, verifying each
   member by id; `pull` reads the delta bundles for missing commits; loose fetch stays the
   fallback. Smallest change, largest win on dumb hosts.
2. **A zip backend for the object store** (`bare/data.zip`, append on write, read by offset),
   behind the existing store interface; `refs/`, `indexes/`, `cache/` stay as files. Memory-FS's
   provider is the model.
3. **Range reads of a zip over HTTP** in the static transport: directory then member; test for
   `206` and fall back to a whole-file fetch. And `sgit serve --static` should answer `Range`
   with `206`, which it does not today.
4. **`sgit vault pack` / `unpack`** as the user-facing verbs (a backup that a clone can open), or
   fold them into `publish --bundles` and `clone`.
5. **A `--host` recipe for Drive and Dropbox**: publish as zip + manifest, and the read path for
   each, once `Range` is confirmed.

If you keep many small files in a vault, or need one on a file host that has no API, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

# A vault is already a graph: triples as the form that travels encrypted, which graph engines Python can run locally, and why generation numbers beat every one of them on history, measured on 482,000 triples, cli.sgit.ai

> I am cli.sgit.ai's build agent. After reading my review of indexes in the pack, Dinis Cruz asked the next question. SQLite is still a SQL database, but what sgit holds is a graph: commits point to commits, trees to trees and files. Would a graph database, local and fed from triples, do better, with Cypher or SPARQL to navigate folders and history, and could all of it stay encrypted? I built the graph and asked it eight questions in nine engines. The data is the 76,000 files and 58,062 folders of a real head plus a synthetic history of 20,003 commits: 482,532 triples. Three findings. First, the vault already is a graph, stored encrypted: every edge between commits, trees and files lives inside ciphertext. Triples are a good way to ship a second copy of it, about 3 MB compressed for the whole set or 203 bytes per commit, encrypted as members the way trees are. Second, no engine is best at everything. Python's own dictionaries and SQLite answer folder and file questions in microseconds to milliseconds. The Cypher engines took two to five seconds to walk a deep history, and rdflib could not walk it at all. Third, the algorithm beats the engine. With one number per commit, its generation, as git's commit-graph uses, the merge base and the commits between two heads take 0.1 ms, against 17 ms to 5 seconds in the engines. So sgit's own commands should stay on the standard library, with generation numbers and path-ordered tables. A graph engine is worth having as an optional local view, built from the same encrypted triples, for questions with many hops and many kinds of link: what changed together, who touched what, how sources connect. Oxigraph, with SPARQL and no dependencies of its own, is the one I would choose.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-vault-is-already-a-graph.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

> **Update, 27 October 2026.** This line of work shipped in **sgit-ai 0.26.0**: [the release notes](../docs/update-to-0-26-0.md), and [how it got there, with every document and the measurements](../articles/pack-indexes-shipped.md).

> **Update, 26 October 2026.** Dinis Cruz's design principles for these indexes (the writer pays, cross-references in both directions, one index per question, plain typed JSON loaded on demand, one file per folder) are tested in [Indexes the writer pays for](../articles/indexes-the-writer-pays-for.md), with MGraph-DB and Memory-FS measured and a million-page link graph. Every number from this article and the next is kept in [Graph and index measurements, 26 October 2026](../research/graph-and-index-measurements-2026-10-26.md), with the scripts.

## In short {#in-short}

- **A vault is already a graph, and already encrypted.** Commits point to parents and trees, and trees point to trees and files. Every one of those edges is inside an encrypted object, and the host sees only ids and sizes.
- **Triples are a good form for a second copy.** The whole graph here, 482,532 triples, is 3.0 to 3.7 MB compressed. Split per commit, each commit's triples are a 203-byte encrypted member.
- **Python has no graph database built in.** I measured its dictionaries, SQLite, networkx, Oxigraph, DuckDB, LadybugDB, Kùzu, rdflib and MGraph-DB.
- **No engine is best at everything.** Dictionaries and SQLite answer folder and file questions in microseconds to milliseconds. Walking a 20,000-commit history took the Cypher engines two to five seconds, and rdflib could not do it.
- **The algorithm beats the engine.** One number per commit, its generation, answers the merge base and base..head in 0.1 ms, about 200 to 50,000 times faster than walking the graph in the engines.
- **sgit's own commands should stay on the standard library,** with generation numbers for history and path-ordered rows for folders.
- **A graph engine is worth having as an optional view,** built locally from the same encrypted triples, for questions with many hops and many kinds of link. Oxigraph is the one I would choose.

## The question {#question}

Dinis Cruz asked this on 26 October, after reading [Indexes in the pack](../articles/indexes-in-the-pack.md) (lightly edited from a dictated message):

> "SQLite is still a SQL database, but fundamentally what we have here is a graph. The commits point to this, this points to that. Would it be worth storing them in a big graph database that we can run locally, or a series of graph databases, using triplets, so that we can use Cypher, or at least SPARQL, and benefit from the relationships? If I want to navigate the folder structure, or navigate the commits, can't I use that graph database to do that? And in principle we should be able to do this all with encrypted data: all the data continues to be encrypted, we just break it into other bits."

He also asked which engines Python already has, given the rule against new dependencies, and in which cases a graph engine would actually make sense.

## The vault is already a graph {#already}

sgit stores a Merkle graph, the same shape as git's:
- a **commit** points to its parents and to a tree;
- a **tree** points to its sub-trees and to its files' blobs, each under a name;
- every one of these is an object named by the hash of its ciphertext.

**The edges are inside the encryption.** A commit's parents and tree, and a tree's names and children, are inside the encrypted object. The host stores nodes it cannot open and cannot link. That is the property Dinis wants to keep, and sgit already has it.

What the [index pack](../articles/indexes-in-the-pack.md#correction) adds is a second copy of some of those edges, flattened so a reader does not have to open every object to follow them. Triples are a natural form for that copy:
- **one triple per edge:** (`commit`, `parent`, `commit`), (`folder`, `contains`, `file`), (`file`, `blob`, `id`), (`commit`, `changed`, `file`);
- **no schema to agree on** beyond the names of the predicates;
- **every graph engine reads them,** as rows, as RDF or as nodes and relationships.

## What I built {#built}

- **The file graph** is the head of the vault this site used for the 0.25.0 release notes: 76,000 files in 58,062 folders, each with its blob and size.
- **The history is synthetic:** 20,003 commits, with a side branch of five commits merged back every 50 commits (400 merges). One unmerged branch forks 120 commits back. Each commit changes five files.
- **Together that is 482,532 triples:** 134,061 `contains`, 76,000 `blob`, 76,000 `size`, 58,062 `tree`, 20,401 `parent`, 20,003 timestamps and 98,005 `changed`.

**Eight questions:**
1. a folder's children;
2. every file under a folder, found by walking down;
3. a file's folders up to the root;
4. every ancestor of the head;
5. the merge base of the head and the unmerged branch;
6. the commits in base..head, the list a pull prints;
7. the commits that changed a file;
8. the paths that hold a blob.

A plain-Python reference computed each answer first. **Every engine's answer was checked against it,** and every one matched except where the engine failed outright.

## The engines {#engines}

Python's standard library has no graph database. These are what can be wired in:

| Engine | Language | What it is | Extra dependencies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python dictionaries | Python | adjacency lists in memory | none: stdlib |
| SQLite | SQL, recursive CTEs | the triples as one indexed table | none: stdlib |
| networkx 3.7 | Python API | in-memory graph library with graph algorithms | 19 MB, pure Python |
| Oxigraph 0.5.13 (`pyoxigraph`) | **SPARQL 1.1** | RDF store, on disk or in memory | 21 MB wheel, Rust, nothing else |
| DuckDB 2.0.0 | SQL, recursive CTEs | columnar analytics database | 2.7 MB wheel, C++ |
| LadybugDB 0.15.3 (`real_ladybug`) | **Cypher** | embedded graph database, the community fork of Kùzu | C++ wheel |
| Kùzu 0.11.3 | Cypher | embedded graph database; **archived on 10 October 2025** | 21 MB wheel, C++ |
| rdflib 7.6.0 | SPARQL 1.1 | RDF library, pure Python | 4.9 MB, plus `pyparsing` |
| MGraph-DB 1.18.0 | Python API | Dinis Cruz's typed graph library, built on `osbot_utils`, which sgit already uses | 3.4 MB, pure Python |

**Kùzu is not a candidate,** whatever it measures. Kùzu Inc. stopped sponsoring it and archived the repository in October 2025; PyPI marks it archived. LadybugDB, the community fork, takes its place in this comparison and behaved the same.

## What I measured {#measured}

Milliseconds per query, warm, on a 4-core cloud sandbox:

| Question | Python | SQLite | networkx | Oxigraph | DuckDB | LadybugDB | rdflib |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Folder's children | 0.000 | 0.008 | 0.001 | 0.06 | 4.9 | 1.7 | 4.6 |
| Files under a folder (7,600) | 2.2 | 48 | 24 | 131 | 27 | 16 | 343 |
| A file's folders to the root | 0.002 | 0.013 | 0.006 | 0.09 | 27 | 2.1 | 3.5 |
| Every ancestor (19,999) | 7.8 | 22 | 18 | 107 | 228 | **1,971** | **fails** |
| Merge base | 52 | 89 | 55 | 450 | 553 | **5,307** | **fails** |
| base..head (110) | 17 | 79 | 35 | 231 | 612 | **4,843** | **fails** |
| Commits that changed a file | 0.000 | 0.007 | 0.005 | 0.05 | 6.8 | 1.5 | 3.8 |
| Paths that hold a blob | 0.000 | 0.007 | 0.001 | 0.05 | 5.0 | 1.4 | 4.5 |
| Load | 0.76 s | 3.1 s | 1.8 s | 4.9 s | 0.41 s | 2.1 s | 11.2 s |
| Size on disk | memory | 52 MB | memory | 56 MB | **9.4 MB** | 47 MB | memory |

The SQLite column is the dictionary-encoded table, where every term is an integer. With text terms it is 118.5 MB on disk, the history questions take about twice as long, and the folder walk is faster (14 ms), since it needs no lookup of the terms. Kùzu matched LadybugDB within 20% on every question.

**MGraph-DB** was measured on its own, because loading this set through its typed API would take minutes. It added a node and an edge in 0.44 ms (5,000 of each in 2.2 s), so 482,000 triples would take about three and a half minutes. Following 5,000 edges took 9.7 ms, about 2 µs a hop.

### Three things the numbers say {#lessons}

**1. Commit histories are deep, and that is the hard case.** A history is a chain with short side branches: 20,000 hops one after another. The Cypher engines find reachable commits with a shortest-path search that advances one level per hop, so a deep chain costs them seconds. rdflib follows a property path by recursion, once per commit, and stops at Python's recursion limit, at about a thousand commits. On the newsroom's 1,229 commits all of these would be much faster, but a vault's history only grows.

**2. A query planner can be wrong by a factor of 13,000.** SQLite's first plan for the folder walk read the whole `contains` index on every step: **182 seconds**. Forcing the join order with `CROSS JOIN` returned the same 13,405 rows in **13.9 ms**. A graph engine knows that a walk follows edges from the frontier; with SQL, you have to say so.

**3. The algorithm beats the engine.** The two questions every pull asks, the merge base and the commits between two heads, need not walk the history at all:
- give every commit a **generation number:** one more than its highest parent, 14 ms to compute for 20,003 commits;
- walk from both heads newest-generation first, and stop as soon as every commit still waiting is reachable from both. This is the walk git uses with its commit-graph file;
- the merge base took **0.10 ms**, and base..head **0.09 ms**, exact.

That is 500 to 50,000 times faster than the engines on the merge base, and 180 to 50,000 times on base..head. It is also the exact fix for a cost this site's [0.25.0 notes](../docs/update-to-0-25-0.md#6-still-slow-or-not-covered) list as still slow: a pull's list of new commits reading the clone's whole history. The CLI team's branch since bounds that walk by a day of clock skew; generation numbers make it exact for any clock. The CLI team's [architecture](../research/pack-carried-indexes-architecture.md) already proposes generation numbers in its `graph/` members.

The same holds for folders. A folder is a range of paths. The path-ordered table of [the indexes article](../articles/indexes-in-the-pack.md#measured) answered "every file under `raw/c09/`" in **5.4 ms** with a prefix range, faster than the engines' walks here except plain dictionaries.

## Where a graph engine is worth it {#where}

The two graphs sgit itself runs on have special shapes. **The files are a tree,** and a path is its index. **The history is a deep chain,** and a generation number is its index. For those, the standard library with the right index wins, and needs nothing new.

A graph engine earns its place where questions cross many kinds of link and many hops, and are asked by someone exploring rather than by a command:
- **what changes together:** files changed in the same commits as a given file. That is two hops, and every engine answered it in milliseconds or less;

  | Engine | Files changed with the most-changed file (32) |
  |---|---|
  | Python dictionaries | 0.003 ms |
  | SQLite, one self-join | 0.020 ms |
  | Oxigraph, SPARQL | 0.12 ms |
  | DuckDB | 16 ms |
  | LadybugDB, Cypher | 22 ms |

- **who touched what:** commits, their signing keys, the members those keys belong to, and the folders they wrote. The [PKI work](../articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.md) adds exactly these links;
- **what an application knows:** the newsroom's sources, the entities they mention, the articles that cite them, and the passes that captured them;
- **a question an agent writes for itself.** Agents already know SPARQL and Cypher. A pattern like `?c p:changed ?f . ?c p:changed ?g` is easier to write and review than its SQL self-join.

**Oxigraph is the one I would choose for that view:**
- **standards:** SPARQL 1.1 for queries, and N-Triples or Turtle for import and export;
- **no dependencies of its own:** one 21 MB wheel, on disk or in memory;
- **fast where it matters:** 0.05 to 0.1 ms on point questions, and 4.9 s to load all 482,532 triples;
- **an optional extra,** never something sgit needs in order to run, so the rule against new dependencies holds for every command.

LadybugDB is the choice if Cypher matters more than standards, with the caveat that its fork is a year old. DuckDB is worth knowing for a different reason: it stored all 482,532 triples in **9.4 MB** and loaded them in 0.41 s. MGraph-DB fits where it already works, as the typed model of a graph. It needs a bulk loader before it can hold a vault's history.

## Keeping it encrypted {#encrypted}

There are three ways to put a graph near ciphertext. Only the first keeps the guarantee sgit has now.

**1. Ship encrypted triples, and query them locally.** This is the index pack of the [last article](../articles/indexes-in-the-pack.md#correction), carrying triples:

| Form | Size |
|---|---|
| all 482,532 triples as JSON | 39.0 MB; **3.69 MB deflated** |
| as N-Triples, the RDF text format | 48 MB; 3.8 MB deflated |
| dictionary-encoded: a list of terms and three integer columns | 16.4 MB; **3.02 MB deflated** |
| one member per commit: its parents, time and changed files | 20,003 members, median **203 bytes**, 4.0 MB in all |

Encrypting the whole set with AES-GCM took 3 ms. Decrypting, inflating and parsing it took 351 ms. Rebuilding the dictionaries from it took 0.76 s, and building any of the engines above took 0.4 to 5 s. The host sees members of a few hundred bytes to a few megabytes, as it sees trees today, and **no edge.**

**2. Ship the graph with every name replaced by a keyed hash.** It looks encrypted, but it is not enough. Hashing all 308,151 names took 0.79 s, and the shape that remains tells the host a lot:
- the vault has 58,062 folders, and the largest holds 20 entries;
- one file has changed eight times, and which other files changed with it;
- how many commits arrive per day.

Each hidden name keeps its place in the structure. **Do not ship relations in the clear, even under hashed names.**

**3. Query the encrypted graph on the host.** Research schemes for queries over encrypted graphs exist. Each leaks which parts of the graph a query touches, and none is in Python's standard library. sgit's model is that the host stores and the client computes. Nothing measured here argues for changing that.

So yes, it all stays encrypted, as Dinis said: **break the graph into bits, encrypt the bits as trees are encrypted, and do every query on the reader's machine.**

## What I would build, in order {#build}

1. **Generation numbers,** in the `graph/` member each commit pack carries: the merge base and a pull's commit list become proportional to the answer. This is the largest win here, and it needs only the standard library.
2. **Triples as the format of the index pack:** dictionary-encoded, deflated, encrypted and signed, one member per pack. The local SQLite tables of the [indexes article](../articles/indexes-in-the-pack.md#sqlite) are one view of it.
3. **A fixed list of predicates, with its own namespace,** so the same triples load into SQL, SPARQL or Cypher: `parent`, `tree`, `contains`, `blob`, `changed`, `signed_by`, and the rest. `osbot_utils`, which sgit already uses, has ontology and taxonomy types that could hold it.
4. **An optional graph view:** a command that loads the local triples into Oxigraph, in memory, and answers a SPARQL query. Installed as an extra, never required.
5. **Application graphs in the vault itself:** a newsroom's sources and entities as triples, encrypted like any other file, loaded into the same view.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **Nothing here is built in sgit.** The proofs of concept are scripts against a copy of the data, not sgit code.
- **The history is synthetic.** Its shape, a long chain with short merged branches, is typical of agents' vaults, but real histories vary. At the newsroom's 1,229 commits, every engine is faster than here.
- **The merge base is the newest common ancestor by time,** for every engine and the reference alike. On this history it is the true merge base. The generation walk finds it exactly, whatever the clocks say.
- **Each engine was used as documented, with one rewrite** when its first query form was unreasonably slow: SQLite's join order, Oxigraph's subqueries, and Cypher's path depth limit. An expert in any of them might do better.
- **Timings are warm, on a fast disk,** and for one process. Concurrency, cold starts and memory limits were not measured.
- **LadybugDB is young as a fork.** Its numbers are those of 0.15.3.

If you build on this or think part of it is wrong, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

A message from Dinis Cruz on 26 October 2026. Measured and written by cli.sgit.ai's build agent, cli.build, the same day.

- **The data:** the 76,000-file benchmark vault of the [0.25.0 release notes](../docs/update-to-0-25-0.md), from its flat cache; a synthetic history generated with a fixed seed.
- **The engines:** the versions in the table, installed from PyPI into a separate environment. Kùzu's archiving: [The Register, 14 October 2025](https://www.theregister.com/2025/10/14/kuzudb_abandoned/), the [Kùzu PyPI page](https://pypi.org/project/kuzu/), and a [LadybugDB launch note](https://communityone.io/ar/servers/787399249741479977/neo4j/news/ladybugdb-launch-community-fork-kuzudb-2025-10-16/).
- **DuckDB's recursive queries:** [its documentation of WITH and USING KEY](https://duckdb.org/docs/1.4/sql/query_syntax/with), and [DuckPGQ](https://duckdb.org/library/duckpgq), its SQL/PGQ extension, which was not tested here.

- **The previous article and the design:** [Indexes in the pack](../articles/indexes-in-the-pack.md) and [The pack as the store, and the indexes it carries](../research/pack-carried-indexes-architecture.md).
- **The research topic:** [Big vaults and many agents](../research/topics/scale.md).

# A vault key that never lands: native PKI in sgit, so a key arrives sealed, stays sealed on disk and is opened only in memory, cli.sgit.ai

> pki.sgit.ai has made something work that I did not expect to feel this good. An agent gives me a QR code holding its public key; I open it on the website, check it, and write a message only that agent can read. Agents now hand each other vault keys the same way, with me as the transport: I carry a QR image from one session to the other and never see what is inside. But the last step undoes it. The receiving agent opens the sealed message, writes the vault key to a file, passes it to sgit clone on the command line, and sgit keeps it in clear in the clone's folder, next to a signing key that is also in clear. The key is protected while it travels and exposed the moment it arrives. So I asked how sgit itself could take PKI natively, on an agent running in a Linux container that has its own key pair, so that the clear vault key is never written to disk and exists only in memory. The answer is that most of the pieces exist. sgit already makes the right keys (RSA-OAEP 4096 and ECDSA P-256, the bundle pki.sgit.ai uses), already speaks the same sealed envelope, and already reads a vault key from standard input. What is missing is to keep the key sealed at rest, to open it inside a small agent process the way ssh-agent holds SSH keys, and to let sgit make and show its own identity. Opening a sealed key costs about two milliseconds, so this is not a performance question. The real work is that 27 places in the CLI read the key file directly and need to go through one door. This article maps that out, phase by phase.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

> **Update, 24 October 2026, 13:00.** Later the same day another agent working with me on pki.sgit.ai sent [ten requirements for the same fix](../research/sealed-vault-keys-requirements.md). The two are read against each other, and against the code, in [a side-by-side review](../research/sealed-vault-keys-side-by-side.md). It changes four things here:
> - a plain vault key on the command line is refused on all 14 commands that take one, not only clone;
> - `--to` means the record fingerprint, the signing key's, while sgit today prints the encryption key's first;
> - a key is sealed to a lasting recovery recipient as well as the agent, so a lost session key never loses a vault;
> - trust is checked against an explicit fingerprint first, leaving the register's rules to pki-agent until they are ported.
>
> The text below is as published.

## In short {#in-short}

- **The QR handover works,** and it protects a vault key while it travels: the key is sealed to the receiving agent's public key, and I carry an image I cannot read.
- **The key is in clear the moment it arrives:** a saved file, a command-line argument, then `.sg_vault/local/vault_key` in the clone, next to an unencrypted signing key.
- **Native PKI in sgit closes that.** sgit makes the agent's key pair, accepts a sealed vault key as it is, keeps it sealed on disk, and opens it only in memory.
- **The private key lives in a small `sgit agent` process,** the way `ssh-agent` holds SSH keys. In a throwaway container it is made in memory and never written at all.
- **It costs nothing a person would notice:** opening a sealed key is about 2 ms, against the 108 ms sgit already spends deriving keys on every command.
- **Most of the pieces exist:** the key types, the envelope, the key store shared with pki.sgit.ai's agent tool, and reading a key from standard input.
- **The real work is one door:** 27 places in the CLI read the key file directly, and all of them have to go through a single key source.
- **What it cannot do:** hide a key from a process that can read the agent's memory while it runs.

## What works now {#what-works}

Three things on [pki.sgit.ai](https://pki.sgit.ai/) have become part of how I work.

- **An agent's public key travels as a QR code.** The QR holds strict JSON: `pki.sgit.ai/qr/key/v1`, a fingerprint, a label and a `k1` code.
- **I seal a message to it in the browser.** sgit's own hybrid envelope: RSA-OAEP 4096 wraps an AES-256-GCM key, and the sender signs with ECDSA P-256. Only that agent can open it.
- **Agents hand each other vault keys the same way.** The sender runs `pki-agent seal --from-vault`, which reads the key from `sgit vault show-key` in memory and seals it to the recipient. The result is a QR image I carry to the other session. The handover page, [pki.sgit.ai/handover.md](https://pki.sgit.ai/handover.md), is what an agent follows.

## Where it breaks: the last metre {#last-metre}

The receiving side, read against sgit 0.24.0's code:

| Step | Where the vault key is | In clear? |
|---|---|---|
| The QR image, carried by me | sealed to the receiving agent's key | no |
| `pki-agent open qr.png --save DIR` | `vault-key-<id>.txt` | **yes**, a file |
| `sgit clone <vault key>` | the command line | **yes**: shell history, the process list, often the agent's own transcript |
| The clone | `.sg_vault/local/vault_key`, mode 0600 | **yes** |
| A read-only clone | `clone_mode.json` holds the read key | **yes** (recorded as an accepted risk, AppSec F07) |
| The clone's signing key | `.sg_vault/local/key-rnd-imm-*.pem`, unencrypted PKCS#8 | **yes** |
| The access token | `.sg_vault/local/token` | **yes** |

sgit writes every one of these files through one helper that sets the permissions to 0600 and encrypts nothing. Anything that can read the folder can therefore read every vault the agent holds:
- a backup, or `sgit vault backup --include-key`;
- a zip of the workspace;
- a container image pushed with the folder still in it;
- another process running as the same user.

## What sgit already has {#already}

More than I thought:

- **The right keys.** `sgit pki keygen` makes an RSA-4096 encryption key and an ECDSA P-256 signing key, fingerprinted as `sha256:` plus 16 hex. pki.sgit.ai's browser keys and its agent tool use exactly this bundle.
- **The same key store.** `pki-agent.mjs` keeps its keys in sgit's store, `~/.sg-send/keys/`, so `sgit pki` and the agent tool already use the same key.
- **The same envelope.** `sgit pki decrypt` opens what pki.sgit.ai seals (envelope v2, with the signer inside), and can write to standard output (`-o -`) instead of a file.
- **A key without a command line.** `sgit clone -` reads the vault key from the first line of standard input. The key is then still written to `local/vault_key`.
- **Secure deletion.** `secure_unlink` overwrites a file before removing it, for retiring a clear key file.

Two weaknesses turned up in the same reading, and both should be fixed whatever else happens:

- **The private key's passphrase protection is weak.** A key from `sgit pki keygen` is encrypted with PBKDF2 at **2,048 iterations**, the library's default. Vault keys get 600,000. Argon2id, already in the cryptography library sgit uses, costs 152 ms here.
- **The vault alias store is weaker than it looks.** `~/.sg-send/vaults.enc` derives its key with a fixed salt for every user, and its "auto-lock" only deletes a timestamp file.

## The design {#design}

Four pieces. Each is small, and together they mean the clear vault key is never written anywhere.

### 1. sgit makes its own identity {#identity}

```text
$ sgit id init --session --name "report builder (Claude Code session)"
  identity sha256:3f9c…  (session: in memory only; gone when the agent stops)
$ sgit id show --qr me.png          # the public key as pki.sgit.ai/qr/key/v1 JSON, or a k1 link
```

`sgit id` is `sgit pki keygen` with the right defaults: the same key types, the same bundle and the same store, so pki.sgit.ai and its agent tool read it unchanged. A key is held in one of three ways:

| Kind | Where the private key is | For |
|---|---|---|
| **Session** | Only in the memory of `sgit agent`. It is never written, and it ends with the process. | A throwaway cloud container: a new key per session, a new handover per session |
| **Lasting** | On disk, encrypted under a passphrase with Argon2id. The passphrase is given to `sgit agent` once. | A vault keeper, or an agent that outlives its container |
| **Hardware** | A TPM 2.0, a security key's PIV slot or a Mac's Secure Enclave. The key cannot be copied out. | A laptop or a server that has one |

Hardware mostly speaks P-256, not RSA-4096. So the third kind needs a second envelope: ECDH P-256 with HKDF and AES-256-GCM, the construction the CLI team already drew up for its [sealed files layer](../research/sealed-files-layer.md). The RSA envelope stays, because it is what pki.sgit.ai speaks today.

### 2. A sealed key goes in as it is {#sealed-clone}

```text
$ sgit clone --sealed handover.png work      # or an m1… code, a file, or - for stdin
  sealed to: sha256:3f9c… (this identity)   from: sha256:a1b2… (chains to the root)   expires: 30 Oct
  ▸ Packs fetched (1 pack(s), 2087 objects, 4 request(s) in 6.2s)
```

The clone accepts exactly what the QR handover produces: the strict `pki.sgit.ai/qr/sealed/v1` JSON, or the `m1` code inside it. It checks the same things `pki-agent open` checks:
- it is addressed to this identity;
- the signature verifies;
- it has not expired;
- the sender chains to the pinned root.

It opens the key in memory, derives what it needs, and never prints the key or writes it in clear. Reading a QR image needs a decoder, which can be an optional extra (`sgit-ai[qr]`), so the base install takes the JSON or the code.

### 3. The clone keeps it sealed {#at-rest}

```text
.sg_vault/local/
  vault_key.sealed      the vault key, sealed to this identity (or to several: a person's recovery key too)
  token.sealed          the access token, the same way
  key-rnd-imm-….pem     the clone's signing key, now encrypted under a key sealed the same way
  identity              which identity opens them: a fingerprint, nothing secret
```

- **Clones and pulls.** Every command that needs the key asks the identity to open `vault_key.sealed`, and holds the result only in memory.
- **Read-only clones** seal their read key in the same way, which retires the F07 accepted risk.
- **Existing clones** convert in place with `sgit vault seal-local`. It writes the sealed files, checks they open, and then removes the clear ones with the secure delete sgit already has.
- **Showing the key.** `sgit vault show-key` on a sealed clone refuses unless asked with `--reveal`.
- **Sending a key on.** A new `sgit vault seal --to <fingerprint> --qr out.png` seals the key to someone else without ever printing it, so the agent tool no longer has to read `show-key`'s output.

### 4. `sgit agent` holds the private key {#agent}

```text
$ eval "$(sgit agent start --session)"       # sets SGIT_AGENT_SOCK, like ssh-agent sets SSH_AUTH_SOCK
$ sgit status                                # asks the agent to open vault_key.sealed: ~2 ms
$ sgit agent lock                            # forgets every opened key; the private key stays (or, --session, goes)
```

A small process that holds the private key, and the vault keys it has opened, for a set time, behind a Unix socket only its user can reach. This is the pattern of `ssh-agent` and `gpg-agent`, and it is right for the same reasons:
- **A lasting key's passphrase is typed once,** not exported in an environment variable that every process of the same user can read in `/proc`.
- **A session key never touches disk at all,** because it is made inside the agent.
- **The agent can apply policy:** "this vault opens read-only", "push needs a fresh approval", "forget everything after an hour". That is where [the second factor](../articles/a-second-factor-without-a-server.md) plugs in.
- **The process can be hardened.** It can refuse core dumps, mark itself undumpable, and lock its pages in memory where the kernel allows.

## The flow, end to end {#flow}

```mermaid
%% A vault key handed from one agent to another with a person as the transport. The key is sealed until the receiving agent's sgit agent opens it in memory, and it stays sealed on that agent's disk afterwards.
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Sending agent
    participant P as Dinis (carries the QR)
    participant R as Receiving agent: sgit agent
    participant D as Receiving agent: disk
    R->>R: sgit id init --session (key pair in memory)
    R->>P: public key as a QR code
    P->>S: the QR code
    S->>S: sgit vault seal --to R --qr out.png
    S->>P: sealed QR (expires in a week)
    P->>R: the sealed QR
    R->>R: sgit clone --sealed: check, open in memory
    R->>D: vault_key.sealed, never the clear key
    Note over R,D: every later command: the agent opens it in memory, about 2 ms
```

## What it costs {#cost}

Measured in this sandbox with cryptography 50.0.2, the library sgit uses:

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| Open a sealed key (RSA-OAEP 4096) | **2.1 ms** |
| Seal a key (RSA-OAEP 4096) | 0.1 ms |
| Make a session identity (RSA-4096 + P-256) | about 470 ms, once per session |
| Load an RSA-4096 private key (the library's key check) | 330 ms, once per agent start |
| Unlock a lasting key with Argon2id (3 passes, 64 MiB) | 152 ms, once per agent start |
| What sgit already spends per command (PBKDF2 at 600,000) | 108 ms |

With the agent holding the opened key, every command after the first is about 2 ms slower than today. If the agent also holds the derived keys, it is about 100 ms faster.

## Where the work is {#work}

The code changes are mostly one refactor:

- **The key is read in 27 places in 17 files.** They go through `_read_vault_key`, `load_vault_key` and `vault_key_path`, including copies of `_init_components` in revert, branch switch and diff. Before anything else, they need one interface: a key source that answers "the vault id and the derived keys for this folder". It reads `vault_key` today, and `vault_key.sealed` through the agent tomorrow.
- **Almost nothing needs the clear key after derivation.** I found no consumer of the clear key in the core or workflow code beyond `show-key`, `rekey` and `move`. Everything else runs on the read key, the write key, the vault id and the file ids derived from them. So the key source can hand out derived keys and keep the vault key itself sealed.

**Phases:**

1. **Phase 1, the door.** The single key source, behind the existing behaviour, with tests that the 27 call sites use it. No change for users.
2. **Phase 2, sealed at rest.** `sgit id`, `sgit agent` with session and lasting keys, `vault_key.sealed`, `sgit vault seal-local`, `clone --sealed` for the `m1` code and the JSON, and Argon2id for private keys. This is the phase that closes the gap.
3. **Phase 3, the sending side.** `sgit vault seal --to`, expiry in the sealed message, read-only handovers (the read key alone), QR images through the optional extra.
4. **Phase 4, hardware and identity.** The P-256 envelope for TPM, PIV and Secure Enclave keys, and signing commits with the identity's own key. A commit's author is then a record in pki.sgit.ai's register, not only a key inside the vault.

None of it needs the server to change: what goes to the host is exactly what goes today.

## How this relates to the native PKI vault mode {#vault-mode}

On 9 October the CLI team mapped [a second vault mode built on key pairs](../research/native-pki-vault-mode.md):
- a vault id derived from a signing key;
- a data key wrapped to a read key;
- writes authorised by signatures instead of a bearer secret.

That is a new kind of vault. This proposal is smaller and comes first: it keeps today's vaults and today's keys, and changes only how a key reaches an agent and how the agent keeps it. Both use the same identity, so the identity built here is the one the vault mode would use later.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **It does not hide a key from a process that can read the agent's memory** while it runs: root on the same machine, a debugger, a compromised agent. It shrinks where a key lives, from every copy of a folder to one process's memory for as long as it is unlocked.
- **Python cannot reliably wipe a secret from memory,** because strings are immutable and the collector moves things. The agent can lock pages and refuse dumps; it cannot promise erasure.
- **Expiry on a sealed key is a policy the agent enforces,** not cryptography. A key that has been opened once can be kept by an agent that ignores the rule. Cryptographic expiry needs rotation (`sgit vault rekey`) or a server.
- **A session key dies with its container,** so a restarted session needs a new handover. That is the point for throwaway agents, and the reason for lasting keys.
- **Nothing here is built.** The numbers are measurements of the operations the design uses, not of an implementation. The code facts are from sgit 0.24.0 at `182cfc1`.

If you want to try this on your own agents, or to argue with the design, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

A message of mine on 24 October 2026, written up by cli.sgit.ai's build agent, cli.build, on the same day; the editorial responsibility is mine.

- **The pki.sgit.ai workflow:** its [handover page](https://pki.sgit.ai/handover.md), its [llms.txt](https://pki.sgit.ai/llms.txt), and [Agents, vault keys and the root](https://pki.sgit.ai/articles/agents-vault-keys-and-the-root.md), all at site v0.2.28.
- **The code facts:** SGit-AI__CLI at `182cfc1`, the code of sgit-ai 0.24.0. The places named are:
  - `crypto/Vault__Secret_File.py`, the 0600 helper;
  - `core/Vault__Sync__Base.py`, the key read and derivation;
  - `crypto/Vault__Crypto.py`, PBKDF2 at 600,000 with an in-memory cache;
  - `crypto/Vault__Key_Manager.py` and `crypto/PKI__Crypto.py`, the unencrypted signing PEM and `BestAvailableEncryption`, whose 2,048 iterations were confirmed with `openssl asn1parse`;
  - `secrets/Secrets__Store.py`, the fixed salt;
  - `cli/CLI__Main.py`, `clone -`.
- **The timings:** measured by the agent in a cloud sandbox with cryptography 50.0.2.
- **Earlier designs this builds on:** [the native PKI vault mode](../research/native-pki-vault-mode.md), [read and write keys as PKI](../research/read-write-keys-as-pki.md) and [the sealed files layer](../research/sealed-files-layer.md).
- **The research topic:** [Keys, members and who may write](../research/topics/keys.md).

# A vault you can carry: one zip holds the whole vault, a public key can seal it, and the round trip already works, cli.sgit.ai

> Reading the pack-mode article, I wanted three things made explicit. First, the two modes side by side, the files that exist in each and the order things happen, which is now a section of that article. Second, my understanding that we mix mutable and immutable files and that this is why the architecture works. The code is more precise than my words were: every object's name says its kind, immutable objects are written once and named by their hash, and the few mutable ones come in two sorts, the shared ones that move only by compare-and-swap and the ones with a single owner. Almost everything in a vault is immutable, so it can be copied, cached or zipped in any shape; only a handful of small files say where the history is. Third, the use case that follows: storage that is good at one big file and bad at thousands of small ones, Google Drive, Dropbox, one large object on S3, for vaults that change rarely or in distinct moments. The whole vault is its bare folder, the objects and those few pointers frozen at one moment, and it fits in one zip. Sealed to someone's public key, the host cannot even tell how many objects are inside. I asked whether that works, and it does today, with commands sgit already ships: a published vault cloned, zipped into one 12.7 MB file of 111 members, sealed to a key in half a second, opened, unzipped elsewhere, and cloned from the folder in 0.48 seconds, with the same files and the same history as a clone from the server. What is missing is one command to make the file, a clone that reads it without unzipping, and a smaller envelope: the seal today is 1.78 times the zip.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/a-vault-you-can-carry.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
By [Dinis Cruz](https://sgit.ai/about/) · 2026-10-21 · published

*A vault in one file.
