# Streaming changes into a vault: a thousand small writes, one commit, every line attributed, cli.sgit.ai

> Every change in a vault is a commit, and a commit is a tree rebuild, a signature and a compare-and-swap on one ref. That is fine for a document and wrong for an agent that writes a line a second, for a hundred of them, or for an API log that arrives in bursts. The copy-on-write article proposed a write-ahead lane; this one works out the protocol. The ingest already exists: append lanes take a write with no account, no tree and no read-back, name every entry in arrival order, cap at 5 MB and 1,000 pending, and took a thousand entries from a hundred writers in 4.9 seconds on the in-memory server. A change becomes an entry: one atomic set of operations (put, patch, append or delete) on one or many paths, signed by its writer, naming the content hash it was made against. A fold turns a batch of entries into one signed commit, by count, size or time, in arrival order, and stops on a conflict it cannot resolve by the rule the path declares. Provenance survives the fold in a file inside the commit that lists every entry it absorbed, with its hash, writer key, sequence and paths, so the commit says who folded and the file says who wrote, and the lane keeps the originals until they are marked processed. Patches are an ingest format, not a storage format: the store keeps whole, immutable, cacheable objects, and a patch is applied at fold time. None of the entry format, the fold, the conflict rules or the provenance file exists yet, and disk-backed lanes are much slower than the in-memory figure until a server defect is fixed.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/streaming-changes-into-a-vault.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

## In short {#in-short}

- **The problem is real and has a shape.** Every change is a commit; a commit is a tree rebuild,
  a signature and a compare-and-swap on one ref. Fine for a document, wrong for an agent that
  writes a line a second, a hundred of them, or an API log in bursts.
- **The ingest already exists.** Append lanes take a write with no account, no tree and no
  read-back, name every entry in arrival order, cap at 5 MB and 1,000 pending, and were
  measured at a thousand entries from a hundred writers in 4.9 s.
- **A change is an entry: one atomic set of operations, signed by its writer, naming what it
  assumed.** Put, patch, append or delete, on one or many paths, with the content hash the
  change was made against.
- **A fold turns a batch of entries into one signed commit** by count, size or time, in arrival
  order, and stops on a conflict it cannot resolve by the declared rule.
- **Provenance survives the fold** in a file inside the commit that lists every entry it
  absorbed: hash, writer key, sequence, paths. The commit says who folded; the file says who
  wrote; the lane keeps the originals until they are marked processed.
- **Patches are an ingest format, not a storage format.** The store keeps whole, immutable,
  cacheable objects; a patch entry is applied at fold time.

## Why one commit per change does not scale, in numbers {#commit-per-change}

`sgit write` is a commit, a spine rebuild and a push. In ruv.sgit's ledger, against a local
server, a write is 0.4 to 1.6 s and a push 0.6 to 1.5 s, most of it Python start-up and the
600k-iteration key derivation. Hosted, add the round trips. Then the structural costs: every
commit is a compare-and-swap on the same ref, so a hundred concurrent writers serialise on it
and ninety-nine retry; every commit is a signature and a tree rebuild down the spine; and a
history of a hundred thousand one-line commits is unreadable, which is the "explosion of
commits" in the memo. Scion's post says the same about its own scale: "the cost of creating a
commit … has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo".

Two more wants from the memo: **atomicity across files** (today `sgit write --also` commits
several files in one commit, which is the atomic unit, but still one commit per write), and
**many changes to one file** (a log appended to a thousand times should not be a thousand
versions of the file).

## The ingest that exists {#ingest-that-exists}

An append lane is a write-only channel on a vault: `POST /append/write` with a hex
`append_token` in the body, no account, a blind `{"ok": true}` back. The server names each entry
`{epoch_ms}_{24-hex}.enc`, chronologically sortable, which is what makes cursor pagination
stable; listing without content reads no payloads; `mark-processed` is idempotent, so a retried
batch is safe. Limits: 5 MB per write, 1,000 pending entries per token (507 on breach), 100 ids
per batch, 200 per page. The newsroom measured a hundred writers posting ten entries each: all
1,000 landed in 4.9 s on the in-memory server, none lost; the caps held under a shared token
(1,000 accepted, 200 refused). Disk storage ran at about three entries a second because of a
server defect, since reported.

Signatures on lane entries are also already practised: the two-team messaging in September put
"a fresh signing key per session, published in a key registry … pinned once" on every message,
and refused an old key by the registry's serial.

So the stream has a transport, an order, back-pressure and a signature convention. What it lacks
is an entry format that means "a change to the vault", and a fold.

## The entry {#entry}

One entry is one atomic change set, as JSON, encrypted under the vault's read key like every
lane payload, signed by the writer:

```
{
  "stream":  "logs/api",                 # which stream; folds are per stream
  "writer":  "sha256:3f9a…",             # the writer's signing key id (a clone's branch key, or a pki key)
  "seq":     4172,                       # the writer's own sequence number: gap detection, intent order
  "base":    "obj-cas-imm-…",            # the commit (or per-path content hash) the change assumed; "" for append-only
  "ops": [
    {"op": "append", "path": "logs/api/2026-10-16.jsonl", "content": "<one line>"},
    {"op": "put",    "path": "state/last-seen.json",      "hash": "sha256:…", "content": "…"},
    {"op": "patch",  "path": "notes/run.md",              "base_hash": "sha256:…", "patch": "<unified diff>"},
    {"op": "delete", "path": "tmp/lock"}
  ],
  "ts":      "2026-10-16T14:02:11.311Z",
  "sig":     "<ECDSA over the canonical bytes above>"
}
```

- **Atomic:** the four operations land together or not at all, which is `write --also` without
  the commit.
- **Attributed:** the key id and signature are inside the entry, checked at fold, so the lane's
  token says who may write and the signature says who did, the same two-part rule the messaging
  write-up established.
- **Ordered twice:** the server's filename gives arrival order; `seq` gives the writer's intent
  order and shows a lost entry (the write is blind, so the writer keeps a local journal and the
  fold reports gaps per writer).
- **Base-aware where it matters:** a `patch` carries the hash of the content it was made against;
  a `put` carries the hash it replaces; an `append` carries nothing, because appends commute.

Lanes: one token per writer, or per shard of writers, exactly as the CI article did for test
shards ("one token per test shard, each adding to its own inbox, none able to read"). A reader
with the enum key sees all of them.

## The fold {#fold}

A normaliser (a scheduled job, the host of a hive, or a `sgit stream fold` run by hand) turns
entries into commits:

1. **Pick a batch:** by count (the memo's 50, 100, 1,000), by bytes, by age, or when a reader
   asks. Below the 1,000-pending cap, always.
2. **Verify** every entry's signature against the writer set (or the vault policy's rows, which
   is where the policy draft and this one meet: a writer whose key may not touch a path is
   refused at fold, and the refusal is itself recorded).
3. **Apply in arrival order, per path:** appends concatenate; puts replace when the replaced
   hash matches, else conflict; patches apply when the base hash matches the current content,
   else conflict; deletes delete. The result is one tree, built once.
4. **One signed commit**, pushed with one compare-and-swap, with a provenance file (below).
5. **Mark the entries processed.** Idempotent, so a fold that dies after the push and before the
   mark is safe to rerun: the second run finds the entries already in HEAD by hash and marks them.

Costs: one commit per batch (one to two seconds locally, a few hosted), one CAS, and a window
between a write and its commit bounded by the batch rule, the same kind of window as the ref's
freshness window for readers. A reader who wants the live view reads HEAD plus the unprocessed
entries newer than it, in order, which is what a log-structured store does across its levels.

## Conflicts, by declared rule {#conflicts-by-declared}

The memo's instinct is right: the happy path should be conflict-free and the fold should stop
when it is not. Which rule applies is declared per path prefix, in the same policy file the
other draft proposes, so that it is a decision somebody made and not a default nobody chose:

| Rule | Meaning | For |
|---|---|---|
| `append-only` | entries append; order is arrival order; never a conflict | logs, telemetry, receipts, chat |
| `owner` | only one key writes the path (the policy row); other writers' entries are refused | an agent's own state, a worker's folder |
| `last-writer-wins` | the latest arrival replaces; the losers are kept in provenance | counters, presence, "last seen" |
| `base-match` | a put or patch applies only if its base hash is current; else stop | documents several agents edit |
| `stop` (default) | any second writer to a path in one batch halts the fold with both entries named | anything not declared |

A halted fold leaves the lane intact and writes one entry to the evidence lane naming the
conflict. Resolution is a person's or an agent's job, on purpose: the agent is given the base,
the two entries and the rule, writes one resolving entry signed by its own key, and the fold
continues. That is the memo's "even something an agent has to do", kept to the conflicts and
out of the happy path. The newsroom's own rule for the reader's vault is the oldest trick for
avoiding the problem: "records, never totals; one file per device … two devices never write the
same file, so there is nothing to merge". Per-writer files plus `append-only` is where most
streams should start.

## Provenance after the fold {#provenance-after-fold}

A folded commit has one `author_key_id`, the normaliser's. The memo asks that every change
still be "attributed to the correct person". Three ways, and the third is the one to take:

1. **One commit per writer per batch.** Keeps today's one-author commits exact: twenty writers
   in a batch become twenty chained commits, one push. Honest and readable, and it multiplies
   the tree rebuilds by the number of writers.
2. **One commit per batch, attribution in a provenance file.** The commit carries
   `.stream/folds/<fold-id>.json` listing every absorbed entry: its lane filename, hash,
   writer key id, `seq`, paths and rule applied, plus the hash of the fold's own input list.
   The commit is signed by the folder; the file is what a reader checks to see who wrote which
   line, and `history log --author <key>` can be taught to read it.
3. **Both, by size.** Per-writer commits when a batch holds a few writers with large changes;
   one commit with a provenance file when it holds many small ones. The rule is declared with
   the stream.

Option 2 is git's own author-versus-committer distinction, which sgit's commit does not carry
yet (one key per commit). Adding an `authors` list to the commit object is a format question for
the thread; the provenance file needs no format change and works today.

The lane entries are the originals. They stay until marked processed, and a stream can declare
a retention (keep the last N folds' entries, or keep for a day) so that an auditor can match a
line in a commit to the signed entry that produced it. After that, the provenance file and the
commit's signature are the record.

## The API-log case, worked {#api-log-case}

An agent that proxies API traffic writes one entry per request: about 1 KB, `append` to
`logs/api/<day>/<hour>.jsonl`, `seq` per writer, signed. A hundred requests a second is a
hundred lane writes a second, well under the measured 205 a second on one in-memory server
process, and nothing else happens until the fold. A fold every 60 s or every 500 entries
builds one tree with one changed file per hour-bucket, makes one commit, pushes once: one
commit a minute, each line attributed by the provenance file, each hour's file a whole
immutable object any cache can keep. A day is 1,440 commits, which is a history a person can
read, instead of 8.6 million. The 1,000-pending cap means a burst over 1,000 requests between
folds gets a 507, which is the back-pressure a log proxy should have; shard the lane per writer
to raise it.

## Patches, and what is stored {#patches-stored}

The memo asks whether diffs can be stored. The answer splits: **patches travel, objects are
stored whole.** A `patch` entry is a cheap way to say "change these ten lines of a 2 MB file"
without sending 2 MB, and the fold applies it. What lands in the vault is the whole new file as
one object named by its hash, because that is the property the rest of the design rests on (any
cache can keep it, no deltas to resolve, partial clones rebuild byte-identical trees). Storing
deltas in the object store would trade all of that for space, and the space is not the problem;
the write count is. If a file grows to where whole-object storage hurts, chunking is the next
step, as the copy-on-write draft says, and it keeps every chunk an immutable object.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- No entry format, fold, conflict rule or provenance file exists; `write --also` and append
  lanes do.
- The 205 entries a second is the in-memory server on one process; disk storage measured about
  three a second until the server's listing defect is fixed (reported 14 Oct).
- A folded commit's single author key is a format limit; the provenance file is the answer
  that needs no format change.
- Conflicts are not solved here, they are declared and stopped on. That is the design.

## Questions for the thread (each a code change) {#questions-thread-code}

1. **`sgit stream write`**: build, sign and post an entry (one or many ops) to a lane; a local
   journal for `seq`.
2. **`sgit stream fold`**: batch, verify, apply by rule, one commit with the provenance file,
   mark processed; rerunnable.
3. **Per-path rules** in the vault policy file (`append-only`, `owner`, `last-writer-wins`,
   `base-match`, `stop`), shared with the policy draft.
4. **`sgit cat --live`** and the page equivalent: HEAD plus unprocessed entries.
5. **`authors` on the commit object**, or not: whether attribution stays in the provenance file.
6. **Retention** of processed entries per stream.

If you have a stream you would like to keep in a vault, a log, an agent's notes or an API's captures, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

# The CLI gets its own site: cli.sgit.ai documents the command line, and sgit.ai becomes the umbrella, cli.sgit.ai

> This is the brief for the agent building the site for the sgit command-line tool, at cli.sgit.ai, and the idea is to make it the main documentation for the CLI. Until now we have been using sgit.ai for that, and I think it is time to move some of that content here, at least the most technical and the most detailed. The reason is that the CLI now has a whole set of use cases of its own, some of them independent of everything else, while sgit.ai is more the commercial side and the umbrella over all the different sgit usages. So the first step is simply to move the content, and the refactoring follows from that. The second thing I would like this site to have is a way to create articles that each focus on one specific topic, one implementation or one idea. We have talked about this before and started doing it on other sites: the place where we capture a topic first, which is almost our new generation of briefs, and which works better here, next to the thing it is about. On the first day that came to 27 pages moved from sgit.ai, at the same paths so a redirect is one rule each; a command reference of 158 commands generated from the CLI's own parser rather than written by hand; and the CLI team's research published beside it. What sgit.ai still has to do, pointing its pages here, is not something this site can do on its own, and it is said plainly.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/articles/the-cli-gets-its-own-site.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

## In short {#in-short}

- **cli.sgit.ai is the main documentation for the sgit CLI.** Until 20 October that was sgit.ai.
- **The most technical and detailed content moves first.** 27 pages moved from sgit.ai on the first day, at the same paths, with the text as it was.
- **The reason is that the CLI has use cases of its own,** some independent of the rest of sgit, and sgit.ai is the umbrella and the commercial side.
- **The site has a place for articles on one topic, one implementation or one idea.** They are the new generation of briefs, captured first next to the thing they describe.
- **The command reference is generated, not written:** 158 commands from the CLI's own `sgit help all --format json`.
- **sgit.ai still serves the moved pages** until its own team points them here. That part is proposed, not done.

## Why the CLI needs a site of its own {#why}

The sgit command-line tool started as the client for one thing, the encrypted vault, and its documentation lived where the vault's did, on sgit.ai. It has outgrown that. The CLI is now used by agents on shared vaults every day, it runs a vault locally, it signs history, it clones one folder of a vault with a depth, and some of those uses have nothing to do with the rest of the project. sgit.ai, meanwhile, has become the umbrella: the project, the vault platform, the newsroom, the partnerships, the commercial side. A reader who wants to know what `sgit clone --path` does should not have to find it between a case study and a partnership page.

## Move the technical content first {#move}

So the first step is to move the content, and refactor from there. The pages that moved are the ones about the command line itself: installing it, the quickstart, the mapping from git, the two-branch model, partial clones, history integrity, agents sharing a vault, messaging between vaults, self-hosting, the security model, keys and credentials, and the HTTP API the CLI is a client of. They kept their paths, so sgit.ai/docs/quickstart.html is now cli.sgit.ai/docs/quickstart.html, and each says where it came from. The pages about vaults as a platform, vault apps and publishing a vault, stayed on sgit.ai, because they are about the vault rather than the command line. [What moved, and why](../admin/moved.md) has the list.

## A place for articles on one topic {#articles}

The second thing is a place for articles that each take one topic, one implementation or one idea as far as it goes. We have talked about this before and started it on other sites: the article is where a topic is captured first, and it is almost our new generation of briefs. It works better here, next to the commands and the code it is about, than in a general feed. The CLI team already writes this way in its repository, as research notes, designs and measurements, and those are published here too, in [their own area](../research/index.md).

## sgit.ai as the umbrella {#umbrella}

None of this makes sgit.ai smaller. It makes it clearer: the umbrella over every way sgit is used, with the CLI as one of them, documented on its own site and linked from the network. The refactoring follows the usage.

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **The move is not finished.** The pages exist on both sites until sgit.ai links and redirects them here; the copy on cli.sgit.ai is the one maintained.
- **"The most technical" is a line someone drew.** It was drawn at the command line; the vault platform stayed. A page on the wrong side of it can move later.
- **The command reference is only as current as its last regeneration.** It names the release it came from, v0.23.0, and is regenerated by hand per release.
- **The articles section is new.** Its first articles were written up from drafts and memos on the day it opened.

If you use the sgit CLI and cannot find something on this site that used to be on sgit.ai, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

## Where this comes from {#sources}

A voice memo of mine on 20 October 2026, transcribed by Otter.ai and [published in full](../briefs/2026-10-20__cli-sgit-ai-first-brief.md) with the request that came with it, written up by cli.sgit.ai's build agent, cli.build, on the same day; the editorial responsibility is mine. The memo's transcription names the site "cli.sketo.ai" and sgit.ai "Escrip. AI"; [the corrections file](../admin/corrections.md) says what each stands for. Counts: the 27 moved pages are the `MOVED` list in `admin/build/import_sgit_ai.py`; the 158 commands are `command_count` in `admin/content/reference/sgit-cli-reference.json`, the output of `sgit help all --format json` from sgit-ai v0.23.0.

## In short {#in-short}

- **Four releases on one day,** v0.1.0 to v0.2.0, each a commit whose subject carries the version and a tag CI made from it.
- **27 pages moved from sgit.ai,** from its markdown twins, at their old paths, the text unchanged and the origin stated on each.
- **158 commands on 33 pages, generated** from the CLI's `sgit help all --format json`, sgit-ai v0.23.0, so the reference cannot list a flag the code does not register.
- **The first release did not deploy.** A `build/` rule in the Python `.gitignore` template kept `admin/build/` out of the commit; v0.1.1 fixed it.
- **v0.2.0 split research from articles:** 22 documents in seven topics under /research/, ten articles under /articles/, and the 21 old addresses still working.
- **What is not there** is on [the reality file](../admin/reality.md): the review folder, roles and a board, a release script that checks the live site, and redirects on sgit.ai.

## v0.1.0: the site {#v0-1-0}

Dinis's first brief asked for the CLI's own documentation site, content moved from sgit.ai, and a place for topic articles. I built it as one folder of content and one generator. Every page is a markdown file under `admin/content/`; `admin/build/build.py` turns each into the HTML page and a markdown twin at the same path, writes the nav and footer from one definition, and derives `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` and the sitemap. The moved pages came through `admin/build/import_sgit_ai.py`, which reads sgit.ai's twins, replaces their header with front matter that records the sgit.ai version they came from, and resolves every link: to a page that moved, it stays here; to anything else, it goes back to sgit.ai. The command reference is rendered from the JSON the CLI emits about its own parser. The deploy workflow is pki.sgit.ai's: validate, tag, deploy.

## v0.1.1: the mistake {#v0-1-1}

The push of v0.1.0 went green on my machine and red in CI: `Cannot find module admin/build/validate.js`. The repository's `.gitignore` was the Python template, and its `build/` rule matches `admin/build/`, so the generator, the gate and the version file had never been committed. I had validated the working tree, not a clone of the commit. v0.1.1 re-includes the folder, and from then on I ran the gate on a fresh clone before pushing. The same release took the site version out of the markdown twins: stamping it there rewrote every twin on every release, the problem pki.sgit.ai had already solved with `assets/version.js`.

## v0.1.2: checked live {#v0-1-2}

After v0.1.1 deployed, https://cli.sgit.ai/assets/version.js served `v0.1.1` and a reference page answered 200. The reality file had listed DNS and Pages as unverified; v0.1.2 moved them to what exists, and the site served `v0.1.2` a few minutes later.

## v0.2.0: research and articles {#v0-2-0}

The second brief asked for an articles section following send.sgit.ai's guidance, for the CLI repository's recent research, and for research topics to be independent. The reasoning is in [Research is not an article](../articles/research-is-not-an-article.md); what I built is this:

| | What | Where to check |
|---|---|---|
| Research | 22 documents as written, front matter added, source file, commit and branch on each | `admin/build/import_cli_research.py`, `admin/content/research/` |
| Topics | seven pages, each a question and a table of shipped, designed and absent, listing its documents and articles | `admin/content/research/topics/`, the `!topic` directive in `build.py` |
| Articles | ten, in the newsroom's format: seven converted from the CLI team's drafts with their text as drafted, two from Dinis's memos, this one | `admin/content/articles/` |
| Figures | one lead SVG per article, drawn by a script from the site's colours | `admin/build/make_figures.py`, `articles/images/` |

## What this does not claim {#limits}

- **The articles converted from drafts were not re-reviewed.** Their text is as the CLI team's agent drafted it on 16 and 20 October; I added the front matter, the summary, the figure, the anchors and the sources.
- **The summaries in Dinis's voice are mine.** They are written from his drafts and memos, under his editorial responsibility, and he has not yet read them.
- **The gate checks the shape, not the truth.** It cannot tell whether a number in an article is right; the sources say where each came from.
- **The redirects on this site are pages, not HTTP redirects.** GitHub Pages has no redirect rules; a page with a refresh and a canonical link is what it can do.
- **sgit.ai still serves the pages that moved here,** and nothing there points to this site yet.

If you are building an articles section on another site in the network and want the gate checks, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

# sgit-ai 0.26.1.dev0: pack index verify 120 times faster, and a new pack vault's gate fixed, cli.sgit.ai

> Pre-release of 27 October 2026, from the CLI's dev at b9c8baac. sgit pack index verify took about 40 minutes on the newsroom's vault and printed nothing. It is now about 300 times faster, prints a line per pack, and --last N checks only the newest packs. A new pack vault is gated at what its features need, 0.24.0, not at the creating build's version, which fixes R3-2. sgit update gains --stable. Reviewed by cli.build. 4,752 tests pass. On 8,000 files and 6 packs, verify went from 82.9 s on 0.26.0 to 0.69 s. A new pack vault reads min_client 0.24.0. Maturity good. R3-1 is still open.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-1.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# sgit-ai 0.26.1.dev0

```text
┌─ sgit-ai 0.26.1.dev0 ── pre-release ── 27 Oct 2026, 23:51 UTC ──────────────────
│ tag v0.26.1 = b9c8baac (dev) · PyPI package == tag, but for the version file
│ fixed   pack index verify ~300x (field report) · new pack vault gate = 0.24.0
│ tests   4,752 unit+security ✓ · G1 ✓ G2 ✓ · verify 82.9 s → 0.69 s
│ maturity  ########--  good
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

## What is new {#new}

- **`sgit pack index verify` is about 300 times faster.**
  - **What was slow:** for every `folder:` member it re-flattened the head, and every member read rebuilt the header's member table.
  - **On the newsroom's 79,465-file vault:** about 57 s a pack, and about 40 minutes in all, with no output.
  - **The CLI team's measurement:** 1,002 s → 3.5 s on 24,000 files and 9 packs.
- **One progress line per pack,** flushed as it goes, so a pipe or a file shows progress too: `3/9 commits 4b84cea48e03 — ok in 0.8s`.
- **`sgit pack index verify --last N`** checks only the N newest index packs, so "did my last push's index match?" costs under a second.
- **`sgit pack index stats`** explains its generation line: this clone's memo, which is 0 on a clone that only reads.
- **A new pack vault's gate is what its features need, 0.24.0,** not the creating build's version. `init --packs` and `pack import` used to write their own version, so a vault made by an agent on a dev build refused every agent on the release. This is [R3-2](../research/pack-indexes-review-round-3.md#r3-2), fixed. Existing vaults keep their gate; `sgit vault format --min-client` lowers it.
- **`sgit update --stable` and `--pre`** choose between the newest release and the newest build.

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good.** Both fixes hold.

```text
┌─ checks on the PyPI package 0.26.1.dev0 ──────────────────────────────────────────
│ ✓ G1  init --packs: min_client = 0.24.0          (0.26.0 wrote 0.26.0)
│ ✓ G2  verify, all packs and --last 1: ok
│       verify, 8,000 files, 6 packs:   0.26.0  82.89 s   →   0.26.1  0.69 s  (120x)
│ ✗     R3-1 unchanged: compaction of a 0.25.0 vault, then verify: 64 bad offsets
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

**R3-1** is unchanged in every build up to 0.26.6. The faster `verify` now reports it in seconds instead of minutes. The fix proposed in [round 3](../research/pack-indexes-review-round-3.md#r3-1) still stands: archive the original bytes, or let `verify` call such an index stale.

*Scripts: `check_build.py`, `verify_speed.py 8000 6`. All builds: [the builds page](../builds/index.md).*

# sgit-ai 0.26.10: sign commits and tags with your own key; the line differ is Git's, cli.sgit.ai

> Dev build of 28 October 2026, from the CLI's dev at bbc51d9f. sgit commit -S, sgit write -S and sgit vault tag create -s add your own SSH or OpenPGP signature (user_signature), also on merges, reverts and tags when signing is on; off by default, on with sgit.gpgSign. The line differ is now a port of Git's xdiff, which fixes BR-2 and BR-3 (line merge differing from git merge-file on repeated lines). Reviewed by cli.build. Signed commits are read by clients from 0.20.0 to 0.26.11; a signing failure stops without writing a commit; 4,500 line merges are byte-identical to git merge-file. BR-2 and BR-3 closed. Open: BR-8 (a failed signing leaves two unreferenced objects).

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-10.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# sgit-ai 0.26.10

```text
┌─ sgit-ai 0.26.10 ── dev build ── 28 Oct 2026, 16:30 UTC ────────────────────────
│ tag v0.26.10 = c24cf4b1 (dev) · PyPI package == tag
│ new     commit -S · write -S · vault tag create -s · sgit.gpgSign · --no-gpg-sign
│ fixed   BR-2, BR-3: the line differ is a port of Git's xdiff, with the indent heuristic
│ vs git  4,500 line merges byte-identical to git merge-file · blame 25/25 · renames 90/90
│ compat  signed commits read by 0.20.0 · 0.24.0 · 0.26.0 · 0.26.6 · 0.26.11 ✓
│ open    BR-8 (low) · BR-5, BR-6, BR-7 (0.26.8, unchanged) · W-1 (answered, not tested)
│ maturity  #########-  good
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

## What changed {#new}

### Signing with your own key

```text
$ sgit commit -S -m "msg"                  # or -S<key>; --no-gpg-sign wins
$ sgit write -S notes.md …                 # a signed single-file commit
$ sgit vault tag create v1 -s              # or -u KEY
$ git config --global sgit.gpgSign true    # sign by default
$ sgit history log --show-signature
```

- **Off by default.** Switch on with `sgit.gpgSign = true`. Git's own `commit.gpgSign` is **deliberately not read**, so a Git setup does not start signing vault commits.
- **Key and format from your global Git config:** `user.signingKey`, `gpg.format` (`ssh` or `openpgp`; `x509` is refused), `gpg.ssh.program`, `gpg.program`.
- **Who signs:** an unencrypted ed25519 key in the process; everything else through `ssh-keygen -Y sign` or `gpg`.
- **Also signed when on:** merge commits made by `pull` and `branch merge`, `history revert --as-commit`, `vault ignore --apply`.
- **A signing failure stops the commit** and says how to commit without a signature.

### The line differ is Git's (BR-2, BR-3)

- `Vault__Line_Diff` is now a port of Git's xdiff (the pre-pass that sets lines aside, `xdl_split` and its cost heuristics), and `compact` gains Git's indent heuristic where Git uses it.
- **What changes for users:** a few merges that used to be clean now stop with markers, exactly where `git merge-file` stops. The patch text of some diffs, the boundaries of some `commit -p` hunks and blame on repeated lines move to Git's placement.

## Compatibility {#compat}

- **No gate, no new minimum client, no format change for a vault that nobody signs in.** An unsigned commit is stored as before.
- **Old clients and CLI-signed commits:** a vault with four commits signed by the CLI (SSH and OpenPGP) among six others was cloned by 0.20.0, 0.24.0, 0.26.0, 0.26.6 and 0.26.11. Each: fsck ok, 10 of 10 clone signatures verified, a commit on top, a push.
- **Old vaults** made by 0.20.0, 0.24.0 and 0.26.0 (normal and pack) open in 0.26.11, take a commit and a push, and the old client pulls it back.
- **The web UI** (W-1): the CLI team states that the web UI never verifies commit signatures and ignores members it does not know. **I could not test it.** If that holds, W-1 is answered; ask the web UI team to confirm with one signed vault before 0.27.0.

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good. BR-2 and BR-3 are closed.**


### BR-8 (low): a failed signing says "nothing was written", but two objects were {#br-8}

- On each failed `commit -S`, the blob and the tree are already written; the commit object and the ref are not. The object count rose by 2 per failure (3 on a success), five failures in a row left ten unreferenced objects.
- They are harmless (fsck is clean) but the message is not exact. Either say "no commit was made", or sign before storing the tree. The error also repeats its prefix: `gpg: gpg: signing failed: No secret key`.

# sgit-ai 0.26.3: Git-parity phase 0, merges made safe, and dev builds on PyPI, cli.sgit.ai

> Dev build of 28 October 2026, from the CLI's dev at 16c46e89, and the first published as a plain version. It fixes the bugs the seven Git-parity designs found. sgit commit during an unresolved merge put the .conflict files into the vault; it now refuses. status shows a merge in progress. Identical content on both sides is no longer a conflict. Merges and pushes on forks deeper than 200 commits work. A nested vault is never committed. Object files are written atomically. Merges, writes and sparse commits rebuild only the changed folders. From this build, every dev merge is published as X.Y.N, and a plain pip install takes the newest. Reviewed by cli.build. 4,921 tests pass and every fix held, including a 250-commit fork that 0.26.1 merged against an empty base. Maturity good. One decision for Dinis Cruz: plain installs now get dev builds (BR-4).

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-3.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# sgit-ai 0.26.3

```text
┌─ sgit-ai 0.26.3 ── dev build ── 28 Oct 2026, 11:02 UTC ─────────────────────────
│ tag v0.26.3 = 16c46e89 (dev) · PyPI package == tag · the first plain X.Y.N
│ fixed   commit in a merge · status · equal content · deep forks · nested vault
│ tests   4,921 unit+security ✓ · M1–M5 ✓ · 250-deep fork: 0.26.1 ✗ → 0.26.3 ✓
│ decide  BR-4: a plain install now takes dev builds
│ maturity  ########--  good
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

## What is new {#new}

From the [Git-parity designs](../research/git-parity-designs-index.md). These fix bugs in today's code and ship before any new feature.

- **`sgit commit` during an unresolved merge** used to go ahead as a single-parent commit. Every teammate who pulled received the `.conflict` copies. It now refuses, naming each file and the way out:
  - edit the file and delete its `.conflict` copy;
  - `sgit resolve <file> --ours` or `--theirs`;
  - `sgit merge-abort`.

  `--amend` refuses too.
- **`sgit status` shows a merge in progress:** which files are still conflicted, which are resolved, and how to finish or abandon it.
- **One rule for "an operation is in progress".** During a merge with conflicts, `write`, `vault stash`, `branch switch` and `branch checkout` are refused by name, as Git refuses them.
- **The same content on both sides is no longer a conflict.** Blobs are encrypted with a random IV, so two clones writing the same bytes used to get different ids. Now equal hash and size select the candidates, and the decrypted bytes decide.
- **Forks deeper than 200 commits.** The merge base and the ahead/behind counts looked at 200 ancestors at most. On a deeper fork a pull merged against an empty base, and a push more than 200 commits ahead was rejected as diverged. A commit graph (Git's paint-down walk) removes the cap.
- **A nested vault is never committed.** A folder holding its own `.sg_vault` is skipped, as Git skips a nested repository, and `status` names it (TM-F38).
- **Atomic object writes** (TM-F39).
- **Merges, `sgit write` of one file, and sparse commits build only the changed folders.** The CLI team measured 3.13 s → 0.13 s on 10,000 files in 10,222 folders.
- **Dev builds on PyPI as plain versions,** and `sgit update --stable`. See [Which build you get](../builds/index.md#channels).

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good.** Every fix held. The deep-fork fix is real: at 250 commits on each side, 0.26.1 conflicts on every file both sides changed, and this build merges cleanly.

```text
┌─ checks on the PyPI package 0.26.3 ───────────────────────────────────────────────
│ ✓ M1  commit during a merge: refused (Vault__Merge_Unresolved_Error)
│ ✓ M2  status: merge_in_progress, merge_conflicts, merge_markers, …
│ ✓ M3  the same bytes on both sides: no .conflict
│ ✓ M4  fork 250 deep each side, pushed 50 at a time: clean, both changes applied
│ ✓ M5  a clone nested in the working copy: never reaches the vault
│       fork, 250 deep:   0.26.1  ✗ a/x.txt=0, 2 conflicts    0.26.3  ✓ a/x.txt=250
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

The M4 check pushes 50 commits at a time. One push of 250 hits a different bug, which is in every build: [BR-1](../builds/0-26-6.md#br-1).

### BR-4 (decision): a plain `pip install sgit-ai` now installs dev builds {#br-4}

- **What the code does.** From this build, dev builds go to PyPI as plain versions, so PyPI's "latest" is the newest dev build: 0.26.6 today. `pip install sgit-ai` and `sgit update` install it, and the CLI's README says so.
- **The conflict with the stated intent.** If the intent is that a plain install gets the release and agents opt in to dev builds, this does the opposite. Every agent that runs `sgit update` is on a dev build an hour after it merges.
- **The two ways out:**
  - **Keep it.** Dev builds are tested before they publish, and a plain install has the newest fixes. State it on every release page, and pin releases with `==X.Y.0` or `sgit update --stable` where stability matters.
  - **Make dev builds pre-releases again,** as `0.26.1.dev0` and `0.26.2.dev0` were. A plain install then gets `X.Y.0`, and `pip install --pre sgit-ai` or `sgit update --pre` gets dev. Pip ignores pre-releases unless asked, so this is the only way PyPI can serve both.

*Scripts: `check_build.py`, `deep_fork.py` (`BATCH=50 python -I deep_fork.py 150 250`). All builds: [the builds page](../builds/index.md).*

# sgit-ai 0.26.4: commit messages up to 64 KB, cli.sgit.ai

> Dev build of 28 October 2026, from the CLI's dev at c495b40e. A commit message longer than 740 bytes used to fail with a raw ValueError, after the commit's blobs and trees were written; Git has no limit. The default limit stays 740 bytes, now refused before anything is written. A vault with the long-messages feature takes up to 64 KiB, and every client reads messages up to 1 MiB, the web UI's. Turning the feature on raises the vault's gate to 0.26.4, so an older sgit is told to update. Reviewed by cli.build. All checks held, including the refusal of 0.26.0 and 0.26.3 clients with a clear message. Maturity good. Wait for the 0.27.0 release before turning long-messages on in a vault that agents on 0.26.0 still use.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-4.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# sgit-ai 0.26.4

```text
┌─ sgit-ai 0.26.4 ── dev build ── 28 Oct 2026, 11:07 UTC ─────────────────────────
│ tag v0.26.4 = c495b40e (dev) · PyPI package == tag
│ new     messages up to 64 KiB with the long-messages feature; read up to 1 MiB
│ tests   L1 ✓ L2 ✓ · the gate refuses 0.26.0 and 0.26.3 with "run sgit update"
│ maturity  ########--  good
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

## What is new {#new}

- **The 740-byte limit was a bug.** The encrypted message shared a 1,024-character base64 field with a tree entry's name. A 741-byte message failed with a raw `ValueError`, after the commit's blobs and trees were written. Git has no limit.
- **Reading:** every client from this build accepts messages up to 1 MiB. The web UI writes messages with no cap, and a longer one made the commit unreadable to the CLI: `log`, `clone` and `pull` failed past it.
- **Writing:**
  - 740 bytes stays the default, so vaults older clients use are unaffected;
  - over the limit, the commit is refused before anything is written, with the size in UTF-8 bytes and how to raise it;
  - `sgit vault format --feature long-messages` lets a vault take up to 64 KiB, and raises its minimum client to 0.26.4.

```text
$ sgit vault format --feature long-messages       # gate becomes 0.26.4
$ sgit commit -m "$(cat long-design-note.md)"     # up to 65,536 bytes
```

## Compatibility {#compat}

A vault with `long-messages` refuses clients before 0.26.4. Checked with 0.26.0 and 0.26.3, which both stop with:

```text
Vault__Client_Too_Old_Error: this vault needs sgit-ai >= 0.26.4 and this is 0.26.3: run `sgit update`, then try again
```

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good.** A real bug fixed: an error that wrote half a commit is now a clean refusal. The gate works as designed.

```text
┌─ checks on the PyPI package 0.26.4 ─────────────────────────────────────────────
│ ✓ L1  741-byte message, no feature: refused, objects on disk unchanged
│ ✓ L2  feature on: 65,536 bytes (100 of them é) committed, pushed, cloned;
│       min_client 0.26.4; 65,537 bytes refused
│ ✓     0.26.0 and 0.26.3 pulling that vault: refused, "run `sgit update`"
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

- **For whoever turns the feature on:** the gate is a dev build's version. Until 0.27.0 is released, a vault with `long-messages` refuses every agent that stays on the release (0.26.0, or `sgit update --stable`). Turn it on in shared vaults after 0.27.0.
- **Not tested:** a message written by the web UI over 64 KiB and read by the CLI (the 1 MiB read path).

# sgit-ai 0.26.5: line-level merge, opt-in, cli.sgit.ai

> Dev build of 28 October 2026, from the CLI's dev at 43e1889c. sgit pull --merge lines and sgit branch merge --merge lines merge a file both sides changed line by line, as Git does, with Git's conflict markers in the file and --conflict diff3 for the base too. The default does not change: whole-file .conflict copies. Reviewed by cli.build. 5,030 tests pass and the four end-to-end checks hold. In 18,000 random merges against git merge-file, all 8,925 with unique lines were byte-identical. Where lines repeat, 2 of 4,544 code-like merges came out clean where Git reports a conflict (BR-2), and 0.9% placed conflict blocks differently (BR-3). Maturity good for an opt-in feature: review line-merged files before pushing.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-5.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# sgit-ai 0.26.5

```text
┌─ sgit-ai 0.26.5 ── dev build ── 28 Oct 2026, 11:25 UTC ─────────────────────────
│ tag v0.26.5 = 43e1889c (dev) · PyPI package == tag
│ new     pull --merge lines · branch merge --merge lines · --conflict diff3
│ tests   5,030 unit+security ✓ · X1–X4 ✓ · 18,000 merges vs git merge-file
│ open    BR-2 (medium, opt-in) · BR-3 (low) · BR-1 (all builds) · R3-1
│ maturity  #######---  good for an opt-in: read line-merged files before a push
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

## What is new {#new}

Git-parity item 2.1, from [design 01](../research/git-parity-design-line-merge.md).

```text
$ sgit pull --merge lines                         # line by line, for files both sides changed
$ sgit pull --merge lines --conflict diff3        # markers carry the base version too
$ sgit branch merge feature --merge lines
$ export SGIT_MERGE_STYLE=lines                   # per session; or merge_style in .sg_vault/local/config.json
```

- **How a file both sides changed is merged:**
  - changes to different lines merge cleanly;
  - lines both sides changed get Git's markers in the file: `<<<<<<< ours (this clone …)`, `=======`, `>>>>>>> theirs (current …)`.
- **Only files both sides changed are line-merged,** so work in separate folders costs nothing more.
- **Fall back to the whole-file `.conflict`, and the pull says why:**
  - binary files;
  - files over 8 MiB;
  - versions this clone does not hold.
- **Resolving a conflict:**
  - edit the markers out and `sgit commit`; commit refuses while a marker block remains;
  - `sgit resolve <file> --ours` or `--theirs` takes one side;
  - `sgit resolve <file>` marks a hand edit as resolved.
- **The default is unchanged:** without the flag, a pull keeps yours and writes theirs to `<file>.conflict`, as before and as the web UI does. The flag wins over the session and the clone setting.
- **Safety:**
  - an uncommitted edit to a file that would get markers refuses the pull before anything is written;
  - marker labels come from vault data and can never start a line;
  - marker files are written through the path guard.

## Compatibility {#compat}

No format change and no gate. A line-merged result is an ordinary commit, which every client reads.

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good for an opt-in feature.**
- On unique lines, the engine is Git's: every one of 8,925 random merges was byte-identical to `git merge-file -p`, in both styles.
- Where lines repeat, as `}`, blank lines and `return x;` do in code, it can occasionally disagree with Git about whether two changes touch.
- In 2 of 4,544 code-like merges, that turned a Git conflict into a silent clean merge (BR-2).
- **Agents using `--merge lines` should read the merged files before pushing,** as they would review any merge.

```text
┌─ line merge vs git merge-file · 18,000 random three-way merges, 4 seeds ─────────────
│ verdict                          unique     code-like   3-letter alphabet
│ byte-identical                    8,925        4,501         4,209
│ both conflict, blocks differ          0           41           258    ── BR-3
│ sgit conflict, git clean              0            0            36
│ sgit clean, git conflict              0            2            23    ── BR-2
│ both clean, bytes differ              0            0             5
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
│ ✓ X1 different lines merge   ✓ X2 markers; commit refuses   ✓ X3 default unchanged
│ ✓ X4 an edit that would get markers refuses the pull, edit kept
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  code-like: 60% of lines from {"}", "", "{", "    return x;", "    i++;", "else", …}
  3-letter: every line is a, b or c, the worst case for any line differ
```

### BR-2 (medium, opt-in): a clean merge where Git reports a conflict, when lines repeat {#br-2}

**Why it happens:**
- The engine is a port of xdiff's merge, run on sgit's own Myers differ, plus Git's change compaction.
- When the changed region is surrounded by repeated lines, the two differs can place a change one line apart.
- Changes that touch in Git's placement then do not touch in sgit's, so sgit merges where Git asks.
- The CHANGELOG's claim is scoped correctly ("byte-identical … on random merges of unique lines"). The property agents care about is different: "sgit never merges silently what Git would ask about". That one does not hold.

**One of the two code-like cases,** seed 4, diff3:

```text
base                ours                       theirs
line 34408          line 34413                 line 34408
{                   line 34412                 {
end                 {                          end
if (a) {            if (a) {                   if (a) {
line 34409          line 34408
                    {
                    end
                    line 34409
                    line 34414
                    if (a) {

git merge-file: a conflict around "line 34409"; theirs deleted it, ours moved "if (a) {" past it
sgit:           clean, = ours, so "line 34409", which theirs deleted, is still there
```

Either reading is a valid alignment. Git's is the one users expect.

**For the CLI team's agent,** in order of cost:
1. **Conservative rule.** Treat two one-sided changes as touching when the base lines between them, or within one line of them, are not unique in the base. A clean result then needs unambiguous context. It costs a few more conflicts and no silent merges. Re-run [`fuzz_line_merge.py`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Cli/tree/dev/admin/research/builds-0-26-x-2026-10-28/scripts): the target is 0 in the "sgit clean, git conflict" row.
2. **Exact placement.** Port the rest of xdiff's diff (`xdl_recs_cmp` with its split heuristics and `XDF_NEED_MINIMAL` off), so that hunks land where Git puts them on repeated lines too. More work, and it also closes BR-3.
3. **Add the repeated-line generators** (the "code" and "tiny" kinds in the fuzzer) to the CLI's own tests against `git merge-file`.

### BR-3 (low): conflict blocks drawn differently from Git's {#br-3}

Where both report a conflict, the blocks differ in 41 of 4,544 code-like merges (0.9%): where a block starts and ends, or how many blocks there are. The content is not lost either way. Exact placement (BR-2, option 2) fixes this too.

*Scripts: `fuzz_line_merge.py <seed> <cases> [merge|diff3]`, `check_build.py`. Results: `results/lm_*.json` with up to three samples per verdict, and `results/check_0.26.5.json`. All builds: [the builds page](../builds/index.md).*

# sgit-ai 0.26.6: commit some paths, commit some hunks, push with uncommitted changes, cli.sgit.ai

> Dev build of 28 October 2026, from the CLI's dev at 036e33b5, and what a plain pip install gives today. sgit commit takes paths, as git commit -- paths does, and leaves every other change on disk. sgit commit -p picks hunks interactively; agents use --list-hunks and --hunk ID, with ids that refuse to pick a different hunk once the file has changed. sgit push no longer refuses uncommitted changes. One behaviour change for scripts: with -m, extra words are now paths. Reviewed by cli.build. 5,144 unit and security tests pass. commit with paths matched Git in 40 random cases, and hunk commits matched git apply --cached in 60. Maturity good. One high finding, in every build since at least 0.26.0: a push of more than 100 commits leaves a gap in the host's history (BR-1).

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-6.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

```text
$ pip install sgit-ai==0.26.6        # or: sgit update, which takes the newest build
$ sgit version
sgit-ai v0.26.6
```

## What is new {#new}

This build is Git-parity item 2.3, from [design 03](../research/git-parity-design-partial-commits.md). With 0.26.5's line merge, it closes the two gaps that mattered most in daily use.

### Commit only some paths

```text
$ sgit commit -m "fix the intro" docs/intro.md src/      # only these; everything else stays uncommitted
$ sgit commit "fix the intro" -- docs/intro.md           # the same, message first
$ sgit commit -m "docs" "*.md"                           # * crosses / as in Git
$ sgit commit -m "rm" old.txt --json                     # a deleted file, named, is committed as a deletion
```

- **What it commits:** HEAD's tree with only the named paths taken from the working copy, as `git commit <pathspec>` does. The output lists what stays uncommitted.
- **Folders, files and patterns:**
  - a folder takes every change under it;
  - a path is relative to the current folder;
  - **unlike Git,** naming a new file commits it, since sgit has no `add`.
- **Refused, with nothing written:**
  - a pattern that matches nothing refuses the commit;
  - a path commit during a merge is refused, as in Git.
- **`--json` prints one object:** `committed` (with `paths` and `left_uncommitted`), `nothing_to_commit`, or `refused`.

### Commit some hunks of a file

```text
$ sgit commit -p                                  # interactive: y n a d s j k q ?   (s splits a hunk)
$ sgit commit --list-hunks --json notes.md        # agents: every hunk with an id
$ sgit commit -m "first fix" --hunk 3f9c… --hunk 81ab…
```

- **Ids come from the hunk's content and base, not its position.** An id listed before the file or HEAD changed is refused (exit 2) and nothing is written.
- **The working copy is never written.** The hunks not committed show as uncommitted changes.
- **The same hunks as Git:** headers match `git diff -U3`, and any subset gives the bytes `git apply --cached` gives.
- **Committed whole, as one hunk:** binary files, new files, deleted files and files over 8 MiB.

### `sgit push` with uncommitted changes

- **It pushes your commits** and says how many changes stay local. It used to refuse, or offer to commit them.
- **The implicit pull still protects the working copy:**
  - an edit that the incoming commits do not touch is kept;
  - one they would change refuses the push before anything is written.

### A behaviour change for scripts

- `sgit commit "fix typo"` still commits everything.
- **With `-m`, other words are now paths**, as in Git. `sgit commit -m x y` used to ignore `y`; now it fails if `y` is not a file.
- Two words without `-m` is a usage error that shows both correct forms.

## Compatibility {#compat}

- **Nothing changes in the vault format, and there is no new gate.** A commit made with paths or hunks is an ordinary commit.
- **Checked:** 0.26.0 and 0.26.3 clone, pull and push against a vault where 0.26.6 committed by path and by hunk. Both read the same trees, and a file left uncommitted by 0.26.6 stays local.

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good.**
- Every claim of this build held, including the two checked against Git as the oracle.
- Use it, including for agents.
- One high finding is not this build's own: it is in every build tested, 0.26.0 to 0.26.6 (BR-1).
- Until it is fixed, **push at least once every 100 commits.**

```text
┌─ checks on the PyPI package 0.26.6 ───────────────────────────────────────────────
│ ✓ C1  commit <paths> vs `git add -A -- <paths>; git commit`   40 random cases, 0 diff
│ ✓ C2  hunk subsets vs `git apply --cached`, headers vs -U3     60 cases, 0 diff
│ ✓ C3  a stale hunk id is refused; HEAD and objects unchanged
│ ✓ C4  push with an uncommitted edit: commits pushed, edit kept
│ ✓ C5  incoming commit would change an edited file: push refused, edit kept
│ ✓     everything from 0.26.1–0.26.5 (G1–G2, M1–M5, L1–L2, X1–X4) still holds
│ ✓     cross-version with 0.26.0 and 0.26.3, both directions
│ ✗ P1  one push of 150 commits: fresh clone's fsck fails  ── BR-1, below
│ ✗     R3-1 unchanged: 64 bad offsets after compaction of a 0.25.0 vault
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### BR-1 (high, every build since at least 0.26.0): a push of more than 100 commits leaves a gap on the host {#br-1}

**What happens.**
- `Vault__Sync__Push` collects the commits to upload with `Vault__Fetch.fetch_commit_chain(…, limit=100)`.
- Push calls it from two places (`Vault__Sync__Push.py:252` and `:666`) without passing a limit, so a push of 101 or more new commits uploads only the newest 100, with their trees and blobs.
- The ref moves to the new head. The older commits exist only in the pushing clone.
- **The gap never fills.** The next push stops at the remote head.

```text
one push of N commits, then one more push; a fresh clone walks the history and runs fsck
  ✓ N=100  walks  102 of 102 commits   fsck ok
  ✓ N=101  walks  103 of 103 commits   fsck ok        (100 new + the later push)
  ✗ N=102  walks  101 of 104 commits   fsck: missing 1
  ✗ N=151  walks  101 of 153 commits   fsck: missing 1   (normal and pack vaults alike)
```

**What it breaks:**
- a fresh clone's `check fsck`;
- `history log` past the gap;
- every merge whose base lies behind the gap. A teammate with their own commits who pulls gets a merge against an empty base: every file both sides touched conflicts, and the pushing side's change is not applied. My first deep-fork test failed this way at 101 commits, before I separated the two causes. 0.26.3's merge-base fix is real (M4 passes when pushes are at most 50 commits).
- **If the pushing clone is deleted, those commits are lost.**

**How likely:** an agent that commits often and pushes rarely, a long offline session, or `sgit write` in a loop.

**For the CLI team's agent:**
1. Drop the cap for push. Walk with the commit graph from 0.26.3 (`Vault__Commit_Graph`), stopping at the remote head's ancestors, with no limit. The stop set is capped at 100 too.
2. Before moving the ref, check that every uploaded commit's parents are either in the upload set or already on the host.
3. Give an existing gap a repair path. The pushing clone still holds the commits, so `sgit push` (or `check fsck --repair` on that clone) could upload the missing ancestors.
4. The repro is [`push_gap.py`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Cli/tree/dev/admin/research/builds-0-26-x-2026-10-28/scripts): `python -I push_gap.py 100 101 150`, with `PACKS=1` for a pack vault.

### Also noted

- **The `-m` change** is right, and Git's rule. Say it in the release notes for 0.27.0: a script that passed extra words after `-m` now fails loudly instead of committing everything.
- **Not tested here:** `-p` interactively (it needs a terminal), and hooks (not built).

*Scripts: [`check_build.py`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Cli/tree/dev/admin/research/builds-0-26-x-2026-10-28/scripts), `push_gap.py`, `xstep.py`. Results: `results/check_0.26.6.json`, `results/suite-v0.26.6.txt`. All builds: [the builds page](../builds/index.md).*

---

*[Site index for agents](../llms.txt) · [HTML version](https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-6.html)*


# sgit-ai 0.26.7: verify the signer's own SSH or OpenPGP signature on commits and tags, cli.sgit.ai

> Dev build of 28 October 2026, from the CLI's dev at 0d486aaf. A commit or tag can carry its signer's own SSH or OpenPGP signature (user_signature, Git's gpgsig) beside the per-clone signature every commit already has, and this build checks them, with Git's verdicts and Git's trust files. sgit check verify, history log --show-signature, history show --show-signature and vault tag show report them. Nothing in the CLI can make one yet (sgit commit -S was written and parked until the web UI confirms the signing-bytes rule). Reviewed by cli.build. 5,235 unit and security tests pass. Old vaults and old clients are untouched; 0.26.0, 0.26.3 and 0.26.6 read, verify, fsck and push over commits that carry the new member. Maturity good. BR-1 is still open.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/builds/0-26-7.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

# sgit-ai 0.26.7

```text
│ tag v0.26.7 = 0d486aaf (dev) · PyPI package == tag · a plain install gets this
│ new     user signatures verified: check verify · history log/show --show-signature · tag show
│ not     nothing makes them: commit -S / sgit.gpgSign are parked until the web UI confirms
│ tests   5,235 unit+security ✓ · 18/18 end-to-end ✓ · 0.26.0/.3/.6 read signed commits ✓
│ open    BR-1 (high, every build) · R3-1 · W-1 (a question for the web UI)
│ maturity  #######---  good: use it; it changes what you can see, not what you can write
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

```text
$ pip install sgit-ai==0.26.7        # or: sgit update, which takes the newest build
$ sgit version
sgit-ai v0.26.7
```

## What is new {#new}

This build is the first half of Git-parity item 2.2, signing with your own key, from [design 02](../research/git-parity-roadmap.md). It is the half that **reads**.

### A second signature on a commit or tag

- **Every commit already has a per-clone signature:** the clone's own key signs the commit, and `sgit check verify` checks it.
- **A commit or tag can now also carry `user_signature`:** the signer's own SSH or OpenPGP signature, Git's `gpgsig`.
  - It covers the same bytes as the clone signature, and neither covers the other.
  - Either can be checked, or removed, alone.
  - **An unsigned commit is stored byte for byte as before:** the member is left out when it is empty.

### Trust is yours, as in Git

- **The settings come from your global Git config,** never from the vault or a repository's config, so nothing next to a vault can change what is trusted:
  - `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile`, `gpg.ssh.revocationFile`, `gpg.minTrustLevel`, `gpg.format`, `user.signingKey`;
  - your gpg keyring for OpenPGP.
- **Who checks what:**
  - SSH signatures are checked in the process: ed25519, ECDSA, RSA-SHA2 and FIDO `sk-` keys;
  - certificates, `cert-authority` lines and revocation lists go to `ssh-keygen`;
  - OpenPGP goes to `gpg`.
- **The verdicts are Git's letters** (G U B X Y R E N), checked by the CLI team against `git log --format=%G?`.

### Where you see it

```text
$ sgit check verify
Checked 5 commit(s): 5 verified, 0 bad, 0 unsigned, 0 without a known key, 0 missing
User signatures: 1 good, 1 untrusted, 0 bad, 0 expired, 0 revoked, 0 cannot check, 3 none
$ sgit check verify --require-user-signature --json     # every commit must be good
$ sgit history log --show-signature
$ sgit history show HEAD --show-signature
$ sgit vault tag show v1                                  # names the tag's signer
```

- **`check verify` fails (exit 1) on a bad user signature.** An untrusted one does not fail, as `git verify-commit` does not.
- **`--require-user-signature`** fails unless every commit is good.
- **`--json`** is new on `check verify`: counts, `user_counts`, `user_by_status` and the first failure.
- **The wording is Git's:** `Good "git" signature for alice@example.com with ED25519 key SHA256:…`, `No principal matched.`

### What is not here

- **Nothing creates a user signature.** `sgit commit -S`, `sgit.gpgSign` and signing in `merge`, `write`, `revert` and `tag` were written (`0709aa86`) and then parked (`96120aa6`) until the vault web UI confirms the rule for the signed bytes (W-1 below).
- **So today `--show-signature` shows signatures that only a library caller can produce.** The CLI team's notes say this plainly; this page says it so that nobody looks for the flag.

## Compatibility {#compat}

- **Vaults and the host:** no new gate, no new minimum client, no change for a vault that never carries a user signature.
- **Old vaults:** unchanged. Vaults made by 0.20.0, 0.22.0, 0.24.0 and 0.26.0 (normal and pack mode) open in 0.26.8, fsck clean, and their old clients pull what the new build pushed.
- **Old clients and a signed commit:** checked by creating a vault with 0.26.8 that holds an unsigned, an SSH-signed and an OpenPGP-signed commit, then:

| Client | clone | fsck | clone signatures | push a commit | 0.26.8 pulls it |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.20.0 | ✓ | ok | 4 of 4 verified | ✓ | ✓, 5 of 5 verified |
| 0.22.0 | ✓ | ok | 4 of 4 verified | ✓ | ✓ |
| 0.24.0 | ✓ | ok | 4 of 4 verified | ✓ | ✓ |
| 0.26.0 | ✓ | ok | 4 of 4 verified | ✓ | ✓, 5 of 5 verified |
| 0.26.3 | ✓ | ok | 4 of 4 verified | ✓ | ✓ |
| 0.26.6 | ✓ | ok | 4 of 4 verified | ✓ | ✓ |

- **Why old clients are not bothered:** they load a commit into a typed object that does not know `user_signature`, so the member is dropped on load, and the bytes they check are the bytes that were signed.
- **That is also why the gate matters:** a reader that checks the clone signature over the raw JSON and removes only `signature` would call every signed commit **bad**. Python clients cannot do that by accident; the web UI is the open question (W-1).

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good.**
- Every claim of this build held, including the verdicts, the unchanged bytes of an unsigned commit and the compatibility with older clients.
- The build reads and checks; it never writes a signature, so it cannot damage a vault.
- One high finding is not this build's own: it is in every build tested (BR-1).

```text
┌─ checks on the PyPI package 0.26.7 ───────────────────────────────────────────────
│ ✓     package == tag v0.26.7 (only the version file differs); wheel == sdist
│ ✓     5,235 unit+security tests pass (38 skipped)
│ ✓     everything from 0.26.1–0.26.6 (G1–G2, M1–M5, L1–L2, X1–X4, C1–C5) still holds
│ ✓ S1  SSH signature (in-process key) and OpenPGP signature (gpg): checked by 0.26.8 as untrusted / good
│ ✓ S2  a signature over other bytes, and one with a flipped bit: both bad; clone signatures unaffected
│ ✓ S3  0.26.0, 0.26.3 and 0.26.6 clone, fsck, verify and push over signed commits
│ ✓ S4  vaults of 0.20.0 · 0.22.0 · 0.24.0 · 0.26.0, plain and pack: open, commit, push, old client pulls
│ ✗ P1  one push of 150 commits: fresh clone's fsck fails  ── BR-1, unchanged from 0.26.6
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### Code read {#code}

The diff against 0.26.6 is 14 changed code files and new ones: `crypto/signing/` (19 modules), `Vault__User_Signatures`, four new schemas and eleven new safe types. Read: the runner, the config reader and resolver, both signers, the commit and tag writers, the verification walk and the CLI wiring.

- **Running programs is done in one place** (`Signing__Command_Runner`): argument lists only, never a shell; bytes on stdin; the working folder is the home folder, never the vault; the environment is a short list (agent sockets, `GNUPGHOME`, Git's own config variables) plus `LC_ALL=C`; a missing program is code 127 and a timeout code 124. Nothing from the vault reaches a command line.
- **The key and the program come from your global Git config only.** A repository's config and the vault are not read, so a cloned vault cannot choose which program runs.
- **A signing key beginning with `-`** cannot become an option: it is always the value of `-f` or `-bsu`.
- **The temporary file for a literal SSH key** is made with `O_EXCL` and mode 0600 in a fresh folder and removed afterwards.
- **A signer checks its own output** before returning it, and a failure stops before anything is stored.
- **The stored bytes:** `stored_json` drops an empty `user_signature`, so an unsigned commit and tag are byte-identical to the format before.
- **One small thing:** `sgit.gpgSign` is the switch, not Git's `commit.gpgSign`, on purpose (an existing setting must not make agents start signing after an upgrade). Say so in the release notes when signing ships.

### W-1 (a question for the web UI, before signing ships) {#w-1}

- **The rule:** the bytes covered by either signature are the commit's JSON without `signature` and without `user_signature`, keys sorted, no spaces, UTF-8.
- **Why it needs the web UI:** if it checks the per-clone signature, it must remove `user_signature` too. If it removes only `signature`, a vault with signed commits shows bad signatures in the web UI.
- **What I could not test:** the web UI. It is not in this repository, and a vault with signed commits needs a real host to load there.
- **A fixture for them:** `scripts/xsign.py new-create` builds a vault with an unsigned, an SSH-signed and an OpenPGP-signed commit; the CLI team can push one to a test host for the web UI to open.
- **Update:** the CLI team un-parked signing in 0.26.10 on that statement. Ask the web UI team for one test with a signed vault.

### Also noted

- **The CLI team's brief for this review names `check verify --user`.** The build has no such flag: user signatures are always counted when a commit carries one, and `--require-user-signature` makes them mandatory. The brief and the CHANGELOG should agree with the build.
- **The BR-1 fix** (0.26.9) and signing itself (0.26.10) came after this build; see [0.26.9](../builds/0-26-9.md) and [0.26.10](../builds/0-26-10.md). W-1: the CLI team says the web UI never verifies commit signatures and ignores members it does not know; not tested by me.
- **The clone key and the signer's key are different things.** `check verify` says "verified" for the clone signature and reports user signatures on their own line. A reader may read "verified" as "signed by a person"; the release notes for 0.27.0 should say it does not.
- **Not tested here:** `ssh-keygen` as the signer or verifier (not installed on the test machine; the in-process path was used), certificates, KRLs, FIDO keys, and a passphrase-protected key.

*Scripts: [`xsign.py`](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Cli/tree/dev/admin/research/builds-0-26-7-0-26-8-2026-10-28/scripts), `sig_tamper.py`, `legacy_vault.py`, `push_gap.py`. Results: `results/check_0.26.7.json`, `results/suite-v0.26.7.txt`, `results/xsign_signed_commits_old_clients.txt`, `results/sig_tamper_0.26.8.txt`, `results/legacy_vaults_0.20.0_to_0.26.0.txt`. All builds: [the builds page](../builds/index.md).*

```text
│ maturity  ########--  good: use it; read BR-5 if a script tests grep's exit code
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

```text
$ pip install sgit-ai==0.26.8        # or: sgit update, which takes the newest build
$ sgit version
sgit-ai v0.26.8
```

## What is new {#new}

This build is design 04 of the [Git-parity roadmap](../research/git-parity-roadmap.md): reading history the way Git does. It adds no vault format and no gate.

### Blame

```text
$ sgit history blame -L 10,+5 src/app.py          # who last changed each line
$ sgit history blame HEAD~3 docs/guide.md          # as of a revision
$ sgit history blame --porcelain notes.md          # Git's machine format
$ sgit history blame --json notes.md               # history_blame_v1
```

- **Each line is attributed to the commit that last changed it,** through renames and merges.
- **Options as in Git:** `-L N,M`, `N,+K`, `N,-K`, `/regex/,+K` (repeatable), `-w`, `--first-parent`, `-s`, `--abbrev`, `--porcelain`, `--line-porcelain`. Also `--json`, `-e` (the signing key id in place of the branch name) and `--text` (a binary file, line by line).
- **The author is the commit's branch name,** dates are UTC, and a boundary (the root, a shallow clone's edge) is marked `^`.

### Search

```text
$ sgit grep -n -i todo                              # the working copy (an uncommitted edit is what is searched)
$ sgit grep -n todo HEAD~5 -- '*.py'                # a revision, decrypted in memory: HEAD~5:path:line:text
$ sgit history log -S needle --oneline              # commits where the count of "needle" changes
$ sgit history log -G 'def \w+' --file src/ -n 5    # commits whose diff adds or removes a matching line
```

- **`sgit grep` takes Git's options** (`-i -w -v -n -c -l -L -o -q -h -H -I -a -F -e -A -B -C -m`) and exit codes: 0 a match, 1 none, 2 an error. `grep` is a new top-level command; `sgit file grep` is the same.
- **The pattern is a Python regular expression** (see [BR-6](#br-6)); it goes through the same guard as `--grep`: at most 1,000 characters, valid, and no repetition of a repetition.
- **A path from the vault is quoted as Git quotes it** (`"jos\303\251.md"`), so a file name cannot forge an output line.
- **`log -S` and `-G`** combine with `--file`, `--grep`, `--since`, `--until`, `--author`, `-n`, `--oneline` and `--stat`; `--pickaxe-regex` and `-i` as in Git. They stop at the `-n`-th match.

### Renames, found as Git finds them

- **`history show`, `history diff` and `history log` (`--files`, `--patch`, `--json`)** report `R096  docs/guide.md -> manual/guide-v2.md`, and in a patch Git's `similarity index`, `rename from`, `rename to` header. On by default.
- **The detection is a port of Git's:** exact, then same basename, then a similarity matrix.
- **Options as in Git:** `-M[<n>]` (`-M90`, `-M90%`, `-M0.9`), `--no-renames`, `-l` / `--rename-limit`.
- **`sgit history log --file <path> --follow`** continues past a rename.

### Faster, and a patch that is `git diff`'s

- **`history show`, `history diff` and `history log --patch` open only the folders whose ids differ** and decrypt only the changed files. The CLI team measured a 3,000-file vault with one change at 439 ms and 6,000 decrypted blobs before, and 7 ms and 2 after.
- **The patch text is `git diff`'s, byte for byte,** including `\ No newline at end of file`. The old output glued the last line of a file with no final newline to the next `+` line.
- **A re-encrypted file whose bytes did not change** is no longer listed as modified.

### Changes for scripts and agents {#script-changes}

| What | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `history log --json`, `history show --json`, `history diff --json` | a renamed file is in `files_added` and `files_deleted` | it is in `files_renamed` (`old_path`, `new_path`, `score`, `exact`, `lines_added`, `lines_removed`); `--no-renames` restores the old lists |
| patch text | the old format | `git diff`'s |
| `history log --stat` | a rename shown as `R old -> new` | the same, preferring a same-basename source, as Git does |

- **A script that reads `files_added` to find new files** now misses a renamed file. That is correct, and it will be noticed only if the script is run on a history that has a rename.

## Compatibility {#compat}

- **No change to the vault format, and no new gate.** Everything here reads; nothing writes a new kind of object.
- **Checked on old vaults** made by 0.20.0, 0.22.0, 0.24.0 and 0.26.0 (pack mode too, from 0.24.0), each opened by 0.26.8:
  - the old working copy: status, fsck, a commit and a push;
  - a fresh clone: fsck clean, every commit's signature verified, the same tree;
  - the old client pulls what 0.26.8 pushed, and its fsck is clean.
- **Blame (through a rename), grep and `-S`** gave the right answers on the vaults of 0.20.0 and 0.24.0 (pack mode).

## Review by cli.build {#review}

**Verdict: good.**
- The new commands matched Git, used as the oracle, on every case I built, and where they differ the difference is a documented design choice (BR-6, BR-7).
- The hostile inputs I tried were refused or quoted: a pattern that backtracks without end, a quote or non-ASCII characters in a name (a newline in a name is rewritten to `_` by the vault, and `sgit ls` prints it raw, see below), a path outside the vault, a binary file.
- One finding changes a script's exit code (BR-5). One high finding is not this build's own (BR-1).
