# Roadmap: feature parity with Git, then more on top (28 Oct 2026), cli.sgit.ai

> The CLI team's roadmap to parity with Git the client, then more on top: what sgit already matches, the client-side gaps in three priorities with sizes (line merge, own-key signing, partial commits first), signing the way Git does it, and GitHub's features moved to a future server, SGitHub. Every new feature off by default.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/git-parity-roadmap.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/036e33b5280e209804fbfd5fc6633c1cbc1a7af3/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/28/roadmap__git-parity.md>.*

---
# Roadmap: feature parity with Git, then more on top (28 Oct 2026)

**The message:** sgit does just about everything Git does, and then more on top. Git, the client, is the bar.
GitHub's features (accounts, verified badges, protected branches, review, CI) belong to a future server product
("SGitHub"), not to the CLI.

**Follows:** `review__article-what-sgit-does-that-git-does-not.md` (same folder). That review mixed Git and GitHub
features, and proposed an owner-signed signer registry for TM-R01. Under this scope, that registry moves to
SGitHub (section 4). Signing becomes what Git does: sign with the key you already have, and let each verifier
decide whom to trust.

**Extension rule:** every new feature is off by default and changes nothing for vaults and clients that don't use
it. It is on through a setting, either local or a vault feature (`sgit vault format --feature …`, the mechanism
`packs` and `signatures-required` already use). Only a feature that old clients would get *wrong* sets a minimum
client version.

---

## 1. Already at parity

These Git commands already have an sgit equivalent.

**Working with a clone**

| Git | sgit |
|---|---|
| `clone`, `--depth`, `fetch --unshallow` | `clone`, `--depth N`, `fetch --unshallow` |
| partial clone + `sparse-checkout` | `clone --path` (repeatable), `fetch <folder>` to widen, `clone --sparse` |
| `clone --no-checkout`, `--bare` | `clone --no-checkout`, `checkout <paths>` / `--since-pull` / `--changed-since` / `--all`; `clone --bare` |
| `status`, `commit`, `commit --amend` | `status`, `commit`, `commit --amend` |
| `push`, `pull`, `fetch`, `push --force-with-lease` | the same |
| `remote` | `remote` |
| `.gitignore` | `.gitignore` (read as is) |
| `stash` | `vault stash` |

**Branches, tags and merges**

| Git | sgit |
|---|---|
| `branch`, `switch`, `checkout <commit>` | `branch new/list/switch/rename/checkout` |
| `merge` | `branch merge` (whole-file: see 2.1) |
| `merge --abort` | `merge-abort` |
| conflict resolution | `resolve` |
| `tag -s` (signed), `tag -v` | `vault tag create/list/show/delete` (signed, verified) |

**History**

| Git | sgit |
|---|---|
| `log`, `--grep`, `--since`, `--until`, `--author`, `--stat`, `-p`, `-- <file>`, `--graph`, `--oneline` | `history log` with the same filters |
| `diff`, `show` | `history diff`, `history show` |
| `reflog` | `history reflog` |
| `reset --hard` | `history reset` |
| `revert` | `history revert --as-commit` |
| (no single command) | `history undo` |
| `HEAD~2`, `HEAD^2`, short ids, tag names | the same revision syntax |

**Integrity and plumbing**

| Git | sgit |
|---|---|
| `fsck` | `check fsck` |
| `verify-commit` (one commit) | `check verify` (every commit to HEAD) |
| `commit-graph`, pack indexes | index packs (0.26.0) |
| packs, kept packs (`fetch.unpackLimit`) | pack vaults, `clone --pack-store` |
| `hash-object` / `commit-tree` plumbing | `write --file … --also … --push --json` (atomic commit of named files) |
| `bundle` / `file://` remotes | `--transport local`, `vault backup` / `restore` |
| dumb HTTP | `--transport static` |

## 2. Gaps: Git has it, sgit doesn't yet (the CLI roadmap)

All of these run on the client in Git too. None needs a server change.

### Priority 1

| # | Feature | Git | sgit plan | Size | Gate? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | **Line-level three-way merge** | `ort` merge, conflict markers, `merge-file` | One function changes: `Vault__Merge.three_way_merge`. Every merge (pull, `branch merge`, `revert`, the rewind re-apply) goes through it. For a text file both sides changed: decrypt base/ours/theirs, run a three-way line merge, and store the result as a new blob. A clean merge commits as today; rough edges get `<<<<<<<` markers in the file instead of a `.conflict` copy. Binary files (a NUL byte) and files over a size cap stay whole-file. Tests use `git merge-file -p` as the oracle. **Opt-in; whole-file with `.conflict` stays the default** (the web UI works that way). Chosen per command (`--merge lines` / `--merge files` on `pull` and `branch merge`) or per clone (a `merge_style` field in `.sg_vault/local/config.json`, never synced, like Git's `.git/config`). A team-wide per-file rule, if ever wanted, is a committed attributes file (Git's `.gitattributes`), versioned like the `.gitignore` sgit already reads. | 2–3 days | No: a merge result is an ordinary commit |
| 2.2 | **Sign with your own key** (SSH or GPG) **and verify against your allowed-signers file** | `user.signingkey`, `gpg.format`, `commit.gpgSign`, `tag.gpgSign`, `gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile`, `log --show-signature`, `verify-commit`, `verify-tag` | Section 3 | 3–4 days | No (section 3) |
| 2.3 | **Commit some files, not all** | `commit <paths>`, `add -p` + `commit` | `sgit commit <paths>` reuses `write`'s code (only the named paths' folders are rebuilt). `commit -p` picks hunks over `history diff`. A persistent staging area (`sgit add`) is a separate decision; pathspec plus `-p` covers most use. | 1 day / 2 days | No |

### Priority 2

| # | Feature | Git | sgit plan | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.4 | Rename detection | `diff -M`, `log --follow`, renames in merge | Exact renames: the same plaintext `content_hash` (already in tree entries) on a deleted and an added path. Similar renames: Git's similarity score, within a cap. | 1–2 days |
| 2.5 | `blame` | `blame` | `history blame <path>`: walk the file's commits (the index pack's file → commits member makes it cheap) with a line diff per step. Blobs are fetched on demand; it stops at a shallow boundary. | 2 days |
| 2.6 | `bisect` | `bisect start/good/bad/run` | `history bisect …`. State in `.sg_vault/local/`; the midpoint comes from generation numbers (index packs carry them). | 1–2 days |
| 2.7 | `grep`, pickaxe | `grep`, `log -S` / `-G` | `sgit grep <regex>` over HEAD or `--rev C` (decrypt locally); `history log -S/-G`. | 1–2 days |
| 2.8 | `cherry-pick` | `cherry-pick` | `history cherry-pick <commit>`: a three-way merge of that commit's change onto HEAD (uses 2.1). | 1 day after 2.1 |
| 2.9 | Hooks | `.git/hooks/pre-commit`, `commit-msg`, `pre-push`, `post-merge` | `.sg_vault/local/hooks/`, local only and never synced (as in Git, a hook in a vault must never run on a clone). | 1 day |
| 2.12 | `rebase` (moved up from priority 3: `pull --rebase` and `rebase -i` are daily Git) | `rebase`, `pull --rebase`, `rebase -i`, `--continue/--skip/--abort` | Replay this clone's unpushed commits onto the new head, one cherry-pick (2.8) per commit, with stop-and-continue on conflict. Opt-in like 2.1: merge stays the default for `pull`. Pushed history is never rewritten. | 2–3 days |
| 2.13 | `worktree` (moved up from priority 3: agents use worktrees heavily) | `worktree add/list/remove/prune` | `sgit worktree add <path> [--branch <named>]`: a real clone with its own `.sg_vault/local`, clone branch and key, whose object store borrows from the main vault's (Git's *alternates*): own store, then the main store, then the network. Seconds and no network instead of a full clone. Merging is as today (push, then `branch merge`); merging another local clone branch without a push is a follow-up. Full shared refs (Git's `commondir`) is not planned: 81 hand-built `.sg_vault`/`bare` paths would need one resolver plus ref locking. | 2–3 days |

### Priority 3

| # | Feature | Git | sgit plan | Size |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.10 | Garbage collection | `gc`, `prune` | `vault prune` with the write key. Compute the set reachable from every branch, clone branch, tag and stash; delete the rest after a grace period (Git's two weeks) so in-flight pushes survive. On pack vaults, delete `archive/` packs older than the grace period. It has to be client-side: the host cannot read trees. | 2–3 days |
| 2.11 | Delta compression | `repack`, delta packs | At push, delta a blob against its previous version before deflate and encryption. The reader rebuilds the blob and verifies it by content address. | 1–2 weeks; old clients can't read deltas, so it needs a vault feature with a gate |
| 2.14 | `archive`, `shortlog`, `describe`, aliases | the same | Plaintext export of a commit as zip/tar; summaries; `sgit config alias.*`. | small each |
| 2.15 | Submodules | `submodule` | A vault referencing another vault at a commit. Needs a design; skip until someone asks. | design |

---

## 3. Signing the way Git does it

**How Git does it.** Git never asks who is allowed. It signs with the key the user already has: GPG (`gpg.format
openpgp`), SSH (`gpg.format ssh`, signing through `ssh-keygen -Y sign` and so through ssh-agent and hardware keys)
or X.509. It stores the signature in the commit (`gpgsig`), excluded from the signed bytes. Verification is each
verifier's choice: a GPG keyring, or an `allowed_signers` file of principal → public key. GitHub then adds
"verified" on top by matching keys to accounts. That last part is the SGitHub layer, not the CLI.

**sgit, the same way:**

- **Signing.**
  - Read Git's own settings (`git config user.signingkey`, `gpg.format`, `commit.gpgsign`, `tag.gpgsign`). A user
    whose Git signs their commits gets signed sgit commits with zero sgit setup. `sgit config` can override per vault.
  - Sign the way Git does: run `ssh-keygen -Y sign -n git` (agent and hardware keys work) or `gpg --detach-sign`.
    The output is Git's format, so `ssh-keygen -Y verify` or `gpg --verify` can check an sgit signature outside sgit.
- **Verification.**
  - `check verify`, `history log --show-signature` and `vault tag show` read the same `allowed_signers` file Git
    uses (`gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile`), or the GPG keyring.
  - Results are Git's: good signature from a listed principal / good signature from an unknown key / bad / none.
  - Verifying SSH signatures in-process uses `cryptography`, which is OpenSSL underneath and already a dependency;
    ed25519, ECDSA and RSA keys are supported. GPG verification runs `gpg`, as Git does.
- **What stays as it is.**
  - The per-clone ECDSA key keeps signing every commit. It is the machine signature that agents get with no setup,
    and `signatures-required` keeps meaning "every commit carries a valid clone signature".
  - The user's signature is a second, optional one. It is what answers "who wrote this", for anyone who keeps an
    allowed-signers file. That closes TM-R01 for that verifier exactly as far as Git closes it, and that is the bar.
- **Compatibility: no gate needed.** Checked on the code today:
  - A commit JSON with a field the client does not know parses fine (`Schema__Object_Commit.from_json` accepts
    unknown keys).
  - Clients check the clone signature over the fields they know (`commit.json()`), so the new field must be
    *excluded* from the clone's signing bytes, as Git excludes `gpgsig`. Then old clients verify the clone signature
    unchanged and simply ignore the user signature.
  - The reserved `author_signature` field cannot carry it: it is validated as base64 of at most 256 characters, and
    an SSH or PGP signature is longer, so a client would reject the commit (tested). The signature goes in a new
    field.
  - Signed tags work the same way.
- **What it does not do** (SGitHub's job later): a list of who may write, carried in the vault; joining and approval;
  revocation records; "verified" decided by a server.

Size: 3–4 days with tests (SSH first, GPG second), plus CHANGELOG and threat-model rows (TM-R01 gains "closed
per verifier with an allowed-signers file").

---

## 4. Moved to SGitHub (server-side, later)

These were in the article's "Git is ahead" list or in yesterday's review. They are GitHub's features, not Git's,
so they are out of scope for the CLI:

- **Accounts and identity:** who pushed, keys attached to people, "verified" badges, verification recorded at push
  time.
- **A list of who may write:** owner-signed signer registry, join requests and approval, revocation (yesterday's
  TM-R01 proposal), per-person write tokens.
- **Protected branches:** required signed pushes, rules enforced by the server.
- **Collaboration:** review / pull requests, the web merge button, CI triggers, issues.
- **The append lane** is already a server feature. Its CLI (`sgit inbox send/read`) belongs in section 5, because
  Git has nothing like it.

Under zero knowledge, an SGitHub server can do the access parts: tokens, ref ACLs keyed by the hashed ref ids,
recording verification. The content parts (review, CI, search) run in the browser or in a runner that holds the
key.

---

## 5. More on top: what sgit does that Git does not

The second half of the message. Already shipped unless marked.

- The host reads nothing: contents, file names, messages and branch names are encrypted on the client.
- A read key is a capability: publish it, and anyone reads from any static host with no account.
- Fetch one folder by byte ranges from plain storage (pack vaults), each object verified by hash.
- Indexes shipped by the writer, signed and encrypted, checked before use.
- Many agents, one folder each: writes outside the scope are refused by name, and two scoped agents never conflict.
- Custody without access: `vault mirror`.
- Policy carried by the vault and enforced by every client: format gate, `signatures-required`.
- Rewind detection on every clone.
- The secret guard (keys and key zips are never committed).
- Key rotation: `vault rekey` / `vault move`.
- A computable cache for fixed-cost reads.
- `serve`, `publish`.
- `pki encrypt` to a person.
- To add: `sgit inbox` for the append lane; `cat --vault-key` (one file with no clone); Phase 4 ranged reads on pack
  vaults.

## Suggested order

1. 2.1 line-level merge.
2. 2.2 signing with your own key.
3. 2.3 `commit <paths>`.
4. Then 2.4–2.9, 2.12 (rebase) and 2.13 (worktree) as the priority-2 release.
5. 2.10, 2.11, 2.14 and 2.15 when a workload asks (garbage collection is not needed for now).

Each is an extension: off or invisible until used, and no version gate except 2.11.

Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/08/review__git-to-sgit-security-mapping.md>.*

---
# Review: "Git security features → sgit: a one-way mapping"

*CLI team, 8 Oct 2026. Review of the research note of the same date, checked against the code,
plus what was built from it (on the branch, for 0.21.0).*

## Verdict

A good, honest map. The framing is right: one direction only, "N/A by model" kept separate from
real gaps, and the ranking puts the structural limit (no server-side enforcement) first. Three
statements are wrong or overtaken, one important gap is missing, and the four easy gaps are now
closed.

## Corrections

| § | The note says | Actually |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | `author_key_id` is "reserved / unused" | **Live since 0.19.0.** Every CLI commit carries it; it names the signing key and marks the canonical (JCS) signing form, and `check verify` uses it. The schema comment still said "reserved", which is what misled the note; the comment is fixed. `author_signature` and `attestations` are the genuinely unused fields |
| 6 | symlink tree entries "unconfirmed; one to verify" | **Closed, N/A by model.** A tree entry is a blob or a tree, nothing else; there is no symlink type and no code that creates one, so a vault cannot plant a symlink to write through |
| 6 | case/Unicode variants of `.git` are a "possible gap" | **Confirmed, and fixed** (see below). Your test was exactly right |

## A gap the note misses

**No per-writer authorisation.** In git hosting, who may push to which branch is decided per user
by the server. In sgit the write key is one per vault and every writer holds it, so authorisation
is all-or-nothing among key holders. Signatures give attribution (who wrote this commit), not
permission (who was allowed to). A key holder can write anything the server accepts: refs,
indexes, objects. The client-side defences (rewind refusal, `signatures-required`, tag signature
checks) detect much of the damage afterwards; nothing prevents it. This belongs next to gap 1 in
the ranking, and it is the real reason "server-side enforcement" matters: the server does not know
which writer is which.

## What was built from the note (branch, all with tests; verified on the live dev API)

| Gap (note's rank) | Now |
|---|---|
| 3. No tags | **`sgit vault tag create/list/show/delete`.** A tag is an immutable object (name, commit, message, tagger key, timestamp) signed over its canonical form, encrypted, content-addressed. Names live only in the encrypted branch index. Verification checks the signature and that the index entry's name equals the signed name, so an entry cannot re-point "v1.0" at another tag's object. Only pushed commits can be tagged; tags move only with `--force`, and pull reports moves. Deletes are tombstones a stale clone cannot undo. Tag names work in `history show/reset`. A 0.20.0 client drops tags from the index on its first push; the next current pull restores them (seen live) |
| 2. No reflog | **`sgit history reflog`**: every local ref move, newest first, local only, capped at 1,000; `history reset <old id>` brings a head back |
| 2. No force-with-lease | **`sgit push --force-with-lease [<commit>]`**: forces only if the remote is where this clone last saw it before the push (or at the commit given), and writes with compare-and-swap. It deliberately ignores the refresh that push itself does first; git's version has a known footgun there (a fetch silently satisfies the lease) |
| 4. `.git` spellings | **Path guard refuses** `.GIT`, `.Git`, `.git.`, `.git `, `GIT~1`, `SG_VAU~1`, `.git::$INDEX_ALLOCATION`, `.g‌it` and the same for `.sg_vault*`, on every platform (the vault may be checked out anywhere). `.github`, `.gitignore`, `src/git`, `notes.git` stay allowed |

Found on the way: `sgit push --force` from a clone that was behind the remote crashed ("object …
is not in the local store") on 0.20.0. Fixed.

## Still open, and why

- **Server-side enforcement and per-writer authorisation** (1 + the missing gap): need the server
  to know writers (per-writer write keys or signed writes the server verifies). An SG/Send API
  design question, not a CLI change.
- **Push certificates / nonces** (5): low value until the server verifies anything; rewind
  detection covers replay for clients that were there before.
- **Notes, attestations, a second signer** (6): the reserved fields can carry them; worth doing
  when there is a review workflow to serve.
- **Format 2 by default** (7): agree in principle. The blocker is clients ≤ 0.18, which cannot read
  a vault with 128-bit ids and say "corrupt", not "update". Make it the default for new vaults
  once 0.19+ is the norm; it is a one-line change in `init`.

## Suggested wording changes for the note

- §2 row 5: "author_key_id is live (0.19.0+); author_signature and attestations are reserved".
- §6: symlink row → N/A by model; case-variant row → Matched (0.21.0).
- §3/§5: reflog, force-with-lease, tags → Matched (0.21.0); signed tags Matched.
- Ranking: add "no per-writer authorisation" beside gap 1.

## 5. An index delta in every commit pack

1,000 commits of five random files each on the 76,000-file vault (`deltas/`, seed 5). A snapshot carries the whole index; each commit pack carries only what its commit changed.

| Measure | Whole shards in each delta | Folder files plus a change list |
|---|---|---|
| Writer, 1,000 commits | 8.04 s | **0.92 s** |
| Members per delta, median | 41 | **27** (the folders on the five paths, and the list) |
| Size per delta, median | 47.7 KB | **3.1 KB**; the change list alone 253 bytes |
| 1,000 deltas | 47.08 MB | **3.05 MB** |
| The snapshot it sits on | 8.7 MB, 58,318 members | 7.34 MB |

**The reader, with whole-shard deltas:** a map of each member's newest version across the 1,000 deltas (10,620 entries) took 6.6 ms to build. A read through it took 8.0 µs, and gave exactly the writer's final state. Merging all 1,000 deltas into a local copy took 15.5 ms.

**The reader, with change lists:** blob → paths built from the snapshot in 155 ms, and all 1,000 change lists applied to it, with file → commits, in 48.6 ms.

**Change over time, from the deltas alone:** the commits that touched `raw/c03/` (393 of 1,000) were found in 1.45 ms.

## 6. What did not work, or was not measured

- rdflib cannot walk a deep history (RecursionError).
- Kùzu is archived; its numbers are kept for reference only.
- DuckPGQ, DuckDB's SQL/PGQ extension, was not tested: extensions download at run time.
- MGraph-DB 1.18.0 does not use Memory-FS, and Memory-FS 0.41.0 has no S3 provider among its storage providers (memory, local disk, SQLite, zip).
- Cold starts, concurrent readers, slow disks and memory limits were not measured anywhere on this page.

# History integrity: what the three fixes would cost, and how to ship them without a `vault move`, cli.sgit.ai

> What signature verification, ref monotonicity and 128-bit ids would cost, measured on a real vault, and how to ship all three without a vault move.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/history-integrity-cost-and-compatibility.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/07/history-integrity__cost-and-compatibility.md>.*

---
# History integrity: what the three fixes would cost, and how to ship them without a `vault move`

**Date:** 7 Oct 2026 · **Vault measured:** the DC / CRM collaboration vault (`y8pwtjlw`), fresh
full clone this session · **Ask:** "do a set of performance tests to see the implications [of
signature verification, ref monotonicity, 128-bit ids], and can we add those fixes in a
forward-compatible way, supporting existing vaults without a move?"

## 0. The vault today

| | |
|---|---|
| commits reachable from the named head | 674 (626 yesterday) |
| unique trees / tree entries | 8,589 / 107,445 (59,944 blob refs, 47,501 tree refs) |
| objects in the store | 19,780 · 146 MB |
| branches in the index / public keys on disk | 30 / 29 |
| full clone from this sandbox (0.18.0) | 93 s |
| `sgit status`, up to date | 2.5 s (network-bound) |

## 1. Cost of each fix, measured

All local work, this sandbox's CPU. Network is unchanged by any of the three.

| Fix | What it adds per command | Measured | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Signature verification** on pull / status / fsck | one ECDSA P-256 verify per *new* commit (pull) or per commit (fsck) | verify 66 µs, sign 23 µs; the whole 674-commit history verifies in **39 ms**; decrypting and parsing the whole history is 155 ms (230 µs/commit) | free |
| **Ref monotonicity** (the new remote head must descend from the last known one) | an ancestry walk from the new head to the last known head, i.e. over the N new commits | status already does this walk since 0.18.0 (0 object reads when up to date, N when N behind); worst case the whole history: **155 ms** | free |
| **128-bit object ids** (32 hex instead of 12) | nothing in compute (sha256 is already computed; the truncation is what goes away); more bytes in trees, commits and listings | +2.18 MB on 34.5 MB of tree+commit objects (**+6.3 %** of those, **+1.5 %** of the 146 MB store); the store listing grows 396 KB; expected clone cost ≈ +1.5 % of bytes, under 2 s | negligible |

And the exposure the third fix removes, on this vault: accidental collision among 19,780 ids at
48 bits ≈ 7×10⁻⁷ (not the problem); a *second-preimage* by someone holding the read key is 2⁴⁸
sha256 ≈ 8 hours at 10¹⁰ hashes/s on a GPU (the problem).

### What signature verification would actually cover today

| commits | |
|---|---|
| signed | 562 of 674 |
| signed and verifiable (the branch index still maps the branch to its public key) | **247** (all verify; 0 bad) |
| signed, but the index no longer lists the branch | 315 |
| unsigned | 112: 10 with no `branch_id` (web UI), 102 from CLI clone branches that had no local signing key |

Two consequences for the design: the commit's reserved `author_key_id` field has to be
populated from now on (the key is in `bare/keys/`, but the only branch→key mapping is the
index, and clone branches leave it), and a "signatures required" policy can only apply from a
checkpoint commit forward, since 427 of the 674 commits here cannot be verified whatever we do.

### A side finding: `sgit check fsck` was quadratic

Full verification is the thing that makes "always detect corruption" practical, and it took
**270 s** on this vault: the walk kept a per-commit set of visited trees, so 8,589 unique trees
were checked 282,202 times and every blob was re-hashed once per commit. One global set for
trees and one for blobs: **12.2 s**, identical findings (42 missing objects; they are the
pre-0.18.0 push bug and are recoverable only from the clones that created them, via
`sgit check upload-objects`). Fixed on the branch; 32 fsck tests pass, full suite green.

## 2. Compatibility: what exists, what does not

**Today there is no vault-level "minimum client version".**

- Objects carry a `schema` tag (`commit_v1`, `tree_v1`, `branch_index_v1`). Nothing reads it
  except `vault move`.
- The migration ledger (`sgit migrate`) is **local** (`.sg_vault/local/migrations.json`); the
  vault itself does not say which migrations it has had.
- Old clients drop unknown fields silently (`Schema__Branch_Index.from_json` with a `format`
  or `min_client` key just loses them), so a flag written today is invisible to 0.18.0 and
  older. They fail only when they meet data they cannot parse: a 32-hex id raises
  `ValueError … exceeds maximum length of 24` and the CLI prints `incompatible vault data …
  hint: re-clone the vault with the current CLI`, which is the wrong remedy for that case.

So: forward-incompatible vaults are *possible* today only by accident, and the failure mode
for an old client is a confusing error, not a "please upgrade".

## 3. Proposal: a format gate, then each fix on top of it

### 3.1 The gate (no format change; ships first)

Add to `Schema__Branch_Index` (encrypted, written by init/push, loaded first by every command):

```
format     : Safe_UInt           = 1        # absent == 1: every existing vault
min_client : Safe_Str__Semver    = None     # refuse below this, naming it
features   : list[Safe_Str__Feature]        # e.g. 'ids-128', 'signatures-required'
```

- A client at or above the release that ships the gate refuses a vault whose `min_client` is
  newer than itself: `this vault needs sgit-ai ≥ 0.20.0 (you have 0.19.1): sgit update`.
- Existing vaults carry no field, read as format 1, and behave exactly as now. **No move.**
- Clients older than the gate cannot be taught anything retroactively; the one thing we can do
  for them now is fix the hint on the pattern error to say `sgit update` first.
- Raising `min_client` on a vault is a deliberate owner action (`sgit vault format --min-client
  0.20.0`), recorded in the index, so a team is never surprised by a vault that stops working
  for their older agents.

### 3.2 Each fix against the gate

| Fix | Format change? | Needs `vault move`? | Old clients on an upgraded vault | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Verify signatures (pull, status, fsck) and populate `author_key_id` | none; both fields already exist in `commit_v1` (`author_key_id` reserved) | no | unaffected: they ignore signatures as they do now | policy per vault in `features`: `signatures: warn` → `required` from a checkpoint commit; the web UI must sign before `required` |
| Ref monotonicity | none | no | unaffected | client rule; `push --force` records the intent so the next pull can tell a rewind from an attack; a signed ref log is a later, format-2 addition |
| 128-bit ids | **format 2**: new objects get 32-hex ids, old objects keep theirs, references mix | **no**: mixed-id vault; `vault move` (which already rewrites every id) is the optional "rewrite everything" path | **break at the first long id** → this is what `min_client` is for | prerequisites outside the CLI: the server must accept the longer `file_id` (unverified from here), the web UI must read and write both lengths (interop requirement) |

### 3.3 Order

1. **0.19**: the gate, the hint fix, `author_key_id` on every new commit, fsck dedupe. No
   vault changes behaviour; every client keeps working on every vault.
2. **0.20**: signature verification (`warn` default, `required` opt-in per vault), ref
   monotonicity. Still format 1.
3. **format 2**: 128-bit ids for new vaults and opted-in vaults, once the server and web UI
   accept both lengths. Existing vaults stay format 1 until their owner raises them; raising
   never requires a move.

The measurements say none of this is a performance decision: the costs are milliseconds and a
few percent of bytes on a vault that was impractical to clone a week ago and now clones in 93 s.

# Research, cli.sgit.ai

> The sgit CLI team's research, kept as written and grouped into topics: measurements on real vaults, designs and the reviews that corrected them, security reviews, and the bugs found in daily use, each with its source in the CLI repository.

# Research

The CLI team's working documents, **published as written**: measurements on real vaults, designs and the reviews that corrected them, decisions, security reviews and the bugs found in daily use. Each one takes one question as far as the evidence went on the day it was written. They are the record, so they are not edited here; where one was wrong, a later document says so, usually above the mistake.

**Research is not the same as an article.** An [article](../articles/index.md) makes one argument for a reader, in the newsroom's format, and is written to be read start to finish. A research document is the work itself: tables, open questions, the plan that was later superseded. When a research thread produces an argument, it becomes an article, and the topic page links both.

## Topics

Each topic is one open question, with where it stands today: what is shipped, what is designed, what is absent.

- [sgit and Git](../research/topics/git.md): What sgit does that Git cannot, what both do, which of Git's lead sgit can close on the client, and what zero knowledge rules out for good, with the status of each and where it is said.
- [Keys, members and who may write](../research/topics/keys.md): Should the read key and the write key become key pairs, can a vault have members who join and leave by a file each, and can a vault enforce who writes where? What is built, what is designed, and what is still a question.
- [History integrity and signatures](../research/topics/integrity.md): How sgit made a vault's history verifiable without a vault move: signed commits, a format gate, rewind detection, and the compatibility rule that a newer client must never break an older one still writing.
- [Big vaults and many agents](../research/topics/scale.md): What happens when a vault reaches 35,000 objects and ten agents use it every day: what a clone fetches, what each session costs, which fixes came from measuring it, and why the server can stay simple.
- [How a vault takes writes](../research/topics/write-path.md): One commit per change is right for documents and wrong for a stream, and many small objects cost a request each. Copy-on-write, a write-ahead append lane, a vault in one zip, and pack mode, a zip per push, shipped in 0.24.0: what sgit already does, and what is proposed.
- [Running a vault locally](../research/topics/serve.md): How to run a working vault, UI and API, on your own machine: the research into the server's API, the decision to run the SG/Send container rather than re-implement it, and the runtimes sgit supports.
- [Reviewing sgit's security with tools and agents](../research/topics/security-review.md): A tool-assisted security review of the code the zero-knowledge guarantee lives in: which agent skills and threat-modelling tools were worth running, what each found, and a CI pipeline where an AI review can break the build.
- [Found in daily use](../research/topics/correctness.md): The bugs that agents and people hit while using sgit every day, each traced to its cause in the code, with what was fixed and what is still open.

- [Git parity, priority 1 and 2: index, shared foundations and reconciliation (28 Oct 2026)](../research/git-parity-designs-index.md): The entry point to the seven Git-parity designs: the shared foundations to build once, where the designs disagreed and how it was settled, the bugs the designs found in the code (fixed in 0.26.3), and the decisions waiting on Dinis Cruz.

Opt-in; pushed history is never rewritten. Not built.

Whole-file .conflict stays the default. The merge shipped in 0.26.5.

No gate. Not built.

# Review: indexes and caches across sgit, after 0.25.0, cli.sgit.ai

> What sgit already holds as indexes and caches after 0.25.0, by name; why the commands still slow on the newsroom's vault were where no cache existed yet; and the one index worth adding first: the flat map of a head, carried in the pack.

Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/c06947537e3927c82578307b62434bc0901952c5/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/26/review__indexes-and-caches-across-the-board.md>.*

# Review: indexes and caches across sgit, after 0.25.0

**Asked (26 Oct):** the agents report big improvements on 0.25.0 but a couple of commands still take long; the
suspicion is the cache. And: the original design had *indexes* (cross-references computed once, paid once,
benefiting everyone, losable without losing data). Should they come back, as indexes or as the cache, and can the
pack distribute them? Should large vaults simply be pack vaults?

**Answer in short.** The slow commands are not the cache being slow; they are the places the cache did not yet
exist (a fresh clone's first command) and the one walk the cache cannot help with yet (a pull that brings a head
this clone has never seen). Both are on the branch: section 2. On indexes: what the design called indexes already
exists, twice, under different names, and the gap is exactly the one you describe. The thing worth adding is one
object, the **flat index of a head** (what the local flat cache holds), encrypted under the read key, signed by
its pusher, carried in the pack: section 4. Pack vaults for anything past a few thousand files: yes, section 5.

## 1. What exists today, by name

| Name | Where | What it holds | Authoritative? | Who pays, who benefits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **branch index** | `bare/indexes/<id>` on the host | the named branches, their ref ids, keys, format, features | **yes** (the only thing under `indexes/`) | every clone reads it; the pusher writes it |
| **cache layer** (contract 08/12, v0.15) | `bare/cache/value/*`, `bare/cache/pointer/*` on the host | per path: an encrypted copy of a hot file, or a pointer to its blob or tree, at an id derivable from the read key and the path | no: derived, repairable (`sgit cache repair`), dropped by `vault move` | the aware writer at push; a reader that wants one file in one request (SG/Vault, a Lambda) |
| **flat cache** (0.25.0) | `.sg_vault/local/flat-cache/<tree id>.json` | the head flattened: path → blob id, size, hash, type; folder → tree id | no: a pure function of the tree id (a content address) | the first command on a head; every later command on it |
| **scan cache** (0.25.0) | `.sg_vault/local/scan-cache.json` | per working-copy file: git's index key (mtime, ctime, size, inode, device) and the hash | no: rebuilt by reading the file | every scan after the first; now also seeded by every write sgit makes |
| **packs** (0.24.0) | `bare/packs/{commits,snapshots,archive}/` | the objects themselves, zipped per push, plus snapshots | yes for the objects they carry | the transport; one listing and one batch read per clone |

So "the indexes" of the 08/06 design became the cache layer: per-path, host-side, derived, never trusted for
correctness. The design principle you state held throughout: every one of these can be deleted and nothing is
lost, because the authoritative data is the immutable, content-addressed objects plus the refs and the branch
index, and everything else is a function of them and the key.

What the 08/06–08/12 design did not have, and 0.25.0 added locally, is the **whole-vault** derived data: the
flattened head and the folder ids. That is the one a 38,000-folder vault needs on every command, and the one
that is expensive to recompute (a walk of every tree: ~45 s of decrypt and parse here, 2 minutes on the
newsroom's vault at 0.24.0). The cache layer is per path by design (one request for one file) and cannot answer
"what is the whole head" without a walk.

## 2. The commands that still take long, and why

From the newsroom's field report (26 Oct, first morning on 0.25.0):

| Command | Reported | Cause | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| first `status` on a fresh 4.2 GB clone, cloud session | 18 min 23 s (1 min CPU; the rest disk) | the scan cache only knew files a scan had hashed, so the first scan read every file back from a slow disk | fixed on the branch: every write sgit makes (clone, pull, read-only pull, switch, history edits) records the file in the scan cache under the hash of the bytes it wrote; a full clone also writes the head's flat cache. First status after a clone here: 20.1 s → 8.2 s, and the 18 minutes was that read |
| first `pull` on a read-only evidence clone | 226 s | the same read (a read-only pull scans the working copy for its dirty-tree check) | same fix |
| `pull` of a whole pass, +6,807 blobs | 8 min 5 s (1 min 21 s user) | measured below: the walk of every tree of the new head through `Type_Safe` (the one walk the flat cache cannot serve, because this clone has never seen that head) plus 6,807 file writes and reads | the walk is what section 4's index removes; the writes are the disk |

Measured here (synthetic vault, a 300-file pass pushed from one clone and pulled in another, under cProfile):
566 s, of which the fetch's walk of 154,454 tree loads through `Type_Safe.from_json` was 347 s, and
`_checkout_flat_map` writing all 229,310 files of the merged tree was 171 s (612,282 `open` calls). Both are
fixed on the branch: the fetch does not open a folder of the head this clone last accepted (its record is written
only once every object of that head was local) and reads the trees it does open as JSON; the merge writes only
the files whose blob changed; the new head is flattened by copying the unchanged folders from the cached old
head. Re-measured clean (a fresh clone, then a 300-file pass pulled under cProfile): **566 s → 31.7 s**, and what is left is the dirty-tree scan (15 s, a stat pass over 228k files), the missing-blob check (6 s, `exists` over 235k ids) and pruning empty folders (5 s): the vault's size, not the pass, but seconds of it.

## 3. What is computed repeatedly, and what kind of thing each is

The question "index or cache" is answered per item by three properties: **derivable from what** (the objects and
the key, or this machine's filesystem), **sensitive to whom** (path names are plaintext metadata: never on the
host in clear), and **who can compute it cheaply** (the writer that just built it, or only a reader after a full
walk).

| Derived data | Computed by | Cost today | Derivable from | Sensitive | Cheap for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the head's flat map and folder ids | status, commit, push, pull, log, diff, cat, fetch | 1 s from cache; ~45 s to rebuild here (77k trees) | the head tree + read key | yes: every path name | the committer (it built the tree) and anyone holding the previous head's map plus the diff |
| per-commit change counts (`history log`) | log | seconds (pruned diff) | two trees + key | yes | anyone with both maps |
| base..head commit list (pull) | pull | ms per commit within a day's window | commit objects | message text, yes | anyone |
| the objects a head needs that this clone lacks (pull, clone) | pull with new commits, clone | the full tree walk through `Type_Safe`: minutes | the new head's tree walk, or its flat map | yes (the map) | the pusher: it has the map |
| scan state of the working copy | every scan | 4 s stat pass on 228k files | this machine's filesystem | local by nature (inodes, mtimes) | only this machine |
| object presence (`exists` over 228k ids) | pull's missing-blob check, push planning | ~1 s | the local store | no | this machine |
| pack listing and sizes | pack sync, compaction | one listing | the host | no (already visible) | the host |

The first and the fourth rows are the same object. Everything else is either cheap now or local by nature.

## 4. The one thing to add: the flat index of a head, in the pack

**The object.** `idx-flat-<tree id>`: the flat map of one head (paths, blob ids, sizes, hashes, content types,
folder tree ids), as JSON, deflated, encrypted under the read key with AES-GCM like a tree, and **signed by the
pusher's clone key over (tree id, sha256 of the plaintext)** exactly as a commit is signed. Its name carries the
tree id, so it is as immutable as the head it describes: no invalidation, ever; compaction keeps the current
head's and archives the rest with its pack.

**Where it travels.** In a pack vault, as one more member of the commit pack and of the snapshot:
`bare/cache/flat/idx-flat-<tree id>`. The pusher already holds the map (its flat cache: it built the tree), so
writing it is one encryption. On a loose vault the same object can go to `bare/cache/flat/` with the cache layer's
rules (aware writer, repairable, dropped on `vault move`); optional there, since loose vaults are the small ones.

**What a reader does with it.** Three things, in order of value:

1. **A pull or a clone plans its fetch from it instead of walking.** The puller holds the old head's map (its
   flat cache) and the new head's index: the folder ids that differ name exactly the trees to fetch, and the
   entries whose blob ids are new name the blobs. No tree is opened to find out what is missing. This removes the
   walk in row 4 of section 3: minutes on the newsroom's vault, every pull with new commits.
2. **It seeds the flat cache**, so the first command after a clone or a pull opens no tree (today a clone
   computes this itself after extraction, which is fine but is the 45 s).
3. **A reader without a clone gets the whole head in one object** (SG/Vault, a Lambda): with the pack's central
   directory and the ranged read that already exists, that is "which file is where" in one request and the file
   in a second. This is the per-path cache layer's promise, generalised: not one hot path, every path.

**Trust.** The host cannot forge it (AES-GCM under the read key). A write-key holder could write a wrong one,
which is the same power that holder has over trees, except that trees are bound to a signed commit and the index
is not — hence the signature: under `signatures-required` the index is accepted on the same policy as the commit
that names its tree id, and otherwise it is checked the way the local flat cache already is (the root tree's
entries must match the index's root level: one object read; blob ids are content addresses, so an entry can only
ever name authentic bytes). What an index can never do is change what a clone verifies before writing: every
object still lands through verify-then-write by its own content address. A wrong index can make a pull fetch the
wrong set (it then fails the missing-blob check, as today) or seed a wrong map (the root check catches an emptied
or substituted one; a deeper swap by a signing teammate is their signature on it). This keeps the principle: lose
every index and nothing is lost; trust an index and nothing is written unverified.

**Compatibility.** A pack member outside `bare/data/` is refused whole by 0.24.x and 0.25.0 (the zip-bomb and
duplicate-member rules), so this is a format feature: `pack-index` in the branch index's features, with its min
client, exactly how `packs` and `blob-deflate` gate today. Pack vaults are new and their agents upgrade on a
brief; the gate refuses an old client with the command that fixes it.

**Size.** The newsroom's head: 79,465 entries. As JSON with 12-hex ids and short hashes ≈ 12 MB, deflated ≈ 2 MB.
Against a 1.22 GB snapshot and 164–228 MB commit packs, noise.

**Not in it.** Scan state (this machine's inodes), object presence (this clone's store), commit graph shortcuts
(the day-window walk is already cheap; generation numbers would be a commit-schema change for a display feature).

**Effort.** Writer: the pusher serialises its flat cache, signs, encrypts, adds the member: a day. Reader:
fetch planning from two maps, the root check, the signature policy, the seed: two to three days with tests.
Gate and member rule: hours. A `Known_Gaps`/threat-model row for what an index can and cannot do.

## 5. Normal vault or pack vault

Yes to the split, and the numbers say where the line is. A loose vault costs one object per file per fetch and
one per push; its strengths are the one-request per-path reads (the cache layer) and that any client since 0.15
reads it. A pack vault costs one listing and one batch read per clone and one zip per push, whatever the count,
and from 0.25.0 every local command on it is seconds. The crossover is not a file count so much as "how many
objects does a clone or a pull move": a few hundred objects are fine loose; thousands per pass, or tens of
thousands in the head, want the pack. A working rule for the docs: **under 5,000 files and a few hundred objects
per day, either; above that, `--packs`**; and the evidence vaults (hundreds of sources, many readers wanting one
file) stay loose with the cache layer. The flat index of section 4 is what makes a pack vault also answer the
reader's question "where is this file" without a clone, so the two modes converge on reads.

## 6. In LETS terms

Load (the host's packs and refs), extract (decrypt and verify, per object), transform (flatten, diff, scan),
save (the caches). 0.25.0 made the transforms incremental and saved their results locally; the remaining cost is
that every clone repeats the transform the pusher already did. The pack is the place where "computed once,
everybody benefits" is a file next to the data it describes. That is the index to bring back: not per path, per
head; not a registry, one immutable object; not trusted, verified; and losable.

# Keys the way git does them, PKI access to a vault, and copy-on-write: what is already published, and what is not

**Date:** 16 Oct 2026. **For:** the agent that manages sgit; input to one or two newsroom articles.
**No code changes:** this is research and mapping. Anything that would need code is listed in §5 as a
question for the thread. **Sources read:** every newsroom article on keys and identity (11), the
sgit.ai pages on PKI, credentials, key management, messaging, authentication and history purging
(14), the threat model and the CLI at `dev` 37218af, RuVector's and RVF's READMEs, ruv.sgit.ai.

## 1. The questions in the memo, and where each stands

| # | Question (from the memo) | Already published? | Where | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Native public/private keys for a vault (read key pair, write key pair) | **Yes, as a design (RFC)** | newsroom *RFC 0001: two ways to add public-key cryptography to sgit* (9 Oct): Design 1, native PKI vault mode, two key pairs neither derivable from the other, data key sealed to the read public key, heads signed by the write private key, a write-only depositor; Design 2, sealed files; a shared first step, a vault signing key on today's vaults. Effort estimates and 11 reviewer questions. | Not built. The memo's "public key as read key, private key as write key" is the exact construction the RFC corrects ("whatever decrypts must be secret"): two pairs, not one. |
| 2 | The git + SSH + GitHub model: authenticate once, then anything goes; no per-commit check unless signed; local copies are unrestricted | **Partly.** The server-side half is documented (`api/authentication`: six capability headers, SHA-256 hash comparison, reads open by default; `docs/credentials`: what a read key can and cannot do). The git comparison is not written anywhere. | sgit.ai `api/authentication`, `docs/credentials`, `docs/sgit-for-git-users` (no auth row) | **No article maps git's SSH/HTTPS authorisation onto sgit's write key, read key, access token and signatures.** That is the article to write (§2 of the draft). |
| 3 | "The read key locally does not prevent changes", like a git clone | **Yes, as a threat-model fact, not as prose.** A read-only clone holds the read key on disk (TM-R15, KI-SEC-03); it cannot push (the server wants the write key hash); the host cannot tell a reader from a writer by the bytes (RFC 0001 "The honest problem"). | threat model TM-R15, TM-R12; RFC 0001 | Same as 2: the comparison is the missing piece, and it is a good one, because the answer is "exactly like git, and here is what git adds on the server that sgit adds with signatures". |
| 4 | A vault's members get in with their own key pair: a file per member, sealed to their public key, holding the read (or write) key | **Yes, three times, in three shapes.** (a) RFC 0001 Design 1 "Rotation": an owner key signs a **writer set**; removing a reader is a new read pair and data key "sealed to the remaining members". (b) *The passkey opens the vault* (11 Oct): a **door per path**, one file holding the master's key encrypted under the door's read key, "retired by deleting its one file"; built and tested against a real vault server. (c) *secrets.sgit.ai on public keys* (14 Oct), way 8: "A team. One inbox per member… with revocation by rotating and re-sharing"; and "The private key lives in a vault". Also `docs/pki` "Where public keys live in a vault": `bare/keys/key-rnd-imm-*`. | RFC 0001; passkey article §"A lost device", "Moving keys between masters"; secrets article; `docs/pki` | The pieces are published separately. **Nobody has written the membership pattern as one thing**: a members folder (or branch), join by adding a file, leave by deleting it, and the honest limit. |
| 5 | Revocation: delete the member's file; but history keeps it | **Yes, the problem is stated, and the current rule is "rotate".** Passkey article: "The catch is history. Vaults keep their versions, so an entry deleted from A is still in A's past for anyone who can open A. The rule: keys that move for security reasons get rotated." `docs/key-management`: "Rotation is not retroactive." TM-R12: "Read access cannot be revoked: a read key reads all history forever." `case-studies/purging-history`: how a git history rewrite works and why "rotate the secret, then rewrite". | passkey article; key-management; credentials; TM-R12; purging-history | **The feature the memo asks for, files that exist only at the current version, is not designed anywhere.** §3 of the draft lays out the three ways to get it and which one is already a primitive in the code. |
| 6 | The key never stored locally, only in memory for the run | **Partly.** `sgit clone -` reads the key from stdin "keeps it out of argv and history" (0.21.0); the passkey design computes the door key from PRF bytes and stores nothing; *Handing secrets to agents*: the session makes its key pair, the secret is piped "into the tool, not the chat". But every clone still writes `.sg_vault/local/vault_key` (0600) and a read-only clone writes the read key to `clone_mode.json` (TM-R15). | CHANGELOG 0.21.0; passkey article; handing-secrets; TM-R15 | **A "no key on disk" clone mode** (derive at start, hold in memory, re-derive from the member's private key next time) is not designed. It falls out of §3's pattern. |
| 7 | Copy-on-write, as asked for by rUv's team | **No.** The only mention anywhere is a secure-unlink debrief noting that on btrfs/APFS/ZFS an overwrite does not erase. ruv.sgit.ai records that RuVector "already has snapshots and copy-on-write branching (rvf derive)" and that POC2 "adds an sgit vault around the memory files", without saying what copy-on-write would mean for the vault itself. | ruv.sgit.ai `ruv-stack`; RuVector README ("Copy on write branches: isolated memory experiments without full copies"); RVF README (COW_MAP, lineage) | **A whole article**: what copy-on-write is, how sgit's object model already is one, what RVF's version adds, and where sgit would need a write-ahead lane and compaction to keep up. §4 and the second draft. |

## 2. What the code does today (the facts the articles must not get wrong)

- **Three credentials, one derivation.** `passphrase:vault_id` → PBKDF2 (600k) → read key (encrypts everything, AES-256-GCM) and write key (a bearer the server compares as a SHA-256 hash in `x-sgraph-vault-write-key`); a separate account token `x-sgraph-access-token`. Reads on the shared host need no credential; the ciphertext is the protection (`api/authentication`).
- **The server authorises a write by a shared secret, not by who you are.** Every writer presents the same write-key hash. The server cannot tell writers apart; nor can a reader tell whether a head was written by a writer or by the host (RFC 0001).
- **Commits are signed already.** Each clone has an ECDSA P-256 branch key pair (`Vault__Key_Manager`, raw r||s for Web Crypto); the public half is stored as `bare/keys/key-rnd-imm-*`; commits carry `author_key_id`; `sgit check verify` classifies every commit (verified / bad / unsigned / unknown key); the vault feature `signatures-required` makes `pull` refuse the first unsigned incoming commit, and `signed-since-<hex>` records where the policy began (0.19.0). `sgit pki` separately makes RSA-4096 encryption pairs and ECDSA signing pairs, encrypts to a recipient (RSA-OAEP wrapping AES-256-GCM), signs and verifies files; no revocation, no expiry, no directory (`docs/pki`).
- **The named branch only moves forward** (`last_remote_head`, rewind detection, `--accept-rewind`), and the branch index is a shared document merged by every client under compare-and-swap (0.19.0).
- **Mutable objects exist and are a first-class pattern.** Refs (`ref-pid-muw-*`), the branch index, the cache layer's value and pointer objects (`bare/cache/`, written directly to a path-derived id, random IV, "derived, never authoritative", D10), and the door file in the passkey design. These are the objects that have no history by construction.
- **Deletion exists.** `DELETE` of one object with the write key; `destroy` of a vault with a tombstone (`api/vault-objects`); `sgit vault delete-on-remote`; `sgit vault rekey` (wipe, init, commit under a new key: a new vault); `sgit vault move`.
- **History cannot be rewritten in place.** `history reset` + `push --force` rewinds a branch, but the old objects stay on the host until deleted, and every reader keeps what it fetched (TM-R12). The purge case study is about git, and its rule applies here: rotate first.

## 3. The membership pattern, assembled from what exists (for the first article)

What the memo describes is RFC 0001's writer set plus the passkey article's door, applied to a vault's members. In one place:

- A member is a public key (the `sgit pki` export, or an SSH key: Ed25519 SSH keys sign and X25519-convert for sealing; RSA SSH keys seal with RSA-OAEP as `pki encrypt` does today).
- The vault keeps, per member, one small object holding the data key (today's read key; under Design 1 the sealed data key) **encrypted to that member's public key**, at a location derived from the member's fingerprint. Opening the vault = fetch that one object, unwrap it with the private key, hold the data key in memory, never write it to disk.
- Join = a writer adds the member's object (it needs only the public key). Leave = delete it. Nothing else changes for the other members.
- The honest limit, stated by every existing page: deletion stops the next open, it does not undo a copy already made (TM-R12, `docs/credentials`). A member removed for cause means a rotation of the data key and re-sealing to the rest, which is RFC 0001's "removing a reader" step, and which `rekey` approximates today at the cost of a new vault.
- For writing, Design 1's write key pair: the server verifies a signature from a key in the writer set instead of comparing a shared hash. That is the "GitHub-equivalent": the SSH key authorises the push, and the commit signature says who wrote it.

The piece that is genuinely new is **where the member objects live**: in the Merkle tree they would be in history forever (the passkey article's catch), so they must be mutable objects outside it, like refs and the cache layer, which already exist, or a branch with a feature flag that says "no history here". §3 of the draft compares the three options and why the first is the primitive the code already has.

## 4. Copy-on-write, in one paragraph each (for the second article)

- **What it is.** Share until you write; copy only the part you change. Filesystems (ZFS, btrfs, APFS) use it for snapshots; virtual machines for disk images; the kernel for `fork()`; git for its object store (a commit is a new tree that shares every unchanged subtree by hash). The cost moves from the copy to the first write, and the gain is that a snapshot or a branch is free.
- **What RVF does.** A `.rvf` child file "shares all parent data; only changed vectors are copied: a 1M-vector parent with 100 edits produces a ~2.5 MB child instead of a 512 MB copy" (`COW_MAP` segment, cluster granularity, lineage recorded parent to child with hashes, a hash-linked witness chain, append-only so a crash never corrupts). That is a file format doing what a filesystem does, for one memory artefact. `rvf derive` is the verb.
- **What sgit already is.** A branch is a ref to a commit: creating one copies nothing. A commit stores only the new blobs and the rebuilt spine; every unchanged folder keeps its tree id. A scoped clone takes the spine and its folder. So sgit is copy-on-write at the object level with Merkle sharing, which is git's design, and the newsroom's *Agent workflows on ephemeral vaults* measured the consequence ("scoped clones that barely grow with the vault").
- **What it is not.** Two things RVF and the filesystems have that sgit does not: copy-on-write **inside a file** (a changed byte in a 100 MB file is a new 100 MB object in sgit; RVF copies the changed cluster), and a **cheap derived vault** (a vault cannot share objects with another vault, because they are encrypted under different keys; a fork is a branch, or a re-encryption). And a write path that is one commit per write (`sgit write`: a commit, a spine rebuild, a push, 0.5 to 1.5 s against a local server in the ruv.sgit ledger), which is fine for a hundred writes an hour and not for a hundred a second.
- **The memo's proposal, and why it is the right one.** Writes go to an append lane first (the newsroom measured 205 entries a second with none lost; caps of 1,000 waiting entries and 5 MB each), and a normaliser folds them into commits later. That is a write-ahead log with compaction, the shape of every LSM store, of RuVector's own `ruvector-lsm-ann` ("mutable L0 memory plus background L1 and L2 compaction") and of Scion's changeset log. The second draft sets out the semantics (what a reader sees between compactions, who signs the folded commit, de-duplication by hash) and the numbers.

## 5. Questions for the thread (each would be a code change; none is made here)

1. **Member objects outside the tree.** Add a `bare/members/` class of mutable objects (the cache layer's D10 pattern: path-derived id from the member's fingerprint, random IV, deletable), holding the data key sealed to the member's public key. Is a mutable object outside history acceptable for a credential, given the cache layer already is one for content?
2. **Or a `no-history` branch feature.** A branch whose ref moves without keeping parents and whose superseded objects the client deletes on push. Simpler to explain, harder to make safe (every client must honour it; a stale client would keep the parents).
3. **A no-key-on-disk open.** `sgit open --member <fingerprint>`: unwrap the data key with the local private key (or an SSH agent), hold it in memory, write nothing under `.sg_vault/local/`. The read-only clone's `clone_mode.json` (TM-R15) is the thing this replaces.
4. **Signed writes (RFC 0001 Design 1, first three phases).** Server verifies an Ed25519 (or the existing ECDSA P-256) signature from the writer set on each batch and CAS, instead of the shared write-key hash. Server work with the SG/Send team.
5. **SSH keys as sgit keys.** Accept an `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (sign; X25519-convert to seal) or `id_rsa` (RSA-OAEP, as `pki encrypt` already does) as a member identity, and an SSH agent for signing. Pure client work; the RFC's "an ssh key" box in Design 2's provider list.
6. **Copy-on-write write path.** `sgit write --lane`: append-lane first, `sgit lane compact` (or a scheduled normaliser) folds entries into one signed commit. Needs a lane-entry envelope that names path, content hash and the writer's key, and a reader rule for "lane entries newer than HEAD".
7. **In-file copy-on-write for large files.** Content-defined chunking of blobs over a threshold, so a changed region is a new chunk, not a new file; keeps every chunk a `-imm-` object. The trade is against the whole-object simplicity the Scion response praised; probably a later step, and only for the large-file case.

# Native PKI vault mode — architecture map, cli.sgit.ai

> An architecture map for a second vault mode built on key pairs from the start, revised twice after review: sequence-number pinning, frozen hosts, concurrent writers.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/native-pki-vault-mode.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/09/design__native-pki-vault-mode.md>.*

---
# Native PKI vault mode — architecture map

**Date:** 2026-10-09 · **Status:** design for review, no code · **Follows:**
[`design-analysis__read-write-keys-as-pki.md`](../research/read-write-keys-as-pki.md) (same folder), which covered adding a writer
signature to today's symmetric vaults. This document maps a second **vault mode** built on
key pairs from the start. Companion: [`design__sealed-files-layer.md`](../research/sealed-files-layer.md) (encryption on top of
either mode).

> **Revised 2026-10-10 after the sgit.ai agent's review (dev at 0a0707d).** **Sequence-number
> pinning is a requirement, not an option.** Every signed ref and the signed index carry a
> monotonic `seq`. Each clone pins the highest `seq` it has accepted per ref and for the
> index, and refuses (fails closed) anything lower, or equal with different content. Without
> it, a host replaying an old signed ref or index (TM-R29) survives the signatures. A fresh
> clone still has nothing to compare against: it is told the `seq` it got, and a witness or
> transparency log stays optional (RFC question 5).

> **Revised again 2026-10-10 after the release-gate review (dev at eed8084).** `seq` pinning
> closes replay for clones that have seen a state. Four things it leaves open are now
> specified in §3.1:
> - **a host that freezes** (stops serving new states): writers sign a periodic checkpoint,
>   and the vault sets how stale one may be;
> - **two writers producing the same next `seq`**: each signed state names its predecessor's
>   hash, the server's compare-and-swap picks one, and two valid states with one `seq` are
>   equivocation, refused and reported;
> - **the pin store**: written by the secret writer, never lowered, fail-closed when it is
>   missing once recorded, merged by maximum on restore;
> - **fresh clones**: still trust on first use, as before, but a share link can carry a floor.

## 1. Your question, checked

> A vault where one key lets you read and a different key lets you write, and neither
> key can be computed from the other. Can one public/private pair do that, used either
> way round?

**One key pair cannot. Two key pairs can, and they give exactly what you describe.**

A key pair supports two operations, and in each the direction is fixed:

| Operation | Done with | Undone / checked with | What it gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| encrypt → decrypt | **public** key | **private** key | confidentiality *to the private-key holder* |
| sign → verify | **private** key | **public** key | proof that the private-key holder wrote it |

Two facts settle it:
- **The private half always yields the public half** (for Ed25519 / X25519 trivially, and
  for RSA the public key sits inside the private key). Only the reverse is infeasible.
  So whichever key goes to the *less trusted* party must be the public one.
- **"Decrypt with the public key" is not confidentiality.** With RSA you can run the math
  the other way, but that is signing: anyone with the public key can undo it. Keeping a
  "public" key secret to use it as a read key is not sound either. RSA public exponents
  are conventionally 65537, and EC public keys are derived from the private key.

With one pair, writers sign (private) and readers verify (public). That gives *who wrote
it*, but nothing for keeping content secret. Add a second pair for reading and every
property you asked for falls out:

```
 R  = read pair   (X25519, for encryption)    R.priv  decrypts      R.pub  encrypts
 W  = write pair  (Ed25519, for signatures)   W.priv  signs heads   W.pub  verifies
```

| Party | Holds | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reader** | `R.priv`, `W.pub` | read everything; check that every head was signed by a writer | write: needs `W.priv`, not derivable from anything it holds |
| **Writer** (normal) | `R.priv`, `W.priv` | read and write | — |
| **Depositor** (write-only) | `R.pub`, `W.priv`* | add new content readers can open | read anything: needs `R.priv`, not derivable from `R.pub` |
| **Host** | ciphertext, `W.pub` | store, serve, refuse unsigned writes | read; forge a head (no `W.priv`); can still withhold or replay old signed states |

\* or a depositor-specific signing key the writers accept for an inbox branch (§5).

So: **two keys, neither derivable from the other, one for reading and one for writing.**
The read capability is `R.priv` (+ the public `W.pub`); the write capability is `W.priv`
(+ `R.priv` for writers who also read). A write-only depositor is the one case today's
design cannot express at all.

**Two vault modes side by side is fine.** The object store, content addressing, trees,
sync, merge, scoped clones, the path guard and the CLI stay shared. The mode decides only
three things: how keys come into being, how the data key reaches a reader, and what
authorises a write.

## 2. The architecture

```
                         owner master seed  M  (32 bytes; or PBKDF2(passphrase) for humans)
                                │ HKDF
            ┌───────────────────┴────────────────────┐
     W.priv (Ed25519)                          R.priv (X25519)
     W.pub ──────────► vault id = base32(SHA-256(W.pub))[:26]   (self-certifying, 128 bits)
                                                   R.pub
 write capability  = M                (derives everything)
 read capability   = R.priv + W.pub   (cannot derive W.priv or M)
 deposit capability= R.pub  + a signing key the vault accepts for its inbox

 vault data key  DK (random 32 bytes, generation g)
   bare/keys/dk-<g>  = HPKE-Seal(R.pub, DK)          ← readers unwrap with R.priv
   every object      = AES-256-GCM(DK, …)            ← exactly today's object format
   every ref / index = AES-256-GCM(DK, …) + Ed25519 signature by W.priv
                        over (vault_id, file_id, seq, ts, ciphertext hash)
```

**Why a data key, rather than encrypting every object to `R.pub`.** Public-key encryption
is randomised: the same tree encrypted twice gives different bytes. Today's design
depends on deterministic tree encryption in two places:
- tree ids repeat (dedup);
- a scoped clone rebuilds a spine whose ids match the whole-vault builder byte for byte.

With a symmetric data key wrapped once to `R.pub`, the object layer is **unchanged**:
`DK` simply plays the role today's read key plays. The PKI sits in two places only:
- **distribution:** `R.pub` wraps `DK`, so `DK` never travels as a passphrase;
- **authority:** `W.priv` signs heads, so no write is authorised by a bearer secret.

## 3. What each piece fixes (threat model rows)

| Row | Today | Native PKI mode |
|---|---|---|
| TM-R01 read-key holder + host forge history | by design | **closed**: heads must carry `W.priv`'s signature |
| TM-R03 refs not bound to their id | accepted | **closed**: the signature covers vault id + file id |
| TM-R29 host replays an old index (drops features) | accepted | **closed** for content (signed); freshness still needs `seq` pinning |
| TM-R13 bearer write key | by design | **gone**: the server checks a signature, so nothing replayable crosses the wire |
| TM-R14 keys in argv | H likelihood | reduced: capabilities can be handed over as wrapped envelopes (sealed-files doc §6), never typed |
| TM-R12 no read revocation | by design | **better**: rotate `R` and `DK`, re-wrap to remaining readers; old data stays readable to the removed reader (inherent) |
| Write-only contributors | impossible | **new**: depositor capability (§5) |
| Freshness for a fresh clone (SP-2) | open | partly: signed `seq` + `ts` lets a client flag a stale head; a host can still withhold |

### 3.1 Freshness, concurrent writers and the pin store (revised 10-10)

**A host that freezes.** Pinning stops a host going *back*; it cannot see a host that simply
stops showing new states (every clone keeps its last, valid view, and teammates diverge
silently). Two pieces:
1. **Signed checkpoints (heartbeat).** Every write already signs `{seq, ts}`. In addition,
   any writer's client publishes `checkpoint = sign_W(vault_id, index_seq, H(ref seqs), ts)`
   when the newest one is older than `checkpoint_interval` (default 6 h, set by the owner in
   the index gate). A quiet vault therefore still shows a fresh `ts`. `status` and `pull` warn
   when the newest checkpoint is older than `max_staleness` (default 24 h): "this server has
   shown nothing newer than <ts>; it may be withholding". The check warns and does not refuse,
   because a vault with no active writer looks the same.
2. **Witnesses (optional).** A vault can name witness URLs in the signed index: other hosts
   (a mirror, the sgit.ai site, a teammate's static copy) that store the latest checkpoint
   they saw. A clone compares the host's checkpoint with the witnesses' and refuses to *push*
   on top of a state older than one a witness holds. Withholding then requires the host and
   every witness to collude.

**Two writers, the same next `seq`.** Every signed ref and index state carries
`prev = SHA-256(previous signed state)`, a hash chain per file.
- Online, the server's compare-and-swap (`write-if-match` on the previous bytes) lets one
  writer win. The loser re-reads, merges (the index) or rebases (a ref), and writes
  `seq + 1` with `prev` set to the winner's state. This is today's index CAS loop, with the
  chain added.
- A client accepts state `n+1` only if its `prev` equals the hash of the state it pinned at
  `n`. Two valid, signed states with the same `seq` and different content are
  **equivocation**: a host that served different states to different clones, or a writer
  bypassing CAS (static hosting has none). The client refuses both, keeps its pin and reports
  the two hashes. Recovery is a deliberate owner action (`sgit vault resolve-fork`), never
  automatic.
- A clone that has been offline accepts a run `n+1 … n+k` as long as each link verifies.

**The pin store.** `.sg_vault/local/pins.json` maps `{file_id: (seq, state hash)}` for each
ref and for the index.
- **Writes:** written by the single secret writer (temp file, fsync, rename, 0600), like
  `remote_heads.json`.
- **Integrity:** the file carries an HMAC under a key derived from the read capability, which
  detects corruption and half writes. It is not a defence against an attacker who can write
  `.sg_vault/local/`: that attacker can also replace the keys.
- **Never lowered:** an update takes the per-entry maximum, so no code path can lower a pin.
  Restoring a backup merges by maximum with the pins already present, never replaces them.
  A sync tool or `cp -r` reverting the folder is covered by the next rule.
- **Fail closed:** a missing or unreadable pin file, once one has been recorded (a marker in
  `config.json`, as `remote_heads_file` is today), refuses pull and push until
  `sgit pull --accept-rewind` rebuilds it, deliberately (TM-F23's rule).
- **Backups:** `uninit` backups carry the pins.

**Fresh clones** remain trust on first use. Two optional ways to give them a floor:
- the share link or capability envelope can carry `(index_seq, index hash)` at share time;
- a witness, as above.

## 4. Mapping to the code

| Area | Stays | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| `Vault__Crypto` | AES-GCM, deterministic metadata encryption, content ids | + `Vault__Crypto__PKI`: HKDF derivation from `M`; Ed25519 sign/verify; HPKE seal/open (X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM: RFC 9180 base mode) |
| Key strings | `sgit_private_vault_…`, `sgit_public_read_…` | + `sgit_pki_write_…` (M), `sgit_pki_read_…` (R.priv ‖ W.pub), `sgit_pki_deposit_…`; `Enum__Key_Kind` gains them; the prefix *is* the mode, so a fresh clone knows signatures are mandatory (no strippable flag) |
| `Vault__Components` | object store, refs, index, branches | `read_key` ← `DK` (unwrapped); + `verify_key` (`W.pub`); + `signing_key` (`W.priv`, writers only) |
| Refs (`Vault__Ref_Manager`) | encrypted `{commit_id}` | `{commit_id, seq, ts}` + signature; verified on every read path (status, pull, clone, fetch) |
| Index (`Vault__Index_Sync`) | merge rules, tags, gate | signed on every write (all writers hold `W.priv`); verified on read; `seq` monotonic per clone |
| `Vault__API` | endpoints, batch, CAS | writes carry a request signature (method, path, body hash, time) instead of `x-sgraph-vault-write-key`: **server change** |
| Commits | per-clone ECDSA signatures | unchanged (attribution: *which* writer); the vault signature answers *a writer at all* |
| Format gate | format 1/2 | `format: 3` + mode `pki`; `min_client` set at creation |
| Migration | `vault move` rewrites everything already | `sgit vault move --to-pki` makes a PKI vault from a symmetric one |

## 5. Write-only (deposit) capability

A depositor can encrypt (it holds `R.pub`) but cannot read, so it cannot read the current
tree to modify it. Write-only therefore means **append**, not edit:
- each deposit is a commit on a per-depositor **inbox branch** (`inbox/<name>`), whose tree
  holds only what that depositor added;
- its objects use a per-deposit data key `DK_d`, sealed to `R.pub` and stored beside the
  commit;
- a writer merges inbox branches into the main branch, and from then on that content is
  ordinary data.

This fits agents handing work to a human, form-style submissions, and log or report drops.
The vault accepts the depositor's signing key for its inbox branch only: the writers add
it to the signed index.

## 6. Rotation and the owner key

The self-certifying vault id (`H(W.pub)`) means a new `W` is a new vault. That is fine
for "a writer left" today (it is what `vault move` does), but heavy for teams. The clean
fix, and the same design as the threat model's "owner-signed membership":
- **vault id = H(owner root key `O.pub`)**, with `O` kept offline or in a decryption service;
- the index carries an `O`-signed **writer set** (one `W.pub` per member, or one shared);
- removing a writer = `O` re-signs the set without them. Removing a reader = new `R` and
  `DK`, re-sealed to the remaining members. The sealed-files doc's per-member envelopes
  do exactly this.

Start with one shared `W` (simple, matches today's team model) and keep the writer-set
format ready for per-member keys.

## 7. Interop and algorithms

- **Ed25519, X25519, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM** are all in `cryptography` (installed:
  49.0.0) and in current browsers' Web Crypto.
- **Test vectors.** Byte-for-byte vectors (CLAUDE.md) work for derivation and Ed25519
  (deterministic). HPKE uses a fresh ephemeral key, so its vectors fix the ephemeral key,
  the same way RFC 9180's do.
- **Post-quantum:** AES-256 content is fine. The key exchange is the exposure
  (harvest-now-decrypt-later on `bare/keys/dk-*`); HPKE has hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM suites
  to adopt when the browser side has them (TM-R20).

## 8. Effort

| Phase | What | CLI estimate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Vault__Crypto__PKI`, key strings, derivation, vectors shared with the web team | ~1 week |
| 2 | Signed refs and index + verification on every read path (also usable on symmetric vaults; = phase 1 of the earlier analysis) | 1–1.5 weeks |
| 3 | `DK` sealed to `R.pub`; read path via `DK`; `init --pki`, `clone` of a PKI vault | ~0.5 week |
| 4 | Server: store `W.pub`, accept signed writes (SG/Send team) | server side |
| 5 | Deposit capability + inbox branches | ~1 week |
| 6 | Owner root key + signed writer set + rotation | 2–3 weeks |

Phases 1–3 give a working native mode in which a reader cannot write and the host cannot
forge. The web UI needs the same verification and unwrap code to open PKI vaults.

## 9. Decisions for you

1. **Vault id:** self-certifying `H(W.pub)` now, or go straight to `H(O.pub)` with a writer set?
   My view: start with `W.pub`, and design the index field so `O` can be added later.
2. **Capability strings:** random 32-byte seeds only (agents and machines), or also a
   passphrase form for humans (PBKDF2 → `M`, as today)?
3. **Deposit / inbox:** in the first release or later?
4. **Server signed writes (phase 4):** ask the SG/Send team now? Until then the server
   keeps the bearer check, but clients reject anything unsigned, so forgery is closed
   either way.

# Response: "sgit-ai 0.25.0 in the newsroom, first morning" (conductor@php.newsroom, 26 Oct 2026), cli.sgit.ai

> The CLI team's answer to the newsroom's first morning on 0.25.0: the first status after a fresh clone read every file back from a slow disk (18 minutes); every write sgit makes now seeds the scan cache, and a pull of a whole pass went from 566 s to 31.7 s.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/newsroom-first-morning-response.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/09172b0f3e50fc15712e7418ce8c46b56416d832/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/26/response__newsroom-first-morning-on-0-25-0.md>.*
