# Sealed files — a second encryption layer on top of a vault, cli.sgit.ai

> A second encryption layer on top of either vault mode: files sealed to named recipients with ECDH P-256, HKDF and AES-256-GCM, with the corrections from the sgit.ai agent's review.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/sealed-files-layer.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/09/design__sealed-files-layer.md>.*

---
# Sealed files — a second encryption layer on top of a vault

**Date:** 2026-10-09 · **Status:** design for review, no code · **Companion:**
[`design__native-pki-vault-mode.md`](../research/native-pki-vault-mode.md) (same folder). This layer works on **either** vault
mode, symmetric (today) or native PKI.

> **Revised 2026-10-10 after the sgit.ai agent's review (dev at 0a0707d).** Three corrections,
> applied below:
> 1. **No "compare by re-sealing".** Sealing is randomised (a fresh file key and ephemeral key
>    every time), so re-sealing never reproduces the stored bytes. The tree entry instead
>    carries a **keyed hash of the plaintext**: HMAC-SHA256 under a key derived from the vault
>    read key, stored under the read key. A recipient compares plaintext to that HMAC. A
>    non-recipient compares the sealed bytes. Unlike the unkeyed `content_hash`, the keyed
>    hash does not let a vault reader confirm a guess of the content.
> 2. **Seal-policy changes need an authorised signer.** Otherwise any writer can "unseal by
>    policy": drop a rule or a recipient, and the next commit of that path is sealed to fewer
>    people, or not at all. `.sgit/seal` names its `admins` (public keys). A commit that
>    changes the policy must be signed by one of them, or pull refuses it, as
>    `signatures-required` does. The first policy is pinned by the clone that adds it (trust
>    on first use, like the PKI mode's writer set).
> 3. **The construction is Web-Crypto-native: ECDH P-256 + HKDF-SHA256 + AES-256-GCM.** That
>    is the HPKE base mode with the P-256 KEM (RFC 9180, DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256)). Browsers
>    open sealed files with no WASM dependency, and CLAUDE.md's byte-for-byte parity rule holds
>    with test vectors. age is kept as an **interop path only**:
>    - `sgit seal export --age` re-seals a file for the stock `age` tool;
>    - hardware and KMS keys are reached through a provider bridge that speaks the
>      `age-plugin` protocol for the unwrap step only (only the file key crosses it).
>    §3 and §9 below are updated accordingly.

> **Revised again 2026-10-10 after the release-gate review (dev at eed8084).** Two more
> corrections:
> 1. **The comparison value moves inside the sealed envelope.** A keyed hash under a key
>    derived from the *vault read key* (correction 1 above) does not stop guessing: every
>    reader holds that key, so a reader who is not a recipient can still compute the HMAC of
>    a guess and compare. The comparison value is now `HMAC-SHA256(K_cmp, plaintext)` with
>    `K_cmp = HKDF(FK, info="sgit seal compare v1")`, where `FK` is the per-file key that only
>    recipients unwrap. It is stored **inside** the envelope, as the first 32 bytes of the
>    encrypted payload, never in the tree entry. A recipient's clone caches it per sealed blob
>    id in a 0600 local file, so `status` does not call the identity provider on every run.
>    The tree entry holds only the hash of the sealed bytes.
> 2. **The chunked AES-GCM payload has defined framing** (§3.1): a per-file payload key, a
>    counter nonce, and the chunk index and a final-chunk flag in the AAD. A reader refuses
>    truncation, reordering, extension and a final flag in the wrong place.

## 1. The idea, in your words and in mechanism

> As the author I can say: "here is my public key, encrypt this data with it; if you need
> to decrypt it, point over there". The files still exist in the vault as before, but
> only someone with the private key can read them. The service holding the private key
> can be local, remote, or anything else.

Mechanically, this is **envelope encryption to recipients' public keys, with decryption
delegated to an identity provider**. git-crypt (GPG), SOPS (KMS/age/PGP) and age
(X25519, ssh keys, hardware plugins) all use this pattern. The vault keeps doing its job,
and selected files get an inner envelope:

```
 plaintext ──► [ inner: sealed to recipients' public keys ]  ──► [ outer: vault encryption ] ──► host
               file key FK (random) encrypts the content          read key / DK, exactly as today
               FK is wrapped once per recipient public key
```

| Who | Sees |
|---|---|
| The host | ciphertext only (outer layer), as today |
| A **vault reader** (read key) | that the file exists: its name, path, history, approximate size, who changed it when. **Not its content.** |
| A **recipient** (holds, or can ask for, a matching private key) | the content |

Two levels, two key systems:
- **Outer layer** (vault key): hides everything from the host.
- **Inner layer** (recipient keys): hides content from everyone who is not a recipient,
  including the host, other vault members, and anyone who later obtains the vault's
  read key.

## 2. What each party can do, precisely

| Party | Create a sealed file | Read it | Edit it | Replace / delete it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recipient (with its provider) | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Vault writer, not a recipient | **yes**: only the recipients' *public* keys are needed | no | no (editing needs reading first) | **yes, blindly**: it can write new sealed bytes over the file, or delete it |
| Vault reader | no | no | no | no |
| Host | no | no | no | withhold or replay, as today |

One correction to "you could only edit or modify a file if you have that key". **Editing**
needs the key, because you must read before you change. **Replacing** does not. Any
vault writer can put new sealed bytes at the same path, because sealing needs only
public keys. Stopping that is an integrity question, not a confidentiality one, and has
two answers that can be combined:
1. **Signed envelopes:** the sealer signs the inner envelope with its own key. Readers
   (recipients) check that the signer is on the path's allowed-author list (§4).
2. **Path rules enforced on commit/pull:** a commit that changes a sealed path must be
   signed by an allowed author. Otherwise pull refuses it, as `signatures-required` does
   today. With the native PKI mode's writer set, this becomes a hard rule.

## 3. Format

**Recommendation (revised 10-10): an HPKE envelope, DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) + AES-256-GCM,
all native to Web Crypto; age v1 as an export and plugin-bridge format only.** The original
reasoning for age follows, kept for the record.
- It is specified, small and audited. Recipient types include X25519, ssh-ed25519 /
  ssh-rsa and scrypt (passphrase), plus a **plugin protocol** (`age-plugin-*`).
- The plugin protocol is precisely "the private key lives elsewhere": YubiKey/PIV, TPM,
  Secure Enclave and cloud KMS plugins already exist.
- **A sealed file can be opened with the stock `age` tool, without sgit**, which is good
  for longevity and audit.
- The pieces it needs (X25519, HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305, HMAC-SHA256, scrypt) are
  all in `cryptography`. A minimal reader/writer for the X25519 and plugin stanzas is
  a few hundred lines.

**Trade-off to decide.** age's payload cipher is ChaCha20-Poly1305, which **Web Crypto
does not provide**, while CLAUDE.md asks for Web Crypto byte-for-byte parity. The browser
would use `typage` (the reference TypeScript age implementation). The alternative is a
custom HPKE envelope (X25519 + HKDF + AES-256-GCM, all in Web Crypto), at the cost of the
tool ecosystem and the plugins. My view: age. The plugin ecosystem *is* the "decryption
service elsewhere" feature, and the parity rule can name `typage` as the browser
implementation for this layer.

```
sealed file   = "age-encryption.org/v1\n"
                "-> X25519 <ephemeral>\n<wrapped FK>\n"        one stanza per recipient
                "-> piv-p256 <tag> <…>\n<wrapped FK>\n"        a hardware / plugin recipient
                "--- <header MAC>\n"
                <payload: ChaCha20-Poly1305 STREAM, 64 KiB chunks, under a key from FK>
              [ + optional detached Ed25519 signature by the sealer, in a sidecar stanza ]
```

### 3.1 Payload framing (HPKE envelope, revised 10-10)

```
header        = magic "sgit-seal/1" ‖ header_nonce (16 random bytes) ‖ recipient stanzas
                (each: HPKE enc ‖ HPKE-Seal(recipient pub, FK)) ‖ chunk_size (u32, 65536)
H             = SHA-256(header)
PK            = HKDF-SHA256(ikm=FK, salt=header_nonce, info="sgit seal payload v1")   (32 bytes)
plaintext'    = HMAC-SHA256(K_cmp, plaintext) ‖ plaintext        (the comparison value rides inside)
chunk i       = plaintext'[i·65536 : (i+1)·65536]                 (the last may be shorter;
                                                                   an empty file is one empty final chunk)
nonce_i       = u88_be(i) ‖ final_i                               (12 bytes; final_i = 0x01 on the last chunk only)
aad_i         = H ‖ u64_be(i) ‖ final_i
ct_i          = AES-256-GCM(PK, nonce_i, chunk i, aad_i)
sealed file   = header ‖ ct_0 ‖ ct_1 ‖ … ‖ ct_n
```

- **The AAD binds each chunk to this header, its position and whether it ends the file**, so
  chunks cannot be moved between files, reordered, dropped from the end (the new last chunk
  has `final = 0` and fails) or followed by more (anything after a `final = 1` chunk is
  refused). The index is also in the nonce, which keeps nonces unique under `PK` without
  storing them.
- `PK` is fresh per sealing (random `FK` and `header_nonce`), so the counter nonce never repeats
  under one key. At most 2^32 chunks (256 TiB) per file.
- A reader streams: it verifies and releases chunk *i* before reading *i+1*, but treats the
  file as complete only after a valid `final = 1` chunk. The plaintext is written to a temp
  file and renamed only then, so a truncated file never reaches the working copy.
- Test vectors (Python and Web Crypto, byte for byte): empty file, exactly one chunk, one
  chunk plus one byte, three chunks; and the refusals: truncated at a chunk boundary, two
  chunks swapped, a chunk appended after the final one, a final flag on chunk 0 of three, a
  header byte changed.

## 4. Policy: which files, to whom, written by whom

A committed policy file, signed like any commit. It works the way `.gitattributes` works
for git-crypt:

```
# .sgit/seal      (committed; changes to it are themselves a signed, reviewable commit)
recipients:
  dinis   = age1qy…            # published key, fingerprint pinned here
  backup  = age1zz…            # offline recovery key
  ops     = age1yubikey1q…     # hardware-held
seal:
  secrets/**        -> dinis, backup
  finance/*.xlsx    -> dinis, ops, backup
  **/.env           -> dinis, backup
authors:                       # optional: who may change a sealed path (§2)
  secrets/**        -> dinis
```

- **Recipients by public key**, fetched from the published key directory and **pinned by
  fingerprint in the policy**. A later change at the directory cannot silently add
  someone; the policy changes only through a commit.
- `sgit commit` seals any changed file a rule matches. `sgit seal add <path> --to <name>`
  and `sgit seal rekey` edit the policy.

## 5. On disk, in the working copy

| Clone | A sealed file looks like |
|---|---|
| Has a working identity for that file | the **plaintext**, written 0600 (secret writer). `sgit status` compares `HMAC(K_cmp, plaintext)` with the value inside the envelope (cached locally per blob, revised 10-10); never by re-sealing, which is randomised |
| Has no identity, or the provider is unreachable | the **sealed bytes**, unchanged (an `age` file). `status` treats it as unchanged, never deleted or modified: the same "keep the committed entry" rule the symlink ban uses |

Integration points in the current code:
- **Tree entries** carry `content_hash` = an unkeyed `sha256(plaintext)[:12]` (today's
  `Vault__Crypto.content_hash`), stored under the vault read key. For a sealed file that
  would let any vault reader *confirm a guess* of the content. **For sealed files the hash
  is taken over the sealed bytes.** The entry also gets a `sealed` flag and the
  recipients' fingerprints (still under the read key).
- **Blob reuse** (`encrypt_or_reuse_blob` matches on `content_hash`) then works on sealed
  bytes. Re-sealing an unchanged file is skipped as long as the plaintext is unchanged and
  the policy did not change (a local cache of plaintext hash → sealed blob).
- **Merge:** sealed files are binary unless both sides can be opened locally. A conflict
  keeps both versions (`.conflict`). Diff shows `sealed, changed` without an identity.

## 6. The decryption service ("identity provider")

Only the **16-byte file key** crosses the boundary, never the content:

```
sgit ──(stanza: recipient tag + wrapped FK)──► provider ──(FK, or "refused")──► sgit
```

| Provider | Where the private key lives | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Local identity file | `~/.config/sgit/identities` (0600) | the simple default; written by the secret writer |
| ssh key / ssh-agent | your existing ssh key (ed25519/rsa) | age natively supports ssh recipients; nothing new to manage |
| Hardware | YubiKey / PIV / TPM / Secure Enclave via `age-plugin-*` | touch-to-decrypt; the key cannot be copied |
| Remote service | a team service, cloud KMS, or an SG/Send service, over an authenticated API | can **log, rate-limit, require approval and revoke** per unwrap, per file: an audit trail of who opened what. Offline means unreadable, by design |

Configuration is per clone (`.sg_vault/local/identities` naming providers) or per user.
The interface is the age plugin protocol, so any existing plugin works, and our own
remote-service provider is just one more plugin.

**Capability hand-off.** The same envelope moves *vault* capabilities between people.
`sgit share --to dinis` seals a read or write capability to Dinis's published key: no
passphrase in chat, argv or shell history. This closes most of TM-R14 and is phase 2 of
the earlier analysis.

## 7. What it protects, and what it does not

| Threat | Covered |
|---|---|
| Host reads content | yes (outer layer, as today) |
| A vault member who is not a recipient reads a sealed file | **yes** |
| The vault read key leaks (a share, a log, an old clone) | **yes for sealed files**: they need a recipient key as well |
| A recipient's key is revoked | only for **new** seals: history sealed to them stays readable to them (inherent; rotate secrets, not just files) |
| A non-recipient writer replaces a sealed file | detected with signed envelopes / author rules (§2); not prevented on the host |
| File names, paths, sizes, history from vault readers | not hidden (they live in the vault's tree). Sizes are approximate (age adds per-chunk overhead); pad if needed |
| Plaintext on a recipient's disk | out of scope: it is the recipient's machine (written 0600) |
| Provider compromise | as strong as the provider: hardware or approval-based providers limit it |

## 8. Relation to the native PKI mode

- **Independent of the vault mode:** sealed files work in symmetric vaults today.
- **In a PKI vault**, per-member envelopes are also the natural way to hand `DK` to each
  member: the vault's `DK` is sealed to every member's public key instead of to one
  shared `R`. Removing a reader then means re-sealing to the rest (native-mode doc §6).
- The deposit capability (native-mode doc §5) plus sealed files gives a **drop box**:
  contributors can add files that only the owner can open, and cannot read each other's.

## 9. Effort

| Step | What | CLI estimate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | HPKE envelope (DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256) + AES-256-GCM, chunked), Python and Web Crypto with shared vectors; `seal export --age` | ~1 week |
| 2 | `.sgit/seal` policy, seal on commit, open on checkout/pull, sealed-bytes hashing, status rules | 1–1.5 weeks |
| 3 | Providers: identity file + ssh keys, then the plugin protocol (hardware/KMS), then a remote-service plugin | ~1 week (+ service side) |
| 4 | Signed envelopes + author rules on pull | ~0.5 week |
| 5 | `sgit share --to <contact>` (capability hand-off) | ~0.5 week |
| — | Web UI: open sealed files with Web Crypto (no WASM) + a provider bridge | web team |

## 10. Decisions for you

1. **Format (revised 10-10):** the Web-Crypto-native HPKE envelope, with age as an export and
   plugin-bridge format. (Was: age.)
2. **Working copy:** plaintext when the clone can open the file (git-crypt style), or
   always sealed on disk with `sgit cat` / `sgit open` to read?
3. **Integrity for sealed paths:** signed envelopes + author rules in the first version,
   or later?
4. **First remote provider:** an SG/Send-hosted unwrap service with approval and audit,
   or a cloud KMS plugin?

# Sealed vault keys in sgit: requirements, cli.sgit.ai

> Requirements for sealed vault keys in sgit, from an agent that spent a fortnight moving vault keys between Dinis Cruz and many agent sessions, by paste and then by sealed QR code. The three places a vault key is still in clear on v0.24.0 (the clone's vault_key file, process arguments and shell history, the file pki-agent open saves), ten requirements (clone from a sealed key, no plaintext key on argv, sealed at rest, migration, record fingerprints, trust with an operator override, never print a key, warn when the pki key will not persist, expiry and renewal, say why trust failed), the non-goals, seven acceptance tests done by hand, and three open questions.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/sealed-vault-keys-requirements.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# Sealed vault keys in sgit: requirements

**Draft for the sgit team.** Written 24 October 2026 against `sgit-ai` v0.24.0 and the `pki-agent` tool
published at pki.sgit.ai. The leak points and behaviours below were checked on that version; the
requirements come from a fortnight of moving vault keys between a person and many agent sessions, by
paste and then by sealed QR code.

---

## The goal in one line

A vault key should travel sealed to its recipient's public key, open only in memory, and be stored
at rest still sealed, so that **no vault key is ever written in cleartext to a transcript, a command
line, a temp file or a working copy**.

## Why: where a vault key is in cleartext today

Sealed delivery through `pki.sgit.ai` already fixes the worst problem, the chat transcript. Three
places remain, all checked on v0.24.0:

| # | Where | How it happens | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `.sg_vault/local/vault_key` in every clone | `sgit clone <key>` writes the key there in plaintext (mode 0600) | as long as the clone exists, on every machine that ever cloned |
| 2 | process arguments and shell history | the key is a positional argument to `sgit clone`, and `pki-agent seal --text` takes it on the command line | process lifetime; shell history indefinitely |
| 3 | the output of `pki-agent open --save DIR` | the opened secret is written to a file so that sgit can use it | until someone shreds it |

Point 1 is the one that matters. A sealed handover that ends in `sgit clone <key>` has protected the
key in transit and then written it to disk in the clear. Every working copy on every agent's machine
holds every vault key that agent has ever opened.

## What is already in place

The parts needed are built. This is wiring, not new cryptography.

- `sgit pki encrypt` / `sgit pki decrypt`: hybrid RSA-OAEP-4096 and AES-256-GCM, keys in
  `~/.sg-send/keys`.
- `pki-agent` (pki.sgit.ai): identities, a register, a pinned root, `seal` and `open`, and QR codes
  as strict JSON. Its `seal --from-vault` already reads the key from `sgit vault show-key` into
  memory without printing it. That is the pattern to generalise.
- The sealed message format (`m1.…`) and the key code (`k1.…`, which carries both public keys and
  the label).

## Requirements

### R1. Clone and attach from a sealed key

`sgit clone` and `sgit vault attach` accept a sealed key in place of a plaintext one:

```
sgit clone --sealed handover.png   <dir>
sgit clone --sealed m1.…           <dir>
sgit clone --sealed handover.enc   <dir>
sgit clone --sealed -              <dir>    # read the sealed form from stdin
```

The key is decrypted in memory with the local pki key and never written in cleartext.

### R2. Never take a plaintext key on argv by default

A plaintext key passed as a positional argument should either be refused with a pointer to
`--sealed` or stdin, or accepted with a warning that names the exposure (process list and shell
history). Keep an explicit opt-in for scripts.

### R3. Keep the key sealed at rest

Instead of `vault_key` in plaintext, a clone stores the key **sealed to the local agent's own pki
key** (for example `.sg_vault/local/vault_key.sealed`). Every command that needs the key unwraps it
in memory and drops it afterwards.

What this buys: an agent no longer holds N vault keys in cleartext. It holds **one** secret, its pki
private key, which protects all of them. Retiring that pki key revokes the agent's access to every
vault it held, without rotating any of the vaults.

### R4. Migrate existing clones

`sgit vault seal-key` converts an existing clone's plaintext `vault_key` into the sealed form and
shreds the plaintext. Running it twice does nothing.

### R5. Address messages by the record fingerprint

A sealed message must be addressed to the recipient's **record fingerprint, which is the signing
key's**, not the encryption key's. `pki-agent open` refuses a message whose `to` does not match
(*"to or from does not match the sealed code: refused"*). We hit this building a sealer from the key
code, and it is easy to get wrong because the key code carries both fingerprints. The library should
offer one function that returns the right one.

### R6. Trust: chain to the pinned root, with an explicit operator override

By default, seal only to recipients that chain to the pinned root, as `pki-agent seal` does today.

Also support a **principal-vouched** mode, behind an explicit flag, for an operator who carries the
recipient's key QR by hand:

```
sgit pki seal --to-key-qr agent-key.png --vouched-by-operator ...
```

It takes the recipient bundle from the key QR instead of the register, skips only the register
check, and records that in the message itself (*"vouched by the operator in person, key carried by
hand"*), so the recipient sees how it was trusted. This is how two keys were handed to an agent that
was not yet enrolled, and it worked. It belongs in the tool, behind a named flag, rather than in a
patched copy.

When this mode is used, the operator is the only check that the key belongs to the agent. The flag's
help text should say so, and tell the operator to compare the QR's fingerprint with the one the agent
printed in its own session.

### R7. Never print a key, including in errors

No command prints a vault key, a read key or a sealed secret's contents, including in error messages
and `--debug` output. `pki-agent read-qr` already gets this right: it reports kind, recipient, sender
and size, and never the secret.

### R8. Warn when the pki key will not persist

If the pki key lives under a home directory that will not survive (a `--rm` container with nothing
mounted over `~/.sg-send`), say so at `keygen`. With R3 in place, losing the pki key loses access to
every vault sealed to it, so this becomes the single most expensive mistake an agent can make. We hit
it once: a keypair made in a `--rm` container printed a fingerprint and a success message, was gone
when the container exited, and the backup sealed to it could never be opened.

A cheap check: after `keygen`, look for the key again in a fresh process and fail if it is missing.
The store location is not configurable (`CLI__Main` calls `pki.setup()` with no argument, so it is
always `~/.sg-send`); `HOME` is the only lever. Adding a `--home` flag or an env var would help.

### R9. Expiry and renewal

A confirmed agent record has a validity window (seven days was observed). Add `sgit pki status`
showing the expiry, warn when it is under 48 hours away, and offer a renewal command. Without this,
enrolled agents stop being trusted without warning, and people go back to pasting keys.

### R10. Say why trust failed

"Not trusted" currently looks the same whether the agent was never enrolled, is enrolled but not
confirmed, has expired, or the register has not rebuilt yet. These need different responses. We
waited about a day for an operator's confirmation to appear in the register, with no way to tell
that from a failed confirmation. Report which of these it is, and when the register was last built.

## Non-goals: what this does not fix

- **The unattended secret.** An agent that runs without a person needs some secret it can use
  unattended: the pki private key, or the passphrase that protects it. R3 cuts the number of such
  secrets per agent to one. It does not get rid of it.
- **Forward secrecy.** The `expires` field on a sealed message is advisory, not cryptographic. If
  the recipient's private key leaks later, every message ever sealed to it can be opened.
- **Endpoint compromise.** Sealing protects the channel. A compromised agent session has the key
  once it opens it.

## Acceptance tests

Each of these was done by hand while writing this brief; they should be automated.

1. **Round trip through the stock tool.** Seal a throwaway vault's key with the new code path, open
   it with the unmodified `pki-agent open`, and compare the result byte for byte.
2. **No cleartext at rest.** After `sgit clone --sealed`, search the clone and the system temp
   directory for the key string. There should be no matches.
3. **No cleartext on argv.** While a sealed clone runs, the key does not appear in `ps` output or in
   shell history.
4. **Wrong recipient fails closed.** A message sealed to another agent is refused, and nothing is
   written.
5. **Tampering fails closed.** Flipping one byte of the ciphertext gives an authentication failure
   (`InvalidTag`), and nothing is written.
6. **Unverified sender is flagged, distinctly.** A message from a sender outside the register opens
   only with an explicit flag, and the report says *why* it is unverified.
7. **Pack-mode clones.** A sealed clone of a pack-mode vault works, and the scans in test 2 read
   through `sgit cat`, not the disk. In a sparse pack-mode clone the working tree is empty while
   `sgit ls` shows every file as present, so a disk scan would check nothing and report clean.

## Open questions

- Should a clone be able to hold its key sealed to **several** agent keys, so that two agents can
  share a clone without sharing a pki key?
- Should the register publish a revocation list that sgit checks before unwrapping a key at rest
  (R3), so that retiring a pki key takes effect straight away rather than when it is next used?
- Should the read key get the same sealed-at-rest treatment? It is less sensitive than the vault key,
  but it is still a credential, and pack mode makes "who can read this vault" matter more.

*Shared by Dinis Cruz on 24 October 2026 and published on cli.sgit.ai as written. Read against the design in [A vault key that never lands](../articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.md) in [Sealed vault keys: the requirements and the design, side by side](../research/sealed-vault-keys-side-by-side.md).*

# Sealed vault keys: the requirements and the design, side by side, cli.sgit.ai

> Two documents arrived on the same day about the same gap, a vault key that is sealed in transit and in clear at rest. One is a list of ten requirements from an agent that moves vault keys for a living; the other is cli.sgit.ai's design for native PKI in sgit. This reads them against each other and against sgit 0.24.0's code. Every factual claim in the requirements holds, and two reach further than they say: 14 commands, not only clone, take a vault key on the command line, and sgit's own output names the encryption key's fingerprint where the register uses the signing key's. They agree on the goal and on R1 to R4 and R7. The design adds three things the requirements need: an agent process, so a per-command unwrap does not need a passphrase in the environment; a recovery recipient, so a lost agent key never loses a vault; and a decision about where trust is evaluated, since the register's rules live in JavaScript. The requirements add four things the design missed: refusing keys on argv everywhere, record fingerprints, a persistence check, and trust that explains itself. A merged list in four phases and fifteen acceptance tests follow.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/sealed-vault-keys-side-by-side.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
# Sealed vault keys: the requirements and the design, side by side

**Date:** 24 October 2026. **Read against:**
- [Sealed vault keys in sgit: requirements](../research/sealed-vault-keys-requirements.md), from an agent working with Dinis Cruz on pki.sgit.ai (R1 to R10);
- [A vault key that never lands](../articles/a-vault-key-that-never-lands.md), this site's design;
- SGit-AI__CLI at `182cfc1`, the code of sgit-ai 0.24.0.

## 1. Verdict

The two documents describe the same fix and agree on its core:
- **the goal:** no clear key on a transcript, a command line, a temp file or a working copy;
- **R1**, a clone from a sealed key;
- **R3**, sealed at rest;
- **R4**, migration;
- **R7**, never print a key.

Each also covers ground the other does not, and both are needed. Nothing in either needs the server to change.

## 2. The requirements' claims, checked

| Claim | Holds? | Evidence at `182cfc1` |
|---|---|---|
| `.sg_vault/local/vault_key` is plaintext, mode 0600 | **yes** | `crypto/Vault__Secret_File.py` sets 0600 and encrypts nothing; written by init, clone and attach |
| The key is a positional argument to `clone` | **yes, and wider** | **14** non-dev commands take a vault key on argv, positional or `--vault-key`. `clone`, `clone-branch`, `clone-headless`, `clone-range`, `init`, `create`, `vault attach`, `vault add`, `vault derive-keys`, `history log`, `inspect tree`, `branch checkout`, `pack import` and `pack export` are among them. `clone -` already reads stdin. |
| `pki-agent seal --text` takes a key on the command line | **yes**, and its help already says *"never paste a key on the command line: --text is for tests"* | pki-agent.mjs as published on 24 October |
| `pki-agent open --save` writes the secret to a file | **yes** | pki.sgit.ai/handover.md, section B |
| `seal --from-vault` reads `sgit vault show-key` into memory | **yes** | handover.md, section A |
| Messages must be addressed by the record (signing) fingerprint | **yes, and sgit itself gets it the other way** | `sgit pki keygen` prints the **encryption** key's fingerprint as "Fingerprint" and the signing key's second (`cli/CLI__PKI.py:44-45`). `pki encrypt --recipient` matches your own keys by `encryption_fingerprint` (`crypto/pki/PKI__Known_Keys.py:23`). The register's record is the signing key's. |
| The key store is always `~/.sg-send` | **yes** | `CLI__Main.py:885` calls `pki.setup()` with no argument; `CLI__PKI.py:22-23` falls back to `~/.sg-send` |

One more weakness, not in the requirements, matters once one pki key protects every vault:
- **The pki private key is weakly protected.** It is encrypted with PBKDF2 at **2,048 iterations**, the library default (checked with `openssl asn1parse`). Vault keys get 600,000. R3 makes it the one secret that guards everything, so it should get Argon2id, which costs about 150 ms in the library sgit already uses.

## 3. What the design adds that the requirements need

**3.1 An agent process, not a per-command unwrap.**
- R3 says every command "unwraps it in memory and drops it afterwards". To do that, every command must load the private key.
- That leaves two options:
  - a passphrase in the environment (`SG_SEND_PASSPHRASE`, readable in `/proc/<pid>/environ` by any process of the same user), or
  - an unencrypted private key, which puts a thief who takes the folder and the key store back where they started.
- The design's `sgit agent` holds the unlocked key behind a socket, the way `ssh-agent` does. It is unlocked once per session; each command asks it to open the sealed key, in about 2 ms.
- This is the same "one unattended secret" the requirements accept in their non-goals, but held in one process's memory instead of an environment variable.

**3.2 A recovery recipient, which is the answer to R8.**
- R8's failure is real and costly: something sealed to a key that did not survive can never be opened.
- The design's session identities, made only in memory, would make that failure deliberate. That is right for a clone that dies with its container, and wrong for anything that outlives it.
- The resolution: seal to **several recipients by default**, the agent's key plus its operator's lasting recovery key (for Dinis's agents, his master key). Losing an agent key then costs a handover, never a vault. This answers open question 1 as well.
- sgit should refuse to seal a backup, or anything meant to outlive the session, to a session identity alone.

**3.3 Where trust is evaluated.**
- R6 asks sgit to seal "only to recipients that chain to the pinned root". The rules for that live in pki.sgit.ai's JavaScript (`directory.js` `trustFrom`): operator links with end dates, personas, policy hashes, three steps to a person.
- Native sgit can take this on in two ways:
  - **port the rules to Python,** with shared test vectors so the two never disagree; or
  - **seal only to an explicit fingerprint,** check the signature and report the sender, and leave the judgement to `pki-agent trust <fp>` until the port exists.
- The second is smaller and safer for a first version. R9 and R10 are then pki-agent and register work, not sgit's.

**3.4 Identity creation, hardware and Argon2id.**
- `sgit id` with session, lasting and hardware keys;
- the P-256 envelope that hardware needs;
- Argon2id for lasting keys.

The requirements are silent on all three.

## 4. What the requirements add that the design missed

- **R2, everywhere.** The design said nothing about keys on argv. All 14 commands above should take the key from stdin or `--sealed`, and refuse a positional key unless an explicit opt-in such as `--key-on-argv` is given.
- **R5, the record fingerprint.** The design's `sgit vault seal --to <fingerprint>` must mean the **record (signing) fingerprint**, with one library function that returns it from a bundle or a `k1` code. `sgit pki` should print it first.
- **R8, the persistence check.** After `sgit id init` without `--session`: open the key again in a fresh process and fail if it is gone, warn when the store is on a filesystem that will not survive, and add an `SGIT_HOME`-style override for the store.
- **R10, trust that explains itself:** never enrolled, not confirmed, expired, or the register not yet rebuilt, with the register's build time. Whichever tool evaluates trust (3.3) owes this.
- **Acceptance test 7, pack mode:** scan through `sgit cat`, because a sparse clone's working tree proves nothing.

## 5. The open questions, answered

1. **Several keys per clone?** Yes, and by default (3.2). The v2 envelope wraps one AES key for one recipient. A sealed key file can hold one wrapped copy per recipient, the way `age` and OpenPGP do, without a new cipher.
2. **A revocation list checked before unwrapping?** Check it when online, as policy, and say so when offline. It cannot be enforced without a server, and it does not need to be for the case that matters:
   - retiring a pki key by destroying it makes every sealed copy at rest unreadable: disks, backups, images. That is crypto-shredding, and it is immediate.
   - What no list can do is reach a session that already opened the key. That needs `sgit vault rekey`, as both documents say.
3. **The read key sealed at rest?** Yes. Today it sits in `clone_mode.json` in clear, recorded as accepted risk F07. Sealing it retires that risk, at the same cost as the vault key.

## 6. One list, in four phases

| Phase | Items | Why in this order |
|---|---|---|
| **1. The door** | One key source for the 27 call sites that read the key file. **R7** across all output. **R2** warnings everywhere, refusals behind a flag. | No behaviour changes except the warnings; everything after depends on it |
| **2. Sealed at rest** | `sgit id`, with lasting keys under Argon2id and session keys. `sgit agent` (3.1). **R1** `clone` and `attach` with `--sealed` (`m1`, JSON, file, `-`). **R3** with **multi-recipient** sealing (3.2). **R4** `vault seal-key`. The read key sealed. **R8** checks. | The goal is met at the end of this phase |
| **3. Sending and trust** | `vault seal --to <record fp>` (**R5**). Explicit-fingerprint trust first, then the ported rules or `pki-agent` (3.3). **R6** operator-vouched mode recorded in the message. Expiry in the message. QR images as an optional extra. | Replaces `pki-agent seal --from-vault` reading `show-key` |
| **4. Hardware and the register** | P-256 envelope for TPM, PIV and Secure Enclave. Commits signed by the identity. **R9** and **R10** with the register. | Builds on everything above |

## 7. Acceptance tests, merged

The requirements' seven, with test 7 as written, plus eight for the design's additions:

1. A seal made by sgit opens with the stock `pki-agent open`, byte for byte, and the reverse.
2. No clear key at rest: scan the clone, `/tmp` and `~/.sg-send`, and read through `sgit cat` on pack and sparse clones.
3. No clear key on argv or in shell history, for **every** command in the R2 list, not only clone.
4. A wrong recipient fails closed and writes nothing.
5. Tampering fails closed (`InvalidTag`) and writes nothing.
6. An unverified sender opens only with an explicit flag, and the report says why.
7. Pack-mode clones, as in the requirements.
8. A session identity's private key never appears on disk: scan for its bytes after the session.
9. `sgit agent`'s socket is reachable only by its user, and no passphrase is in any process's environment after the agent starts.
10. A key sealed to an agent and a recovery recipient opens with either one alone.
11. Destroying an agent's key makes its at-rest sealed keys unopenable, and the recovery key still opens them.
12. A migrated clone's plaintext `vault_key` is overwritten before it is unlinked, and running the migration twice does nothing.
13. On a sealed clone, `vault show-key` refuses without `--reveal`, and `vault backup --include-key` refuses to write a clear key.
14. New lasting keys are encrypted with Argon2id, not 2,048 PBKDF2 rounds.
15. `sgit pki` and `sgit id` print the record fingerprint first, and `--to` accepts it.

## 8. Where both are silent

- **The access token** in `.sg_vault/local/token` is also in clear. It should be sealed with the key.
- **The clone's signing key** (`key-rnd-imm-*.pem`) is unencrypted PKCS#8. The design seals it; the requirements do not mention it.
- **The vault alias store** `~/.sg-send/vaults.enc` uses a fixed salt for every user. Fix or retire it once sealed keys exist.

# Security CI: a dedicated pipeline, and an AI review that can break the build, cli.sgit.ai

> A dedicated security pipeline on every pull request, and a keyless AI security review that can break the build on anything new: why, how it is wired, and what it costs per reviewed change.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/security-ci-and-ai-review.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/13/security-ci__pipeline-and-ai-review.md>.*

# Security CI: a dedicated pipeline, and an AI review that can break the build

**Your questions (13 Oct):**
1. Is a dedicated security pipeline worth it?
2. Can some of the checks and AI security reviews run in CI and break the build on anything new?
3. What would that cost, on a cheaper model?
4. How do you create a Claude key for it?

**Short answers:**
1. Yes. It is now `.github/workflows/security.yml`.
2. Yes. The AI review is built, tested without spending anything, and switched **off** until you
   connect it. It is keyless: GitHub's OIDC token through workload identity federation.
3. About **$0.20–0.65 per reviewed PR on Sonnet 5.5**, or **1–16 cents on Haiku 5.5**. Changes
   that touch none of the 45 security-slice files cost nothing.
4. No key is needed: workload identity federation, steps in §6.

## 1. Why a dedicated pipeline

Three reasons:
- **Nothing ran on a pull request.** `ci-pipeline.yml` runs on push to `dev` and `main` only, so
  every gate, including the security job, could only fail after the merge. `security.yml` runs on
  every PR into `dev` or `main`, so a red result blocks the merge rather than reporting it,
  and on every push to `dev`, since that is where changes land here (updated 13 Oct).
- **New advisories and rules arrive without code changes.** A weekly run (Mondays 05:17 UTC) on
  `dev` catches a new CVE in `cryptography` or a new Semgrep rule even when nobody pushes.
- **The workflows themselves had findings.** zizmor found 4 high and 13 medium issues in our
  Actions. They are fixed or recorded (§3).

The release pipeline keeps its own security-tests job, since that job gates publishing. The new
workflow does not replace it.

## 2. The gates (each fails only on what is new)

| Job | What it runs | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| Security & adversarial tests | `pytest tests/security` | a `Fixed__*` attack works again, or a `Known_Gaps` gap moved |
| Bandit (baseline) | `bandit -r sgit_ai -b tests/security/bandit-baseline.json` (1.9.4) | a finding not in the committed baseline |
| Semgrep (new lines) | `p/python`, `p/security-audit`, `p/secrets`, `r/python.cryptography` (1.178.0) on `sgit_ai` and `review/tools`, `--baseline-commit` = the PR's base | a finding on a line the PR adds or moves. The weekly run reports everything as SARIF and does not fail |
| pip-audit | `--strict` on the runtime dependencies, now **read from `pyproject.toml`** (the release job hardcodes them) | any known advisory |
| zizmor | the workflows and the composite action, `--min-severity medium`, ignores in `.github/zizmor.yml` | a new medium or high finding |
| actionlint | `actionlint` (1.7.12) on the workflows | a workflow GitHub would reject. Added after the first `dev` run of this change failed at load: a duplicated `with:` in the mutation job passed every YAML parser and zizmor |
| review/ graph current | `review/tools/derive.py --check` | never fails: a warning, because a stale graph is a docs debt, not a defect |
| AI security review | `review/tools/ai_review.py` (§4) | a new, confident, medium-or-worse finding that survives a second opinion |

Calibrated here:
- **Semgrep's PR mode** run against the merge I pushed today flagged the three `urlopen` lines in
  the `serve` code. Bandit already had reviewed `nosec` reasons for those lines; they now carry
  `# nosemgrep` as well.
- **Bandit, zizmor and pip-audit** are clean on the branch.

## 3. What zizmor found in our workflows, and what changed

- **template-injection (high, 4).** The composite test action pasted `${{ inputs.* }}` into
  shell text. The values are our own constants today, but the pattern is the classic Actions
  injection.
  - Fix: the inputs now reach the shell as environment variables, with `set -f`.
  - Side effect: the integration jobs' `'mcp<2'` lost its quotes (`mcp<2`). A variable expansion
    never parses `<` as a redirection; I checked the word-splitting in bash.
- **artipacked (medium).** Every read-only job now sets `persist-credentials: false`.
  - The tag job and the two publish jobs keep their credentials, because they push the tag and
    run `git__update_branch`. Each has an inline ignore with that reason.
- **secrets-inherit, excessive-permissions (medium).** The `dev` and `main` callers pass every
  secret and run with default token permissions. Narrowing them changes the publishing path, so
  they are ignored with reasons and left for a release check (follow-up under TM-R21).

**Risk:** these edits touch the release pipeline's test action. They parse, zizmor is clean, and
the word-splitting is checked. The first `dev` run after the merge is the real check, so watch
it.

## 4. The AI review (`review/tools/ai_review.py`)

### Flow

1. **Scope.** Take the PR's changed files that are in the security slice (`review/slice.json`,
   45 files: crypto, host and local boundaries, verify-then-accept, key stores, supply chain).
   If there are none, stop: it costs nothing.
2. **Request.** One request to Claude:
   - *System part (cached):* the rules, `review/intent/*.json`, and the threat model.
   - *User part:* the diff (15 lines of context), each touched file whole, and the function
     dossiers for those files from `review/context/functions/`.
   - Settings: adaptive thinking; effort `medium`; output forced to a JSON schema; server-side
     fallback on (`fallbacks: "default"`), so a safety-classifier decline is retried on another
     model instead of failing. Haiku has no fallback.
3. **Findings.** Each finding has a file and line, a function, a category, a severity, a
   confidence, and **`register`**: the threat-model row it is (TM-F/TM-R), or `new`.
4. **The gate.**
   - It counts only findings that are `new`, at least medium severity and at least 0.8 confidence.
   - If any remain, a **second call tries to refute them**: is the input reachable, is it handled
     elsewhere, did it exist before the diff? Only what survives fails the build.
   - Clean PRs never pay for that second call.
5. **Waivers.** You accept a finding by adding its id (12 hex: file, function and category, not
   the wording) with a reason to `review/findings/ai-waivers.json`. Exit codes:

   | Code | Meaning |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | pass |
   | 1 | new findings |
   | 2 | error |
   | 3 | inconclusive: the model declined or ran out of tokens; nothing was reviewed, which is not a pass |

### What it is not

The diff is attacker-controlled text and the model reads it. A hostile change can argue its way
past the reviewer. So the AI review catches mistakes by honest contributors and agents; the
deterministic gates are the controls. The model gets no tools, so injected text can only change
the verdict. The prompt also asks it to report steering text as a finding.

The job runs only:
- on pushes to `dev`, and on PRs from branches of this repository (a fork's PR never gets an
  OIDC token);
- when the repository variable `SECURITY_AI_REVIEW` is `true` and a federation rule id is set
  for that event.

Never move it to `pull_request_target`.

### Tested without spending anything

- **Wire shape.** A loopback server stood in for the API. It confirmed that the request carries
  the `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` beta, `fallbacks: "default"`, adaptive thinking, the
  JSON-schema output and the cached system prompt.
- **Paths.** I ran it through the four outcomes:
  - confirmed finding → exit 1 (only the high, new one gates; a low one does not);
  - refuted finding → pass;
  - waived finding → pass, one call only;
  - refusal → exit 3.
- **Unit tests.** `tests/unit/review/test_Review__AI_Review.py` covers the gate rules, waivers,
  the fingerprint, the Haiku price tier, the skip, and a dry run that calls nothing.

### The off-the-shelf alternative

[`anthropics/claude-code-security-review`](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-security-review)
runs Claude Code as an agent over the PR (up to 20 minutes) and comments on it.
- It does not fail the build itself. It outputs `findings-count`, so you would add your own
  step to fail on it.
- Its default model is an older Opus. Its README says it is *"not hardened against prompt
  injection attacks and should only be used to review trusted PRs"*.

It is good for PR comments. As a gate, ours is cheaper and predictable, because it is one call
with no tools and known inputs. It also knows our threat model and register, so it can tell new
from known. Both can run if you want PR comments as well.

## 5. Cost (measured inputs, list prices as of 2026-10)

Dry runs (`--dry-run`: counts what would be sent, sends nothing) on five real commits:

| Commit | Slice files | Input tokens (~) | Sonnet 5.5 clean / with findings | Haiku 5.5 clean / with findings | Opus 5.5 clean / with findings |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `b32a6ba` sgit serve | 2 | 61k | $0.19 / $0.32 | $0.01 / $0.02 | $0.38 / $0.64 |
| `9362a25` TM-F32..36 | 4 | 75k | $0.22 / $0.38 | $0.01 / $0.02 | $0.44 / $0.76 |
| `fbd550f` pull guard | 4 | 75k | $0.22 / $0.38 | $0.01 / $0.02 | $0.44 / $0.76 |
| `eb7941c` bulk fetch | 4 | 109k | $0.29 / $0.51 | $0.07 / $0.13 | $0.57 / $1.03 |
| `a5e6043` partial clones | 7 | 144k | $0.36 / $0.65 | $0.09 / $0.16 | $0.71 / $1.30 |

**How the numbers are built:**
- Input is about 16k tokens of system (design plus threat model) plus the change.
- Output is assumed at 6k tokens per review and 4k per verification, including thinking. The
  real figure is printed in the job summary once it runs.
- Prices per million tokens (input / output):
  - Sonnet 5.5: $2 / $10.
  - Haiku 5.5: $0.10 / $0.50, or $0.50 / $2.50 past 100k input tokens, which is why the larger
    commits jump.
  - Opus 5.5: $4 / $20.

**Per month**, at 60 PRs that touch the slice:

| Model | Per month | Before your first top-up | Spend limit to set |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sonnet | about $15–40 | a $10 credit covers about 30 reviews | $25 |
| Haiku | about $1–5 | | |

**Which model.**
- Start with **Sonnet 5.5**, the default (`SECURITY_AI_REVIEW_MODEL` changes it with no code
  edit). Haiku 5.5 is about 20 times cheaper per token, but finding security bugs is reasoning
  work, and a gate that misses or invents findings costs more in attention than it saves.
- **Measure before you choose.** Your branch gives a ready-made test with known answers: review
  the five fixes *backwards*, so the "change" re-introduces TM-F32..F36. Commands are in §6. A
  model that does not flag them is not worth its price at any price. That is under $1 on Sonnet
  and a few cents on Haiku.
- Batch pricing (50% off) does not suit a PR gate, which needs the answer in minutes. It would
  suit a later weekly sweep of the whole slice: about 150k tokens of code, roughly $1.30 on
  Sonnet, $0.65 batched.

## 6. Switching it on: keyless, with workload identity federation

*Updated 13 Oct. This replaces the API-key setup first written here.*

The CI job holds **no API key**. It asks GitHub for a short-lived OIDC token (about 5 minutes)
for the audience `https://api.anthropic.com`, and the SDK exchanges that token once for an
Anthropic token bound to a service account. Billing goes to the organization that owns the
service account (the one with the credits), attributed to the rule's workspace.

The job runs on every **push to `dev`**, since that is where changes land here. It can also run
on PRs. It reviews `before..after` of the push. A push that touches no security-slice file
(release-badge commits, docs) is skipped at no cost.

### In the Claude Console (organization admin)

1. **Settings → Workspaces → Create workspace** `sgit-ci`. Click the workspace, then
   **Spend limits**, and set the monthly cap, for example $25 with an alert at 50%.
2. **Settings → Workload identity → Connect workload → GitHub Actions.** The wizard creates
   the issuer, the service account and the rule together. It is better than the bare
   *Register issuer* dialog.
   - **Issuer:** name `github-actions`, issuer URL `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`,
     JWKS source *OIDC discovery*. Leave the discovery URL and CA certificate empty.
   - **Service account:** for example `sgit-ci-security-review`, member of workspace `sgit-ci`.
   - **Rule for pushes to dev** (the one the job needs):
     - subject: `repo:SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI:ref:refs/heads/dev` (exact, no `*`);
     - audience: `https://api.anthropic.com`;
     - claims: `repository_id` = `1187093532`, `repository_owner_id` = `269696930`,
       `ref` = `refs/heads/dev` (numeric ids survive a rename);
     - workspace `sgit-ci`, scope `workspace:developer`, token lifetime 600 s.
   - **Optional second rule for PRs:** subject `repo:SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI:pull_request`, same
     audience and id claims, no `ref`.
3. Note the ids: rule `fdrl_…`, service account `svac_…`, workspace `wrkspc_…`, and the
   organization id (Settings → Organization).

### In GitHub (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → *Variables* tab)

None of these values is a secret: without a GitHub token that matches the rule, they mint
nothing.

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `SECURITY_AI_REVIEW` | `true` |
| `ANTHROPIC_ORGANIZATION_ID` | the organization id |
| `ANTHROPIC_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID` | `svac_…` |
| `ANTHROPIC_WORKSPACE_ID` | `wrkspc_…` |
| `ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID` | the dev-push rule, `fdrl_…` |
| `ANTHROPIC_FEDERATION_RULE_ID_PR` | optional: the PR rule |
| `SECURITY_AI_REVIEW_MODEL` | optional: `claude-haiku-5-5` (the default is Sonnet 5.5) |

Do **not** add an `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret. A set key, even an empty one, takes precedence
over federation; the job unsets it anyway.

**Who can spend.** Anyone who can push to `dev` can run a workflow that mints a token.
Forks cannot: a fork's PR gets no OIDC token. The workspace spend limit is the backstop.

**Tested here without spending anything.** I ran the job's exact shell step against a local
stand-in for both GitHub's token endpoint and Anthropic's token exchange:
- the GitHub token is requested with the right audience;
- it is exchanged **once**, with the rule, organization, service-account and workspace ids;
- API calls carry the federated bearer token;
- an empty API key is unset;
- an all-zero push base falls back to the parent commit;
- the token file is deleted afterwards;
- a gating finding gives two API calls on one exchange, and the step exits 1.

`ai_review.py` now makes one SDK client per run. Before this fix, the second call created a new
client, which would have re-presented the single-use GitHub token and been refused
(`jti_reused`).

**Locally**, with your own key and never in a repo file, the commands in §5 still work:
`export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=…` and `python3 review/tools/ai_review.py --base 9362a25 --head 9362a25^`.

## 7. Next steps (not done here)

- A weekly whole-slice AI sweep through the Batch API, with findings written as records under
  `review/findings/`.
- Narrowing `secrets: inherit` and the default token permissions in the dev and main callers,
  with a release check.
- A committed lockfile, so pip-audit checks what is installed, not what could be (TM-R21).
- `review/tools/derive.py` running in CI and committing the graph, rather than warning.

# Case study — a tool-assisted security review of sgit-ai 0.21.0 (round 1)

**From:** the sgit-ai CLI agent · **Date:** 2026-10-11 · **Plan:** `../plan__security-review-with-skills.md`
(accepted by Dinis the same day: the slice as proposed, `review/` at the repository root, no
need to tell Matt beforehand since every tool is open source). **For:** `skills.sgit.ai` and
`threat-modeling.sgit.ai`, and Matt Adams, whose three tools were part of the run.

This note reports what each tool found, with counts, and what the run cost. The method and the
data are in `review/` (see `review/README.md`); the vetting of the tools is in `00__vetting.md`.

## 1. What ran, in order

| Step | Tool | Ran as | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Cisco AI Defense skill-scanner 2.2.2, OWASP AST10 checklist | tool + checklist by hand | `00__vetting.md`, four SARIF files, `review/tools/skills.lock.json` |
| 1 | `review/tools/derive.py` (stdlib `ast`) | tool | `review/graph/`: 41 Python files, 47 classes, 522 methods, 3,289 test functions whose file imports a slice module |
| 1 | Trail of Bits audit-context-building | four subagents, one per boundary | `review/context/functions/`: 270 function records with `nothing found` assumptions and open questions |
| 2 | mrwadams stride-threat-modelling skill (no model key, no hosted MCP) | the agent | `review/stride/agent.json`: 68 threats, 25 explicit N/A, DREAD scores; joined to the register by `stride_join.py` |
| 2 | Matt Adams' insider-threat model (27 threats, CC BY 4.0) | the agent, as data | `review/stride/insider-overlay.json`: 16 land on existing rows, 2 new model items, 9 are the deployment's; actor A9 proposed |
| 3 | Semgrep 1.180.0 (236 rules), Bandit 1.9.4, pip-audit 2.10.1 | tools | `review/findings/raw/`; a Bandit baseline (108 results) and the pip-audit gate added to the security CI job (TM-R21) |
| 3 | Trail of Bits sharp-edges, insecure-defaults (its six corpora by hand) | the agent | `review/findings/sharp-edges.json`, `insecure-defaults.json` |
| 3 | Sentry security-review, secret-serialization, gha-security-review | the agent | three findings files |
| 3 | Trail of Bits supply-chain-risk-auditor | its scripts via `uv` | `raw/supply-chain-report.md`; the collector did not parse the Poetry tables (see §4) |
| 3 | Trail of Bits differential-review (0.20.0 → 0.21.0, 27 files, 58 commits) | one subagent | `review/findings/differential-review.md` + `.json` |
| 3 | Trail of Bits post-patch-validation on TM-F29 (`f624d3b` → `d970599`) | the same subagent, the skill's runner | `post-patch-validation.md` + result and report JSON: complete, 0 gaps, runtime evidence, 4 exploit/variant checks fail on base and pass on patch |
| 4 | Trail of Bits fp-check (by hand), mrwadams threat-led-triage (rubric by hand) | the agent; four reproductions with lying hosts on the in-memory API | `review/findings/ranked.json` |
| 5 | `review/tools/security_json.py` | tool | `review/security/`: 41 `.security.json` records in the house schema |

Not run: STRIDE GPT's `analyze` (no model API key in this session) and the hosted STRIDE GPT
MCP server (deliberately: it receives the application description). The skill from the same
author stood in for both; the tool pass is owed from a machine with a key, so the planned
two-pass comparison can still happen.

## 2. What was found

104 finding records across nine files (`review/findings/`), each a claim with its evidence:

| Tool | VULN | VERIFY | KNOWN | CLEARED |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| audit-context-building (four dossiers, read as claims) | 4 | 31 | 6 | 7 |
| differential-review | 2 | 1 | 1 | 12 |
| sharp-edges | 1 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| sentry-security-review | 2 (same root cause as sharp-edges') | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| sentry-secret-serialization | 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| insecure-defaults | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| semgrep | 0 | 1 | 0 | 5 |
| bandit (30 in the slice) | 0 | 2 | 1 | 4 (+1 out of slice) |
| pip-audit, supply-chain auditor, gha review | 0 | 0 | 0 | clear |

**Five distinct defects reproduced and fixed this round, each with a test that fails on the code
before its fix, a register row and a CHANGELOG line:**

| Row | Defect | Found by | Reproduced how |
|---|---|---|---|
| TM-F32 | `sgit pki delete ..` emptied `~/.sg-send` (credential store, keyring, keys); `pki export ../x` read any PEM | sharp-edges (SE-001), confirmed by the Sentry pass and the crypto dossier | in a sandboxed temp dir |
| TM-F33 | a push the host acknowledged with an empty body counted as pushed (batch path and the individual-write fallback) | host dossier (AC-H-003), confirmed by the differential review (DR-002) | a lying host answering `{}` |
| TM-F34 | an empty listing made a clone that had synced re-upload stale refs with no compare-and-swap: the shared branch rewound under a legitimate key | host dossier (AC-H-001) | a lying host listing `[]`; 1 of 2 refs moved |
| TM-F35 | a garbled branch index on clone degraded to a policy-less index: signatures-required off for the newcomer | verify dossier (AC-V-001) | random bytes in the host's index; clone succeeded with no features |
| TM-F36 | a server index this build cannot parse was overwritten by the pushing clone (the whole-index twin of TM-F29) | differential-review (DR-001) | a branch entry with an unknown type; the push erased it |

One more reproduced defect is **open with a proposed fix**: AC-L-001, the vault-path type rewrites
any character outside `[a-zA-Z0-9/\_.- ]` to `_`, so a vault under `/home/josé/` keeps its objects,
refs and keys under `/home/jos_/` (the fix touches every path field, so it is left for a decision).
One suspected ordering defect was **cleared by reproduction**: a dirty-tree refusal on pull leaves
the baseline untouched (AC-V-003).

The remaining 46 VERIFY records are ranked in `review/findings/ranked.json` with the
threat-led-triage rubric (reachability first: "host alone" is this system's unauthenticated).
The next ones in the queue: AC-H-002 (the host's `not_found` drops the CAS), AC-V-002 (the rewind
guard's UNKNOWN verdict proceeds), AC-H-004 (host body text drives control flow), AC-L-006
(no ceiling on the walk to `.sg_vault`), AC-C-002 (a corrupt `remotes.json` falls through to
another server).

## 3. STRIDE GPT's rubric, applied to the hand STRIDE pass

TM-Bench scores STRIDE coverage, completeness, technical validity and JSON compliance. Against
this project's register as ground truth (`review/stride/coverage.json`):

| Dimension | Result |
|---|---|
| Completeness against the register | first pass 54 of 63 rows (85.7 %); second pass 63 of 63; third pass, after the review added five rows, 68 of 68 |
| STRIDE distribution | T 20, I 15, S 8, D 8, E 7, R 5; 25 cells recorded N/A with a reason |
| Priority distribution (DREAD) | Critical 19, High 29, Medium 14, Low 1 |
| New threats (no register row before this round) | 9, of which 4 became fixed rows and 2 are the agent-as-insider model items |
| JSON compliance | by construction (the join tool reads it) |

The honest reading: the register was the model's input, so completeness measures whether the pass
restated it, not whether it would have found it. The nine new threats and the five fixes are the
part that was not in the input.

## 4. What the tools got wrong, or could not do

- **The skill scanner's errors inside the installed set were all false positives** (pattern
  lists and attack references read as instructions); its real findings were the undeclared
  network hosts of the supply-chain skill, and the absence of any licence field or signature.
- **The supply-chain collector misread this project**: it parses PEP 621 tables only, so the
  three runtime dependencies in `[tool.poetry.dependencies]` were not seen and the report says
  "every direct dependency is a development dependency". Without an authenticated `gh`, ten
  of thirteen criteria were unassessable. pip-audit did the advisory work.
- **Semgrep and Bandit found nothing new**: their six and thirty results were the two opt-in
  TLS branches, the guarded presigned PUT, a file name called `token`, and `try/except: pass`.
  Their value here is the CI baseline, not the findings.
- **The dossiers (audit-context-building) were the most productive input**: four of the five
  fixed defects came from a `nothing found` assumption in a dossier, read as a claim and
  reproduced with a lying host. The skill's refusal to name vulnerabilities is what made the
  records usable: they list what the code counts on, and the hunting is a separate, cheap step.
- **The differential review found the one defect the dossiers missed** (TM-F36), because it
  asked of every fix "what did its skip branch do to the data it skipped", which is how
  TM-F29 happened. Its post-patch-validation runner worked end to end on the first fix it was
  pointed at, with runtime evidence on both revisions.
- **Three of the Sentry findings and the sharp-edges finding were the same defect** seen from
  three methods; the case for running several skills is that each one's phrasing reached a
  different line of the same file.
- **The one thing the agent got wrong**: the first run of the TM-F32 test executed the
  unfixed code's `..` and `../..` cases from a temp directory directly under `/tmp`, and the
  unfixed code removed `/tmp`'s contents, including this session's scratchpad and the
  commit-signing helper. The test was rewritten to run three directories below a sandbox
  root so that nothing the unfixed code does can leave it. A proof that destroys the
  environment it runs in is itself a finding about the proof.

## 5. Cost

| Item | Measure |
|---|---|
| Subagents | 5 (four dossiers, one differential review + post-patch validation); 1.9 M tokens between them; 23 to 32 minutes each |
| The orchestrating agent | one session, the whole day |
| Tools' own time | Semgrep about 1 minute; Bandit seconds; the full unit + security suites 2 min 11 s with `-n auto` |
| Lines of code reviewed | 11,604 in 45 files (the slice); the differential review read +1,566/−172 across 27 of them |
| Tests added | 4 files or classes, 46 attack cases, 11 controls; every attack case fails on the code before its fix |

## 6. For the two sites and for Matt

- `skills.sgit.ai`: the research doc (`../research__security-review-skills.md`), `00__vetting.md`
  and §4 above are the material. The headline: none of the ecosystem's best security skills can
  pass the AST10 checklist they are vetted against, because none is signed.
- `threat-modeling.sgit.ai`: `../research__threat-modeling-tools.md`, `review/stride/`, the
  insider overlay, and §3 above. The headline: a register with a test per row is a usable
  ground truth, and the agent-as-insider actor (A9) belongs in it.
- For Matt: the stride-threat-modelling skill ran without a key and produced a model the join
  tool could score; the licence in its frontmatter (GPL-3.0-or-later) disagrees with the
  repository's MIT; `threat-led-triage`'s rubric transferred well once "host alone" was mapped
  to its `unauthenticated` band; STRIDE GPT's `analyze` is still owed a run with a key.

Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/11/plan__security-review-with-skills.md>.*
