# Plan — the next security review of sgit-ai, with skills, and the review graphs it produces

**From:** the sgit-ai CLI agent · **Date:** 2026-10-11 · **Status:** proposed, for Dinis to accept
or redirect before step 0 runs. **Companion docs:** [`research__security-review-skills.md`](../research/security-review-skills.md),
[`research__threat-modeling-tools.md`](../research/threat-modeling-tools.md), `map__security-work-already-done.md` in this folder.

## 1. One sentence

Run a tool-assisted, data-producing security review of **one slice** of sgit-ai (the code the
zero-knowledge guarantee and the trust boundaries live in), using five skills and three tools
chosen in the research docs, join every output to the existing register and its tests, and
leave behind the first `review/` graphs and per-file security records, so the case study can
say which tool found what.

## 2. Scope: the slice, and why it is this one

The code-review-graphs brief says not to start an existing repository with a full derivation,
and the `secrets.sgit.ai/review/` page starts from what people actually walk. For a security
review, what people walk is the key path: derive a key, encrypt, send to the host, verify what
comes back, write to disk. Everything the register's High-impact rows touch is in these
packages.

| In scope (round 1) | Files · lines | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `sgit_ai/crypto/` | 9 · 793 | every primitive; the KDF cache; the deterministic metadata mode (KI-SEC-02); PKI |
| `sgit_ai/network/api/` | 13 · 1,504 | the host boundary: presigned URLs, CAS, per-op conflicts, timeouts, scheme rules |
| `sgit_ai/storage/` (`Vault__Path_Guard`, `Vault__Storage`, `Vault__Verified_Write`, `Vault__Object_Store`, `Vault__Index_Reader`, `Vault__Ref_Manager`, `Vault__Branch_Manager`) | 7 of 17 | the local boundary and verified writes; where the path, symlink, baseline and index fixes landed |
| `sgit_ai/core/actions/verify/`, `clone/`, `pull/`, `push/`, `commit/`; `sgit_ai/core/Vault__Secret_Guard.py`, `Vault__Ignore.py` | 5 of 28 action groups + 2 | verify-then-accept, the rewind guard, the secret guard and the always-ignored set |
| `sgit_ai/secrets/`, `sgit_ai/cli/CLI__Main.py`, `CLI__Credential_Store.py`, `CLI__Token_Store.py`, `CLI__Debug_Log.py`, `CLI__Vault.py` | 6 files | where keys are stored, pinned, printed and logged (TM-R14 is High) |
| `.github/workflows/*.yml`, `pyproject.toml`, `sgit update` | 3 + 2 | supply chain (TM-R21) |

41 source files, about 11,300 lines (counted with `wc -l`), out of 469 files. **Out of scope for round 1:**
`plugins/`, `workflow/`, `migrations/`, the rest of `cli/`, `core/serve`, `mirror`, `publish`
(round 2 candidate: their code-stage review is owed since 08/19), `objects/`, `safe_types/`,
`schemas/` (covered by the Type_Safe tests and the round-trip invariant).

## 3. The tools, and what each is for

| Step | Tool | Chosen because | Not chosen |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | OWASP AST10 checklist; `cisco-ai-defense/skill-scanner` | the only published rubric for installing third-party instruction files into a key-custody repository | SkillLedger and skillsign: nothing on our list is signed, so there is nothing to verify |
| 1 | Trail of Bits **audit-context-building** | a per-function dossier with a line for every claim and "nothing found" for unestablished assumptions; no verdicts, so it cannot anchor the later steps | Sentry's "research the code base first" is a paragraph, not an artefact |
| 1 | a parser (Python `ast`) | the code-review-graphs brief: derived structure comes from parsers, never a model | STRIDE GPT's repository stage: it is a model reading code, so its output goes in the intent/explanation layer, not `graph/` |
| 2 | **STRIDE GPT** CLI (`analyze`, JSON, Anthropic via LiteLLM) and the **`stride-threat-modelling` skill** copy | two independent STRIDE passes with the same rubric: one by the tool, one by this agent; stable threat ids; evidence required per threat | the hosted `mcp.stridegpt.ai` endpoint (sends the description off-machine); pytm and Threagile (their libraries are web- and infrastructure-shaped; a pytm model file is a round 2 artefact once the DFD exists as data) |
| 2 | Matt Adams' **insider-threat model** (27 threats) | the agent as actor; thirteen threats already map to register rows after one reading | |
| 3 | Sentry **security-review** (cryptography, file-security, supply-chain, logging guides) and **secret-serialization**; Trail of Bits **insecure-defaults**, **sharp-edges**, **differential-review** (0.20.0 → 0.21.0), **post-patch-validation** (the 0.21 fixes) | method, not pattern list; the diff of 0.21.0 is the largest security diff the project has had and two of its fixes regressed | Project CodeGuard: read its crypto and supply-chain rules once, cite where relevant, do not install; the "Anthropic Cybersecurity Skills" library (not Anthropic's, no code-review domain); Varlock (keep the rule, not the skill); squirrelscan (nothing to audit in a CLI) |
| 3 | **Semgrep** (`p/python`, `python.cryptography.*`, Trail of Bits rules), **Bandit**, **pip-audit**; Sentry **gha-security-review** on the workflows | deterministic, SARIF, and the CI baseline TM-R21 has wanted since 10/08 | CodeQL: worth adding at the CI step if the Semgrep pass leaves gaps; not first |
| 3 | Anthropic **`/security-review`** | already here; diff-scoped; a second opinion on the pending changes of each fix commit | as the whole-slice review: its filter drops DoS-shaped findings by design, and three accepted rows are DoS-shaped |
| 4 | Trail of Bits **fp-check**; Matt Adams' **threat-led-triage** over all findings with the STRIDE GPT model | every finding is a claim to verify; ranking by reachability across *our* boundaries is how the list stays short | CVSS-style scoring |
| 5 | the house `.security.json` schema; the `review/` layout from the code-review-graphs brief | so the output is data the sites can join and the next review can diff | a prose report alone |
| 6 | the TM-Bench rubric (four dimensions) with the register as ground truth | the measurable part of the case study | running TM-Bench itself (no public harness) |

## 4. The steps

Each step names its output. Outputs that are data go under `review/` (new, at the repository
root, per the brief); prose goes under this folder's date; threat-model changes go in the
register with their tests, as §9 of the threat model requires.

### Step 0 — Vet, pin, canary (half a day)

1. Clone each skill source at a commit SHA; record SHA and `sha256` of every SKILL.md.
2. Run `skill-scanner scan-all --format sarif` over the lot; HIGH blocks install. Keep the SARIF.
3. Fill the AST10 table from [`research__security-review-skills.md`](../research/security-review-skills.md) §2 for each skill.
4. Install into this cloud session only (no vault key, no token, no `.env` on disk here):
   Trail of Bits plugins (`audit-context-building`, `insecure-defaults`, `sharp-edges`,
   `differential-review`, `post-patch-validation`, `fp-check`, `static-analysis`,
   `supply-chain-risk-auditor`); Sentry `security-review`, `secret-serialization`,
   `gha-security-review`; `stride-threat-modelling` skill copy; `threat-led-triage` skill;
   `pip install stride-gpt==<pinned>` with hashes; Semgrep, Bandit, pip-audit pinned.
5. Rule for every run: the agent never reads `.sg_vault/local/*`, never prints a key, never
   runs a skill's "fix" mode. Written at the top of the session prompt.

**Output:** `…/10/11/case-study/00__vetting.md` with the table and SARIF.

### Step 1 — Context and the first derived graph (one day)

1. `audit-context-building` over the slice → `audit-context/DOSSIER.md` and one file per function.
   Read the "nothing found" assumptions first; they are the candidate threats.
2. A small `ast`-based deriver (classes, methods, calls within the slice, tests that import each
   module) → `review/graph/{files,classes,methods,tests}.json`, each node with path, lines and
   tree hash, per the brief's grammar. Freshness checked by tree hash. **Parsers only.**
3. Intent for the slice, written from the threat model's §2 assets, §4 boundaries and §5
   mechanisms, each node citing its section → `review/intent/boundaries.json`,
   `mechanisms.json`. This is the top-down half, and it is small because the register already is
   the intent.

**Output:** the dossier; `review/graph/` and `review/intent/` seeds; `review/README.md` with
counts written by the deriver, not by hand.

### Step 2 — Threat model, two ways, plus the insider overlay (one day)

1. `stride-gpt analyze <slice> -f json -o review/stride/stride-gpt.json` with the cost estimate
   recorded first. Also `-f sarif` for the triage step.
2. This agent runs the `stride-threat-modelling` skill over the same slice and the dossier →
   `review/stride/agent.json`, same schema (id, STRIDE class, component, description, evidence
   line, mitigation).
3. Reconcile → `review/stride/join.json`: each threat id ↔ TM-R/TM-F row ↔ test file, or `new`,
   or `out-of-scope-by-model` (the host-and-harness threats). Disagreements between the two
   passes are kept, not averaged (the house two-modes rule).
4. Insider overlay: confirm the thirteen mappings in the threat-modeling doc §1.1 against code;
   add actor **A9** (the agent holding the key) to the register §3, and a column to §6 naming the
   insider threat ids each row answers. Where a mapping proves an *open* gap, write its
   `Known_Gaps` test in the same commit.

**Output:** `review/stride/` (three files); a register change with tests; the first number for
the case study (STRIDE GPT's completeness and coverage against the register).

### Step 3 — Code review (two days)

Run in this order, each writing findings as `VULN-###` / `VERIFY-###` with file, line, evidence:

1. Semgrep, Bandit, pip-audit → `review/findings/semgrep.sarif`, `bandit.json`, `pip-audit.json`.
   These three also become the CI baseline: a new job step in "Run Security & Adversarial Tests"
   that fails on *new* findings only (closes TM-R21's open half).
2. `insecure-defaults` and `sharp-edges` on `crypto/` and `storage/`.
3. Sentry `security-review` on the slice with the cryptography, file-security, supply-chain and
   logging guides; `secret-serialization` on `crypto/Vault__Secret_File.py`, `secrets/`,
   `cli/CLI__Debug_Log.py`, `cli/CLI__Vault.py`, `cli/CLI__Credential_Store.py`.
4. `differential-review` on `git diff 0.20.0..0.21.0 -- <slice>`; `post-patch-validation` on
   the TM-F25→F29 and TM-F27→F30 pairs specifically (the two fixes that regressed).
5. `gha-security-review` on the three workflows; `supply-chain-risk-auditor` on `osbot-utils`
   and `cryptography`.
6. `/security-review` on each fix commit as it is made (step 4), as the PR gate.

**Output:** `review/findings/<tool>.json` per tool, same record shape, each with `tool`,
`confidence`, `file`, `line`, `evidence`.

### Step 4 — Triage and fix (one day, plus the fixes)

1. `fp-check` over every finding; a finding without a reproducing path is `VERIFY`, not `VULN`.
2. `threat-led-triage rank review/findings/*.json against review/stride/stride-gpt.json` →
   `review/findings/ranked.json`, with the "could not determine" list kept.
3. House rule applies to anything real: a `Fixed` test that fails on the current code, the fix,
   the register row, the CHANGELOG line, in one commit. Anything accepted gets a `Known_Gaps`
   test and a `risk_decision` with owner and rationale.

**Output:** fixes with tests; register updated; the per-tool true/false-positive counts for the
case study.

### Step 5 — Per-file records and the skill rule (half a day)

1. One `.security.json` per file in the slice (house schema: `attack_surface`,
   `vulnerabilities` with `risk_decision`, `secrets_exposure`, `dependencies` with
   `trust_boundary_crossings`, `redundant_code`), written from the dossier and the findings,
   every claim with a line → `review/security/<path>.security.json`. The slice is 41 files;
   that is the whole point of the slice.
2. Add to `library/skills/sg-send-cli__SKILL.md` (and the sgit skill on `skills.sgit.ai`) the
   rule Varlock states and the insider model's I4 needs: never print, echo or log a vault key,
   read key, write key or token; read keys from the store, not from argv; prefer the key prompt.
   This is the one thing from the screenshot list that becomes a line in our own skill.

**Output:** `review/security/`; the skill change.

### Step 6 — Publish (half a day)

1. The two research docs → `skills.sgit.ai` and `threat-modeling.sgit.ai` Documents, as they are.
2. The case study: which tool found what (true positives, false positives, time, cost per
   tool), STRIDE GPT scored on the four TM-Bench dimensions against the register, the insider
   overlay result, the vetting table and the signature gap → both sites, and to Matt Adams.
3. Link the 0.21.0 register and the case study from `sgit.ai/security/` (closes "being
   prepared").

## 5. Acceptance

- Every file in `review/graph/` is regenerated byte-identically by the deriver from the tree
  hash it names; a stale file fails the check.
- Every STRIDE threat in `review/stride/join.json` resolves to a register row with a test, or is
  marked `new` with a `VERIFY`, or `out-of-scope-by-model` with the reason.
- Every `VULN` has a test that fails on the code before its fix; every accepted gap has a
  `Known_Gaps` test and a `risk_decision`.
- The security CI job runs Semgrep, Bandit and pip-audit against a committed baseline and is
  green on the head that adds it.
- Suites on the final head: unit, security, integration, QA all pass, with counts in the note.
- The case study reports per-tool counts, not impressions.

## 6. Risks of the plan itself

| Risk | Handling |
|---|---|
| A skill is a supply-chain vector into a key-custody repository (AST01/02) | step 0; cloud session with no keys; pinned SHAs; no fix modes |
| Prompt injection from repository content into a review skill: `tests/security/` and the review-round tests contain adversarial strings by design (hostile paths, `(ſ[a-z]+)+$`, forged objects) | review skills read `sgit_ai/`, not `tests/`; findings cite `sgit_ai/` lines only; the agent treats skill output as claims |
| STRIDE GPT sends the slice to the model provider | the code is Apache-2.0 and public; never run it over a checkout holding `.sg_vault/local`; record the cost estimate first |
| Finding flood: 23 Bandit mediums were counted in March | step 4's ranking and the baseline; only ranked-reachable findings get a test |
| The derived graph becomes hand-maintained | `review/graph/` is written by the deriver only; the freshness check is in the acceptance list |
| Scope creep into `plugins/`, `workflow/`, `serve`/`mirror`/`publish` | named out of scope; round 2 is a separate plan with its own note |

## 7. Decisions needed from Dinis

1. Accept the slice, or swap one package in or out (the obvious candidate to add is
   `core/actions/publish` + `mirror`, owed since 08/19; it would make round 1 about 60 files).
2. Whether `review/` goes at the repository root now (the brief's layout) or under
   `team/explorer/appsec/review/` until the deriver is trusted. The plan assumes the root.
3. Whether to tell Matt before or after the run that his three tools are being test-driven on a
   published register with tests, so he can say what he would like measured.

# Agent skills for security review — what exists, what it would do here, cli.sgit.ai

> Agent skills for security review, each checked at its source, ranked by whether it brings a method, a tool with deterministic output, or vets the other skills, against this code base.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/security-review-skills.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/11/research__security-review-skills.md>.*

# Agent skills for security review — what exists, what it would do here

**From:** the sgit-ai CLI agent · **Date:** 2026-10-11 · **For:** `skills.sgit.ai` (Documents), then
the case study once used.

**Method.** Each entry was checked at its source (the repository README or SKILL.md, the
project site, or the registry page) on 2026-10-11, not from the aggregator listing that
surfaced it. Where a claim could not be confirmed it says so. "On this code" means the sgit-ai
CLI: 469 Python files, Type_Safe throughout, two runtime dependencies (`osbot-utils`,
`cryptography`), AES-256-GCM / PBKDF2 / HKDF / ECDSA P-256 in `sgit_ai/crypto/`, a host
boundary in `sgit_ai/network/api/`, a local boundary in `sgit_ai/storage/`.

**The ranking rule.** A skill earns a place on this review if it does one of three things the
existing work does not already do: (a) brings a *method* (not a pattern list) that reaches
crypto, trust boundaries and file handling; (b) brings a *tool* with deterministic output
(SARIF, JSON) we can join to the threat model; (c) vets the other skills. Skills that only
restate OWASP web-app lists score low here: this code base has no HTML, no SQL, no sessions.

## 1. The catalogue

### 1.1 From the screenshot

| # | Skill | Source, licence | What it is | On this code | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | **security-review** | `getsentry/skills`, `skills/security-review/SKILL.md`, Apache-2.0 (references credit the OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, CC BY-SA 4.0) | A review *method*: research the whole code base first, trace data flow, then report only high-confidence findings (`VULN-###`) with a separate "needs verification" list (`VERIFY-###`). Do-not-flag rules for tests, dead code, server-controlled config. Loads reference guides per topic (17: injection, XSS, authorization, authentication, **cryptography**, deserialization, **file security**, SSRF, CSRF, data protection, API, business logic, modern threats, misconfiguration, error handling, **supply chain**, **logging**) and per language (Python among five) | The cryptography, file-security, supply-chain and logging guides fit. The confidence discipline matches the house rule that a finding needs a reproducing test. Timon Weber's comparison of five Claude Code security skills picked this one as the only one worth installing | **Use.** Primary code-review skill for the slice |
| S2 | **Cisco software.security** → Project CodeGuard | `cosai-oasis/project-codeguard` (was `project-codeguard/rules`), CC BY 4.0; Tessl registry lists `cisco/software-security` at 82 % quality | Secure-by-default *rules* for AI coding agents, eight categories: cryptography, input validation, authentication, authorization, supply chain, cloud, platform, data protection. Ships a `.claude-plugin` and a `skills/` folder; translators to Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf | The cryptography and supply-chain rules are a checklist to read the slice against (safe algorithms, key management, dependency pinning). It is guidance for *writing* code; it has no review loop, no output format, no verification step | **Reference only.** Read its crypto and supply-chain rules once; cite them in findings where they apply. Do not install as a plugin for this review |
| S3 | **"Anthropic Cybersecurity Skills"** | `mukul975/Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills`, Apache-2.0, community project by Mahipal Jangra; README: "Not affiliated with Anthropic PBC" | About 817 skills in 34 domains mapped to MITRE ATT&CK v19.1, NIST CSF 2.0, ATLAS, D3FEND, NIST AI RMF, F3. SKILL.md with When to Use / Prerequisites / Workflow / Verification | No threat-modeling or secure-code-review domain. Cryptography (16 skills) is TLS, Ed25519, PQ migration, key management at the operations level, not code review. Much of it is offensive and dual-use (C2, exploitation). The review queue is self-described as months long | **Skip.** The name misleads; the content is a SOC and red-team library, not a code-review method |
| S4 | **audit-website** (squirrelscan) | `squirrelscan/skills`; the `squirrel` CLI from squirrelscan.com, installed by `curl \| sh` | Site audit: SEO, performance, accessibility, security headers, mixed content, leaked-secret patterns (96). Gen Agent Trust Hub rated the skill **Fail / high risk** for the pipe-to-shell install and agent-run fixes | Nothing to audit in a CLI. Possible later use on the published `*.sgit.ai` sites and on `sgit vault serve` / published static vaults, with the binary installed by hand and the agent never running its fixes | **Skip for the CLI.** Park for the website estate |
| S5 | **Varlock** | `wrsmith108/varlock-claude-skill` wrapping `dmno-dev/varlock` (varlock.dev) | A `.env.schema` with sensitivity flags; the skill's rules are "never echo environment variables, never read `.env` directly, validate with masked output". Thin: no support files in the skill repo | The *rule* is the point, and it is already a sgit concern: TM-R14 (keys in argv and logs, re-ranked High on 10/09 because agents' command lines are read by many tools), TM-R09 (`.env` tracked-wins), the always-ignored set in `Vault__Ignore`. We do not use `.env` at runtime | **Skip the skill, keep the rule.** Fold "never print a vault key, token or read key" into the sgit skill (`library/skills/sg-send-cli__SKILL.md`) as a stated rule; see plan step 5 |
| S6 | **OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 (AST10)** | `OWASP/www-project-agentic-skills-top-10`, incubator, "1.0-2026", leads Ken Huang and Fabio Cerullo, CC BY-SA 4.0 | Ten risks for the skill layer (between model and tools): AST01 malicious skills, AST02 supply-chain compromise (both Critical), AST03 over-privileged, AST04 insecure metadata, AST05 untrusted external instructions, AST06 weak isolation (High), AST07 update drift, AST08 poor scanning, AST09 no governance, AST10 cross-platform reuse (Medium). A pre-install checklist | Not a review skill; it is the rubric for *installing* the others into a repository whose whole point is key custody. Every skill on this list is a third-party instruction file that will run with read access to the code and, in a careless session, to a vault key | **Use as the gate.** Plan step 0 applies its checklist to each installed skill and records the answers |
| S7 | **Behavioral verification** (canary run, signed manifest) | AST10 checklist items; tools: `cisco-ai-defense/skill-scanner` (Apache-2.0, PyPI `cisco-ai-skill-scanner`, SARIF, YARA + dataflow + optional LLM pass, pre-commit hook and reusable workflow), `getsentry/skills` `skill-scanner` skill, `skillsign` (Ed25519 over a skill folder), SkillLedger (content-addressed, SLSA L3) | The checklist asks for a valid Ed25519 signature with a content hash matching the manifest, and a run in an isolated canary environment with a report that observed behaviour matches declared behaviour | None of the skills above ship a signed manifest, so the signature check fails for all of them today (the `skills.sgit.ai` catalogue already shows version and permissions fields undeclared on our own eight). What we *can* do: scan each SKILL.md with the Cisco scanner, pin to a commit SHA, read it, and run it first in this cloud session (which has no vault key) before any session that holds one | **Use the scanner, note the gap.** The gap (no signatures anywhere in the ecosystem) is itself a `skills.sgit.ai` finding |

## 2. What the vetting gate looks like (AST10 applied)

For every skill the plan installs, record this table in the case study before the first run:

| Check (AST10 checklist) | Evidence we can produce today |
|---|---|
| Provenance: author identity, content hash, signature | Repository and commit SHA pinned; `sha256` of each SKILL.md recorded; **no signature exists** for any of them |
| Scan status | `skill-scanner scan-all <dir> --format sarif` output kept under the case study; HIGH fails the install |
| Permissions: files, tools, network | Read from the frontmatter (`allowed-tools`); Sentry's security-review declares `Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Task`. Any skill that fetches remote instructions at run time fails AST05 unless pinned |
| Identity files | Does it ask to write `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, memory? Sentry's `agents-md` does by design; the review skills must not |
| External content | `mcp-stride-gpt` hosted at `mcp.stridegpt.ai` sends the app description off-machine; use the skill copy or self-host on loopback (see the threat-modeling doc) |
| Dependencies pinned | `stride-gpt` from PyPI pinned by version and hash; the scanner itself pinned |
| Risk tier matches scope | A review skill that only reads is Low; anything that writes fixes is Medium and runs with `--dry-run` or not at all |
| Canary run | First run in a session with no vault key, no `.env`, no token on disk (this cloud environment qualifies: `find / -name .sg_vault` is empty) |

The honest finding for `skills.sgit.ai`: **the ecosystem's best security-review skills cannot pass
their own community's checklist**, because nobody signs skills yet. The `skills.sgit.ai` thesis
(skills as packages with version, permissions and provenance) is exactly the missing piece, and
this review is a worked example of the gap.

## 3. Two ideas worth taking, not installing

- **Confidence tiers with a "needs verification" list** (S1). Our house rule already demands a
  test per finding; the Sentry format gives the step before the test a name. Adopt the
  `VULN-###` / `VERIFY-###` split in the review output, then promote a VERIFY only when its test
  exists.
- **Context before verdicts** (S8 audit-context-building). The dossier's "assumption with
  nothing found to establish it" is the single most useful intermediate artefact: it is a
  candidate threat with its line number attached, before anyone has argued about severity. That
  is the `.security.json` row's `attack_surface` and `trust_boundary_crossings` fields, written
  by an agent with a citation, which is what the code-review-graphs brief allows at the
  explanation layer.

# Review: "What sgit does that Git does not", checked against the code, cli.sgit.ai

> The sgit CLI team's review of the newsroom's article "What sgit does that Git does not" (No. 308, 27 October 2026), claim by claim against the CLI at 640069a. The article is accurate on the whole. One headline number is unsourced and one signing line is wrong. Two claims are too strong in sgit's favour: signatures prove a key holder, not a clone (TM-R01), and indexes are checked under the vault's signature policy (TM-R42). It also undersells sgit, missing partial commits with sgit write, one file with no clone on normal vaults, and seven things Git has no equivalent for. Almost everything on Git's lead can be built client-side, with how and at what size. Six things zero knowledge rules out are listed, each with its substitute.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/sgit-and-git-article-review.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift.*

---
> **Published as written.** Dinis Cruz passed it to this site on 28 October 2026; it is now also in the CLI repository, at `team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/28/` on `dev` (`036e33b`), and led to the [Git-parity roadmap](../research/git-parity-roadmap.md). cli.sgit.ai's build agent checked three of its claims against the PyPI release 0.26.0 on 28 October and found all three hold: `sgit write` leaves other edits uncommitted, a zip holding a vault key is refused at commit, and a pull refuses a rewound head that the host accepted ([the script](https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Cli/tree/dev/admin/research/sgit-and-git-2026-10-28)). The site's summary of it, row by row, is [sgit and Git](../docs/sgit-and-git.md).

# Review: "What sgit does that Git does not" (newsroom.sgit.ai, article No. 308, 27 Oct 2026)

**Article:** <https://newsroom.sgit.ai/articles/what-sgit-does-that-git-does-not.html> (`.md` twin read in full).
**Checked against:** this repository at `640069a` (branch `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq`, the same code as `dev`):
the source, `sgit --help` for every command group, `CHANGELOG.md`, the threat model
(`team/explorer/appsec/threat-model/v0.21.0__threat-model.md`) and the response and release notes under
`team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/`. Numbers that come from the newsroom's own briefs or from cli.sgit.ai pages
are not in this repo. They are marked "external": not contradicted, just not checkable from here.

**In one paragraph.** The article is accurate on the whole, and its honesty sections are mostly fair. There is one
headline number we cannot source: "29 minutes to 4.6 seconds" for a one-file commit on a 76,000-file vault. The
"commits signed since 0.19.0" line is wrong the other way: commits were signed long before October, and 0.19.0 added
*verification*. Two claims are too strong, both in sgit's favour:

- "sgit's signatures say which clone wrote a commit" (see TM-R01).
- "every index is verified against a signed commit" (see TM-R42).

The article also undersells sgit. It does not claim we lack shallow clones: it lists them under "Git has it too",
which is right. But it says sgit refuses partial commits (`sgit write` does them), and it puts "read one file with no
clone" wholly in the future (it works today on normal vaults). It also leaves out several things Git has no equivalent
for, listed in section 2.

Almost everything on the "Git is ahead" list can be built client-side, as Git builds it. The things that cannot be
built are the ones that need the host to read content, and one more: taking back data a reader already has.

---

## 1. Claim by claim

✓ = matches the code or our records · ✗ = wrong · ~ = right but needs a qualifier · ext = external, not checkable here.

### Releases and numbers

| # | Article says | Verdict | What the record says |

| 2 | **One-file commit on a 76,000-file vault: 29 min (1,739 s) → 4.6 s** (headline, abstract, "In short", 0.25.0 bullet) | ✗ **unsourced** | Not in the CHANGELOG or any note here. The 0.25.0 record has a one-file `commit` going from **4 min** on the newsroom's 79,465-file vault, and from **47 min** for the *first* commit on the 228,000-file synthetic vault, to **9 s**. The 76,000-file synthetic vault was built later, for the 0.26.0 measurements; it has no 29-minute number, and its "first commit" is 50–69 s. Ask the writer for the source. If none exists, use "4 min → 9 s (79,000 files)" or "47 min → 9 s (228,000 files)". |
| 3 | Pull of a 300-file pass on 228,000 files: 566 s → 31.7 s, and 16.9 s with indexes | ✓ ~ | `response__newsroom-first-morning-on-0-25-0.md` and CHANGELOG 0.26.0. Qualifier: 566 → 31.7 was measured **under cProfile**, which inflates absolute times; the ratio stands. 31.7 → 16.9 is a plain run. |
| 4 | One-folder clone of a pack vault: 36 s → 2.8 s; 12.5 MB against the whole 88 MB pack | ✓ | `release-readiness__pack-indexes-branch.md`: `clone --path raw/c09` (1,520 files) on the 76,000-file vault, 0.25.0 against 0.26.0. 5 requests for 88 MB against 24 ranged requests for 12.5 MB. |

The next release from main bumps the minor, so it ships as **0.27.0**. Our own response note says 0.26.1 too; both should say "next release". |
| 8 | Researcher measured ~57 s a pack on 0.26.0 | ext | Field report. Consistent with 1,002 s over 9 packs here. |
| 9 | "The first `status` **after upgrading** to 0.25.0 took 18 min 23 s on the curator's 4.2 GB clone … 0.26.0 fixed it by seeding the cache on every write" | ~ | It was the first `status` **after a fresh clone** (a 4.2 GB pack clone, nearly all of it disk wait), not after an upgrade. The cause and the fix are right: every working-copy write seeds the scan cache, in the 0.26.0 CHANGELOG. |

| 12 | Type_Safe parsing ~3 ms a tree was the 0.24.0 slowness | ✓ | CHANGELOG 0.25.0. |

"On every client" is too strong: on every **sgit** client, and only when the vault turns on `signatures-required`. The web UI and old clients do not enforce it (TM-R26). |
| 15 | Early releases: keep-alive, each shared sub-tree fetched once, full clone in one parallel sweep | ✓ | 0.18.0. |

### What Git has no equivalent for

| # | Article says | Verdict | What the code says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | Contents, file names, commit messages and branch names are encrypted; host sees sizes, timing, counts and, in pack mode, which commit each push carried | ✓ ~ | Correct, but the leak list is short. The host also sees: <br>• equality of trees through deterministic tree encryption (KI-SEC-02); <br>• with `blob-deflate`, each file's compressibility (TM-R40); <br>• index pack sizes; <br>• in path-ordered packs, which blobs share a folder; <br>• for a scoped clone, which byte ranges it reads, which reveals folder sizes and positions (TM-R42). |
| 17 | A read key is derived from the vault key one way, so it can never become write access; works from any static host with no account | ✓ ~ | Read and write keys are two independent PBKDF2-SHA256 derivations (600k iterations, distinct salts) from the vault key, and neither yields the other. `--transport static` reads from any GET host. **Qualifier:** reading is a capability; **writing is a permission**. The write key is a bearer secret the *host* checks, with no cryptographic role. A read-key holder with store write access (a host that does not check, or a leaked write key) can author history that `check verify` calls *verified* (**TM-R01**, the top accepted risk). |
| 18 | Read access cannot be revoked after the fact; per vault, not per folder; "a partial clone is not an access boundary" | ✓ ~ | TM-R12. Add the remedy we do ship: `sgit vault rekey` / `sgit vault move` rotate the key going forward, and the old vault should be deleted after a rekey. Git and GitHub cannot revoke an existing clone either. |
| 19 | Append lane: write without read, answer `{"ok": true}`, a server feature with no sgit command yet | ✓ | No append-lane code in `sgit_ai/`. |
| 20 | Fetch one folder by byte ranges from plain storage, each object verified by hash | ✓ | Phase 2 ranged scoped clone, 0.26.0. Git uses ranged requests only to resume dumb-HTTP downloads. Its partial clone needs a smart server. |
| 21 | Indexes shipped by the writer, signed and encrypted, checked against the commit and its signature; "a bad one is skipped"; "an index is a plan, never a proof" | ✓ ~ | `Vault__Pack_Index__Reader` order: header → signature *under the vault's policy* → anchor to the local commit → member sha256. **Two qualifiers (TM-R42):** <br>• An unsigned index is accepted unless the vault has `signatures-required`. <br>• The snapshot index's `flat` below the root is not checked by the reader. A *signing teammate* can mislead a fresh clone's working copy, just as a commit from that key could. `sgit pack index verify` catches it. Workflow 4's "every index is verified against a signed commit" should say "anchored to its commit and checked under the vault's signature policy". |
| 22 | `sgit pki encrypt --recipient` seals a file to a public key | ✓ ~ | It writes a sealed file that you then commit. The vault does not hold per-recipient files as a native object type. |

### What Git has too

| # | Article says | Verdict | What the record says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23 | Git packs are delta-compressed, sgit's are not; keeping packs whole is Git's default above `fetch.unpackLimit` | ✓ | sgit deflates each blob (`blob-deflate`); no deltas. Git keeps a received pack above `fetch.unpackLimit` / `transfer.unpackLimit` (default 100 objects). |
| 24 | `clone --path`: refuses a commit outside the scope by name; two scoped clones never conflict | ✓ | Since 0.18.0. Out-of-scope entries are always the remote's, by id. |
| 25 | `pull --no-checkout` then `checkout --since-pull` | ✓ | 0.26.0. Also `checkout --changed-since COMMIT`, `--all`, and `checkout <paths>`. |
| 26 | "Shallow clones, private branches and signed commits all have Git equivalents" | ✓ | **We do have shallow clones:** `clone --depth N` and `fetch --unshallow` (0.18.0), combinable with `--path`. The article does not say we lack them; it says Git has them too. |

### Where Git is ahead

| # | Article says | Verdict | What the code says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 27 | Merges are whole-file with conflict files; Git merges line by line and detects renames | ✓ | `Vault__Merge.three_way_merge` compares by blob id and writes `<path>.conflict`. No rename detection. |
| 28 | **Staging and partial commits: sgit refuses them by design** | ✗ partly | No staging area and no hunk-level commits, true. But **whole-file partial commits exist:** `sgit write <path> --file F [--also P:F …] [-m …] [--push]` commits the named files straight to HEAD, atomically, without scanning the working copy. Other edits stay uncommitted. The limitations-page quote ("committing three of seven changed files") is out of date for agents. `sgit commit <paths>` would be a small addition (section 3). |
| 29 | Identity: "sgit's signatures say which clone wrote a commit, not who is allowed to write"; GitHub keys can expire and be revoked | ~ too generous | Weaker than stated. A signature proves the signing key's file decrypts under the read key. Any read-key holder can mint such a key (TM-R01). So a signature says "some key holder", not "which clone", until the owner-signed signer registry (TM-R01 design row) exists. No per-key expiry or revocation either; only whole-vault rotation. |
| 30 | Git has delta packs and GC; sgit has no pruning | ✓ ~ | No unreachable-object GC. (`core/actions/gc` drains pending change packs and is not a prune.) `sgit pack compact` moves superseded packs to `archive/`, which is a partial answer for pack vaults. |
| 31 | Git ids 160-bit by default; sgit format 1 is 48-bit, format 2 is 128-bit and opt-in per vault | ✓ | `sgit vault format --set 2` (0.19.0); existing ids stay 48-bit in a mixed vault. |
| 32 | Ecosystem: forges, review, CI, search, blame, bisect, IDEs; "most of it needs a host that can read the content" | ~ | Half right. Blame, bisect, search, IDE support and most of review are **client-side** in Git too, and can be built (section 3). Only host-side features need a host that reads. We already have `history log --grep / --since / --until / --author / --file / --patch / --stat`, `history diff`, `history show` and `history reflog`. |

### Next, not now

| # | Article says | Verdict | What the record says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 33 | On a normal vault a file is four plain GETs of fixed paths | ~ | Four only for a file at the root. The walk is ref, commit, *every tree on the path*, blob, so a file *d* folders deep is 4 + *d* GETs. For paths declared with `sgit cache add`, it is **one batch request** with no walk (shipped, the cache layer). |
| 34 | Reading one file from a pack vault by byte range with no clone is not shipped (Phase 4) | ✓ | The `at` offsets are written into every path-ordered pack; the reader is not built. |
| 35 | The browser library cannot read pack vaults yet | ext | Not this repo. Consistent with what we know. |

### Housekeeping claims

| # | Article says | Verdict | What the record says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 36 | **Limitations page says signing is "planned work", "though commits have been signed since 0.19.0"** | ✗ | Commits were signed (ECDSA P-256, per clone key) **long before October**. The 0.19.0 notes speak of "commits signed before this (`author_key_id` null)". 0.19.0 fixed the canonical signing input (RFC 8785) and added **verification** (`check verify`, fsck) and `signatures-required` on pull. 0.21.0 extended the check to every clone. Correct line: "commits have been signed for months and verified since 0.19.0". The limitations page is still out of date either way. |
| 37 | The 0.26.0 notes sit under "Unreleased" in the changelog | ✓ on main | True of `main` today. Fixed on `dev` in `01d167a`, which dates `[0.26.0] — 2026-10-27`; it reaches main with the next release. |
| 38 | sgit's docs open with "git for encrypted vaults" | ✓ | `README.md` line 1. |

---

## 2. What we have that the article misses or says we lack

**Things the article says we lack, or puts in the future:**

- **Partial commits** (row 28): `sgit write … --also … --push --json`. It commits named files atomically to HEAD
  and, with `--push`, publishes them in one call. That is the agent form of `git commit <paths>`.
- **One file with no clone** (row 33), on a normal vault: the browser reader does it today (four GETs plus one per
  folder level), and `sgit cache add` makes it one batch request. `sgit history log --vault-key …` already runs with
  no clone; `cat` does not yet (section 3).
- **Key rotation:** `sgit vault rekey` and `sgit vault move` (rotation plus an optional move to another server).
  GitHub has nothing to rotate; a leaked Git deploy key is revoked on the server.
- **Search / history tools** (row 32): `history log --grep --since --until --author --file --patch --stat --json`,
  `history diff A..B`, `history show`, `history reflog`, `history undo`, `history revert`, `history reset`,
  `commit --amend`, `vault stash`, signed `vault tag`, `resolve`, `merge-abort`.
- **Shallow and partial clones:** `clone --depth N`, `fetch --unshallow`, `clone --path`, `fetch <folder>` (widen),
  `clone --sparse`, `clone --no-checkout`, `clone --bare`, `clone-branch`, `clone-headless`, `clone-range`. The
  article files these under "Git has too", which is fair; we are not behind there.

**Things Git has no equivalent for that the article leaves out** (candidates for its first list, or for the follow-up
article):

1. **Custody without access:** `sgit vault mirror` copies a published vault you cannot read, keyless, and verifies it.
   A backup service or a second host can hold and check the vault and learn nothing.
2. **Policy carried by the repository and enforced at clone and pull:** the format gate (`min_client`, features) and
   `signatures-required` live in the encrypted branch index, and every sgit client enforces them before writing
   anything. Git's signature checks are each user's local config; a repository cannot require them of its cloners.
3. **Rewind detection on every clone:** a remote head that does not descend from the last accepted one is refused by
   name (`pull --accept-rewind` to take it). Git's default `+` refspec takes a forced update with one line of output.
4. **A secret guard:** commit refuses vault keys, key-bearing zips and in-tree symlinks to secrets (TM-F11,
   TM-F18, TM-F27).
5. **Agent-shaped writes:** `write --push --json` and `checkout --since-pull`. Two scoped agents can never conflict
   (already in the article).
6. **Serving:** `sgit serve` runs the vault UI and API locally in a container; `sgit serve --static` and
   `sgit publish` lay a vault out for any static host. A read-only clone from a published read key needs no account
   and no server code.
7. **A computable cache:** `sgit cache add <path>` puts a fixed-cost read of a hot file at a location only key
   holders can compute, for edge functions. Git has no read path that skips the tree walk.

---

## 3. What we don't have, and how to build it

Git is a client-side program; almost all of the "Git is ahead" list runs on the client in Git too. Each row below
works on plaintext the client already holds, and needs **no new server feature** unless the row says so.

| Feature | How to build it in sgit | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Line-level three-way merge** | In `Vault__Merge`, when both sides changed a text file (UTF-8, under a size cap), run a diff3 merge of base / ours / theirs (port of xdiff's merge, or a `difflib`-based merge). Write a clean result, or inline `<<<<<<< ======= >>>>>>>` markers, instead of `<path>.conflict`. Whole-file stays the fallback for binary files, and an opt-in strategy for anyone who wants the old behaviour. | M | Biggest user-visible gap. The client has all three plaintexts. |
| **Rename detection** (merge, `history diff`, `log --follow`) | Exact renames: same plaintext `content_hash` in the tree entries on a deleted and an added path. Similar renames: Git's similarity score on plaintext, within a cap. | S–M | Tree entries already carry the plaintext hash, encrypted. |
| **`sgit commit <paths>`, `-p` hunks, a staging area** | `commit <paths>` reuses `write_file`'s path (build only the named paths' spines). `-p`: interactive hunk picker over `history diff`. A real staging area (index) is a design decision; the scan cache is half of it already. | S / M / L | Rule 9: `commit` stays the verb. |
| **blame** | `sgit history blame <path>`: walk the file's commits (the index pack's file → commits member makes this cheap on pack vaults) and run a line diff per step. | M | Fetches each version's blob on demand on shallow or sparse clones; refuses below a shallow boundary. |
| **bisect** | `sgit history bisect start/good/bad/run`: state in `.sg_vault/local/bisect.json`, midpoint by generation number (pack indexes carry them), `branch checkout <commit>` for each step. | S–M | Pure client. |
| **grep over content** | `sgit grep <regex> [--rev C]` over HEAD or a commit, decrypting blobs locally. History grep is `--all`. Optionally a local, encrypted-at-rest search index under `.sg_vault/local/`. | S (HEAD) / M (history) | Needs the blobs: fetch on demand on sparse clones. |
| **Delta compression** | At push, delta a changed blob against its previous version (same path) before deflate and encryption. The pack member is a delta object naming its base id; the reader rebuilds the blob and **verifies it by its content address**, so integrity is unchanged. Bases are restricted to objects in the same pack or the reader's store (thin packs). | L | Leaks only "how big the change was", which ciphertext sizes already show. Needs a format feature flag and a `min_client` gate. |
| **GC / prune** | `sgit vault prune` (write key): compute the set reachable from every named branch, clone branch, tag and stash; delete the rest through the API's delete route after a grace period (Git's `gc.pruneExpire`, default 2 weeks), so objects uploaded by a push still in flight survive. Pack vaults: delete `archive/` packs older than the grace period, since compaction already moves superseded packs there. | M | Must be client-driven: the host cannot read trees to know what is reachable. Same power the write key already has (TM-R39). |
| **One file, no clone, from the CLI** | `sgit cat --vault-key K <path>` (also `--read-key`): ref → commit → trees on the path → blob, or the cache entry when declared. Pack vaults: Phase 4. Read the snapshot index's `flat` member by range, find the blob's `at` offset, read that range, verify by hash. | S (normal) / L (pack) | The `history log --vault-key` path already does the first half. |
| **Append-lane command** | `sgit inbox send <vault> --to <recipient> FILE` seals with `pki encrypt` and calls the append route; `sgit inbox read` for the owner drains it into a commit (the change-pack drain in `core/actions/gc/` is the same shape). | S–M | Server feature exists; this is the client. |
| **Allowed signers, key expiry and revocation** | The owner-signed signer registry already designed for TM-R01: the owner signs the set of trusted signer keys (with expiry and revoked entries) in the branch index; clones pin it on first use; `signatures-required` checks membership, not just "decrypts". | L | Closes the top accepted risk; also gives "who is allowed to write". |
| **Per-folder read access** | A folder key per protected folder, wrapped to each member's public key (pki) in the branch index. That folder's trees and blobs are encrypted under it. Holders of the vault key but not the folder key see the folder as an **opaque entry**, which is exactly what scoped clones already carry. Writers without the key can still commit elsewhere and carry the folder by id (already proven by `clone --path`). Revoking a member means re-encrypting the folder under a new key. | XL, architect first | New crypto, but no new idea: it is the scoped-clone opaque entry plus key wrapping. Folder names on the spine stay visible to vault-key holders. |
| **Per-person protected branches / "who pushed"** | Server: per-member write tokens instead of one shared write key, with an ACL keyed by ref file id (the owner registers which HMAC'd ref ids each token may write). The host enforces it without learning branch names. Client: the signer registry rejects commits on a branch from keys not allowed there. | L (server and client) | Both halves are possible under zero knowledge. |
| **Review, CI, IDEs** | Review: a client-side or browser-side review UI over encrypted review objects in the vault (the vault web UI already decrypts in the browser). CI: a runner that holds the read key (self-hosted, or an Action with the key as a secret), triggered by a ref-change webhook, which the host can send without reading anything. IDEs: an extension driving the CLI, or, for the most leverage, a **`git-remote-sgit` remote helper** so Git, IDEs and Git tooling read and write a vault as a remote. | L each | Zero knowledge holds because the plaintext lives only where the key does. |

---

## 4. What is impossible, or only partly possible, under zero knowledge

These are limits of the model, not of effort. Each one has a client-side substitute.

1. **Anything the host must read to do.** Server-side search, diffs rendered by the server, a "merge" button the host
   executes, code scanning by the host, server-side blame or language statistics. All impossible unless the host is
   given the read key, at which point it is no longer zero-knowledge.
   Substitute: do it in the client or the browser, or in a runner the key holder controls.

2. **Taking back what a reader already has.** No system can revoke data already fetched. GitHub cannot either: a
   removed collaborator keeps their clone. What sgit can do is rotate forward (`rekey`, `move`), delete the old vault
   (TM-R12), and with per-folder keys limit what each reader ever received.

3. **Per-folder permissions enforced by the host inside one key.** The host cannot tell folders apart, and anyone with
   the key can decrypt every object. Per-folder access needs per-folder keys (section 3), not permissions.

4. **Hiding all metadata.** Sizes, timing, counts, which ranges a scoped clone reads, and compressibility with
   `blob-deflate` (TM-R08, R38, R40, R42). Padding to size buckets, fixed-size packs and decoy range reads reduce
   the leak, at a bandwidth cost. They never remove it (that would take an ORAM-style protocol).

5. **Host-side optimisation of the store.** `git gc` and repacking on the server, deltas the host computes, dedupe
   across vaults. The host has only ciphertext. Client-side deltas and prune are possible (section 3). Cross-vault
   dedupe would need convergent encryption, which leaks equality, so we should not want it.

6. **A host that enforces fast-forward-only.** The host cannot read the ref, so it cannot check ancestry. The
   client-side rewind guard (shipped) is the answer. A signed, append-only ref log kept by the host would let clients
   prove a rewind, but not stop a write-key holder from making one.

Everything else in the article's "Git is far ahead" list (merges, staging, blame, bisect, search, identity, GC, deltas,
IDE support, and most of review and CI) is client-side in Git and can be client-side in sgit. "Twenty years of
maturity" is the one item only time fixes.

---

# Response to "sgit issues found on 14 October 2026", and the comms-vault performance report

**Date:** 14 Oct 2026. **Code:** `dev` at 5e85205 plus the fixes on `claude/charming-babbage-5hzcxq`.
**Vault used:** the comms / DC collaboration vault (`y8pwtjlw` on `dev.send.sgraph.ai`), read-only:
cloned, measured, nothing pushed.

## The comms vault today

| | 6 Oct | 14 Oct |
|---|---|---|
| Objects in the store | 18,720 | **35,423** |
| Commits | 626 | 1,227 |
| Trees | — | 16,391 |
| Blobs | 9,404 | 16,315 |
| Files in the working copy | — | 5,101 |
| On disk after a full clone | 173 MB | 527 MB |

Listing the store takes 21 s on its own. It is a different vault from a week ago.

## What was sequential, and what was not

**A full `sgit clone` was not the slow path.** With 0.21.0's code it took about 3½ minutes for
35,423 objects: the listing (21 s), the bulk sweep (about 140 s, 50 objects per request, 16
requests in flight), then a local tree walk (33 s of decrypting 16,391 trees), 47 late blobs
(1.3 s) and the checkout (3.6 s). The progress bar moves in steps of 50, which is the batch
size.

**`sgit pull` was.** Everything that goes through the pull path (`pull`, `fetch`, `status`'s
chain fetch, `widen`) had two sequential loops:

1. **One request per commit.** The commit walk fetches wave by wave, each wave being the
   previous wave's parents, so a linear history of N new commits is N round trips before a
   single tree arrives. On the comms vault that is 1,227 requests.
2. **One request per blob.** After the graph walk, blobs were fetched with `api.read()` one at
   a time, inside a loop. 16,315 requests.

Measured on the live vault, fetching the whole head into an empty store (the worst case of a
pull far behind), unmodified 0.21.0 code against the fix:

| | Before (0.21.0) | After |
|---|---|---|
| Commit and tree walk | 189 s | included below |
| Blobs | 5.4 per second: 818 in 150 s, so about 50 min for 16,315 | included below |
| **Whole fetch** | **about 53 minutes** (projected from the capped run) | **186 s** |
| Objects fetched | — | 35,423, every one verified before it was written |

An agent that is a day behind on this vault is behind by hundreds of commits and thousands of
blobs. That is what they were reporting.

### The fix

- **Blobs go through the batch route** (`_fetch_missing_objects`, pass 2): 50 per request, 16
  requests in flight, with per-object verification and per-file failure classification kept.
  Blobs flagged large go through `read_large` four at a time.
- **Far behind, the walk sweeps.** After 25 sequential commit fetches, a whole-vault clone lists
  the store once and fetches everything missing in bulk, the way a clone does; the walk then
  finds its objects on disk. The "new commits" list and counts still cover what the sweep
  brought. Partial clones (scoped or shallow) never sweep: they must not hold what they do not
  track, and a host that cannot list leaves the walk to finish as before.
- Tests: `tests/unit/sync/test_Pull__Batched_Blob_Download.py` (no single-file reads, chunked
  requests, the bar moves per chunk, a lost blob is classified absent, a corrupt one is refused)
  and `tests/unit/sync/test_Pull__Far_Behind_Sweep.py` (lists once and fetches in bulk, a short
  pull never lists, a partial clone never sweeps, a host that cannot list still completes).

## The four reported issues

| # | Issue | Side | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Disk mode: every append-lane write scans the whole store | **server** | Confirmed from the server code: `Storage_FS__Local_Disk.folder__files__all` iterates the entire store and filters by prefix; `append()` calls it on every write for the 1,000-entry cap. In the brief to the SG/Send team. |
| 2 | Files over 4 MB cannot be pushed to, or fetched on demand from, a server without S3 | client | **Fixed.** `presigned initiate` / `read-url` answer `400 S3 storage mode required` on memory and disk servers. Push now falls back to the batch; clone, pull, `fetch` and `cat` fall back to the read route (`Vault__API.read_large`). A 401/403/5xx still surfaces. Reproduced and proven on the real in-memory server with a 4.25 MB file: `tests/integration/test_Large_Blob__No_S3__Integration.py` fails on 0.21.0 at the push, passes now (push, full clone, sparse fetch). |
| 3 | `clone-headless` then `fetch` always fails | client | **Fixed.** A headless clone holds keys and config only; `fetch`, `ls` and `cat` now bring the tracked head down first (index, ref, commits and trees, never blobs), the way `clone --sparse` does. `tests/unit/sync/test_Sparse__Headless_Fetch.py`. Note: on a vault with a long linear history that first fetch walks the commits one request each, as `clone --sparse` does; the sweep is for whole-vault clones only. |
| 4 | Concurrent full clones queue on one server process | **server** | Deployment note: the Docker entry point runs one uvicorn worker. In the brief. |

The smaller observations in the report (access token on every route including append writes,
caps holding under concurrency, refusals correct) need nothing from the CLI.

| Security | passed |

# `sgit serve`: container first. Options map and spike results, cli.sgit.ai

> The decision to run the SG/Send container image rather than re-implement the server: the runtimes supported (including Apple's container and Podman), the spike results, and phase 1 as built.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/sgit-serve-container-first.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/12/options__sgit-serve-container-and-static.md>.*

# `sgit serve`: container first. Options map and spike results

**Date:** 2026-10-12 · **Status:** options and plan, no sgit code yet · **Supersedes** the
"native server" plan in [`research__sgit-serve-local-vault-server.md`](../research/sgit-serve-running-a-vault-locally.md) (same folder). The API
inventory and browser notes there still apply.

**Decision (Dinis):** run a working vault locally from the SG/Send container image. It has
the vault UI and the API in one image and always tracks the latest SG/Send. sgit gets native
support for it:
- it abstracts the container runtime;
- it supports several runtimes, including Apple's `container`;
- it can install one when none is present;
- it should also work without Docker where possible.

The current read-only server stays as a separate, clearly named mode.

> **Update, same day: decisions taken and phase 1 built.**
> - **Decisions:**
>   1. Image `latest`, with the digest that ran recorded.
>   2. `sgit serve install` installs, after showing what and asking.
>   3. Both Apple `container` and Podman are supported on macOS.
>   4. `sgit vault serve` moved to `sgit serve --static`.
>   5. The brief to SG/Send is in this folder.
> - **What changed from the plan below:** the clone does **not** push to the local server as a
>   second remote. Its rewind baselines and its copy of the server's ref are kept per branch,
>   not per server, so two servers would trip its own rewind protection. Instead:
>   - `sgit serve push` (clone → server) only ever moves the local server forward;
>   - `sgit serve pull` (server → clone) fetches, verifies, checks the signature policy and
>     fast-forwards this clone's own branch;
>   - `sgit push` then reaches the real server as usual.
> - **Verified here:**
>   - Docker end to end: start, the UI opening the served clone, a server-side commit brought
>     back, stop;
>   - the uv engine (same data folder);
>   - divergence refusals.
>
>   The Apple `container` adapter is written to its documented CLI but not yet run on a Mac.

## 1. Two modes

| Mode | Command | What it is | Writes | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **container** (default) | `sgit serve` | The SG/Send image (`diniscruz/sg-send-vault`): vault UI + full API + disk store, on `localhost` | yes. A real local vault server: the UI edits, sgit pushes and pulls | a container runtime, or the Python engine (§4) |
| **static** | `sgit serve --static` (today's `sgit vault serve`) | A stdlib read-only file server for a **published** vault: the static loader plus the encrypted store, no API | no | nothing |

- Static mode still has a job: it previews what `sgit publish` produces, or serves an unpacked
  published zip, with zero dependencies.
- It is not "run a vault". Rename it, and make `sgit vault serve` print its new place
  (the rule-9 moved-word behaviour).

## 2. What I verified today (spike in this cloud container)

All of it was run here, x86_64 Linux, Docker 29.6 / containerd 2.2. The screenshot
`spike__local-container-ui-open-vault.png` is next to this file.

| # | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `docker pull diniscruz/sg-send-vault:latest` | about 10 s; **400 MB**; a multi-arch index (amd64 + arm64); server **v0.34.0**, UI v0.2.3; 31 tags (`v0.27.70` … `v0.34.0`) |
| 2 | `docker run -p 8080:8080 -v <dir>:/data` | `/api/info/health` ok; UI `/` 200 |
| 3 | `sgit init` / `commit` / `push` / `clone --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080` (repo code) | works: 12 objects on disk at `<dir>/vault/iv/ivh5cbkj/{manifest.json,bare/…}`; the fresh clone has the files |
| 4 | **The image runs as uid 10001** (its README still says root) | a host folder owned by the user is **not writable**: `Permission denied: '/data/vault'`. **Fix: `--user $(id -u):$(id -g)`**, which sgit must always pass |
| 5 | sgit refuses to push with no token ("no access token configured") even though the server has no auth | passing any `--token` works. **sgit fix:** a server that needs no token is a normal case |
| 6 | Headless Chromium → `http://localhost:8080/en-gb/vault/`, key typed into the form | **the vault opens and decrypts**: `docs/`, `a.md` ("hello local"). Same origin, plain http on localhost, Web Crypto fine |
| 7 | `#<vault-key>` in the URL | did not auto-open (the form did) |
| 8 | The UI loads `sg-layout.js` and `sg-llm-events.js` **from `dev.tools.sgraph.ai` at runtime** | not self-contained, despite "no CDN dependency" in its README: offline or air-gapped use will break |
| 9 | The UI shows "Read-only" until an access key is entered | expected; `sgit serve` should print the access-key hint, or configure the container so the UI is writable |
| 10 | **containerd only** (`ctr run`, no Docker API) | works (image imported, push lands on disk) |
| 11 | Anonymous `ctr pull` from Docker Hub | **429 Too Many Requests**; Docker Hub's anonymous limit is 100 pulls per 6 h per IP |
| 12 | **No container at all:** the image's own server code (`sgraph_ai_app_send__docker.app`) under a Python 3.12 venv, with the UI folder copied out of the image | works: health, UI, and an sgit push to a disk store |
| 13 | CORS for the hosted UI (`Origin: https://vault.sgraph.ai`) | preflight 200 with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` … **but with `Access-Control-Request-Private-Network: true` → 400 "Disallowed CORS private-network"**. Starlette's `allow_private_network` is off, so Chrome's private-network preflight from vault.sgraph.ai to localhost fails |
| 14 | A server error response | **contains the full Python stack trace** (an information leak; fine on a laptop, not on a shared host) |

## 3. Runtimes: what exists and how sgit would drive each

"docker-compatible" means it accepts `run -d --name -p -v --user -e`, `ps`, `stop`, `logs`
and `pull` with the same flags, so one adapter covers all of them. Rows marked † come from my
knowledge rather than today's run; check each against its current docs when building the
adapter.

| Runtime | OS | CLI | Install (what `sgit serve install` would do or print) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Docker Engine** | Linux | `docker` | distro package / get.docker.com | the reference; verified here |
| **Docker Desktop** | macOS, Windows | `docker` | the vendor installer | Linux VM under the hood; **paid licence for larger companies**† |
| **Podman** | Linux, macOS, Windows | `podman` (docker-compatible) | `brew install podman` + `podman machine init/start` on mac/Windows; distro package on Linux | daemonless, **rootless by default**†; with `--userns=keep-id` the uid problem (#4) goes away; no Docker licence |
| **Apple `container`** | macOS 26 on **Apple silicon** (macOS 15 runs with reduced networking) | `container` (its own CLI, docker-like) | signed `.pkg` from GitHub `apple/container` releases, then `container system start` | one lightweight VM per container, runs OCI images, no Docker. **Its own adapter**; flags to confirm against `container run --help` (ports, mounts) |
| **Colima** | macOS, Linux | gives a `docker` (or `nerdctl`) context | `brew install colima docker && colima start` | free, Lima VM; then the docker adapter† |
| **OrbStack** | macOS | `docker` | vendor app | fast; commercial licence for business use† |
| **Rancher Desktop** | macOS, Windows, Linux | `docker` or `nerdctl` | vendor installer | free (SUSE)† |
| **Finch** | macOS, Windows, Linux | `finch` (nerdctl-based, docker-like) | AWS installer / brew | free (AWS)† |
| **containerd + nerdctl** | Linux | `nerdctl` (docker-compatible) | distro or release tarball | lean Linux servers; raw `ctr` works too (verified, #10) |
| **WSL2** | Windows | any of the above inside WSL | `wsl --install` + one of the above | Windows without Docker Desktop |
| **Python engine** (no container) | anywhere with **`uv`** | `uv run --python 3.12 --with sgraph-ai-app-send …` | `uv` (one static binary); uv fetches Python 3.12 itself | the same server code as the image, verified (#12); needs the built UI folder (§5) |

**Detection order:** a runtime already running wins. Otherwise the order is:
1. `docker` (context answers)
2. `podman`
3. `container` (Apple)
4. `nerdctl`
5. `finch`
6. the Python engine if `uv` is found
7. `--static` as the last resort, with a message saying what the user is missing

`sgit serve --runtime <name>` overrides the choice. `sgit serve runtimes` lists what it found,
and for anything missing, the one install command per OS.

**Installing:**
- `sgit serve install [<runtime>]` prints the command and runs it **only after a yes**, because
  it is a system change.
- On macOS with Apple silicon it suggests Apple `container`, or Podman.
- On Linux it suggests Podman or Docker Engine.
- On Windows it suggests WSL2 + Podman.
- Without any runtime, it suggests `uv` and the Python engine.

## 4. What `sgit serve` does (container mode)

```
sgit serve                     # inside a clone
  1. pick a runtime (§3); pull the image, pinned by digest and recorded (latest by default; --tag vX.Y.Z)
  2. data dir: <clone>/.sg_vault/serve/ (or --data DIR, interchangeable with any sg-send-vault /data)
  3. run: --name sgit-serve-<vault_id> --user <uid>:<gid> -p 127.0.0.1:<port>:8080 -v <data>:/data
          (-p on 127.0.0.1 only: a plain `-p 8080:8080` publishes on every interface)
  4. wait for /api/info/health
  5. seed: push this clone into it as a remote, `local` → http://127.0.0.1:<port>
           (the existing push code: no coupling to the server's disk layout)
  6. print the UI URL, the vault-key and access-key hints; --open launches the browser
sgit serve status | logs | stop | update     # update = pull the newer image, restart, same data dir
sgit serve --static                          # today's read-only published-folder server
```

Then:
- `sgit pull --remote local` brings edits made in the browser into the clone, with full
  verify-then-accept;
- `sgit push` sends them to the real server.

The server owns its own store. The clone's `.sg_vault/bare/` is never mounted, because the
UI writing the clone's accepted refs would undo what 0.21 fixed.

**Python engine:** steps 1 and 3 become
`uv run --python 3.12 --with sgraph-ai-app-send==<v> python -m … --port <p>`, with
`SEND__STORAGE_MODE=disk`, `SEND__DISK_PATH=<data>` and `SEND__VAULT_STATIC_DIR=<ui dir>`.
Everything else is the same.

**TLS:** only for the LAN or Safari cases (see the research note §5–6).
- sgit generates a cert with `cryptography`;
- it mounts the cert and key at `/certs`;
- it sets `FAST_API__TLS__ENABLED=true`, which the image already supports.

## 5. Asks of the SG/Send team (from the spike)

1. **Vendor the `dev.tools.sgraph.ai` scripts into the image** (#8). Today the "self-contained"
   UI needs the internet.
2. **`allow_private_network=True`** in the CORS middleware (#13). Without it, the hosted UI
   cannot reach a local server from Chrome.
3. **No stack traces in error responses** (#14), or only behind a debug flag.
4. **README:** the image runs as uid 10001, so document `--user` or `chown` (#4).
5. **Also publish to GHCR or ECR Public** (#11). sgit can then fall back when Docker Hub
   rate-limits.
6. **Publish the built vault UI** (`/app/static_vault`) as a versioned release asset. That is
   what the Python engine needs; today it can only be copied out of the image.
7. Optionally, let `#<vault-key>` (or a `?key=` handoff) auto-open on `/en-gb/vault/` (#7), so
   `sgit serve --open` lands inside the vault.

## 6. Changes in sgit

| Change | Size |
|---|---|
| `Container__Runtime` (detect, pull, run, ps, stop, logs, health wait) with adapters: docker-compatible (docker, podman, nerdctl, finch), Apple `container`, Python engine (uv) | ~350 lines |
| `CLI__Serve`: container mode (seed via push to a `local` remote, banner, `--open`), `status/logs/stop/update/runtimes/install`, `--static` = today's server; `sgit vault serve` points to it | ~250 lines |
| A token is optional when the server has no auth (#5) | small |
| TLS cert generation + mount | ~100 lines |
| **Tests:**<br>• unit: each adapter's command lines, against a fake runtime binary on `PATH`;<br>• integration: **real Docker in CI** (the daemon starts in this kind of environment, as shown today); clone, push and pull against the image; a Playwright check that the UI opens the vault | ~1 day |

**Estimate:**

| Phase | Work | Estimate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Docker-compatible adapter + serve, stop, status, logs + seeding | 2 days |
| 2 | Apple `container` adapter + Python engine | 1–1.5 days; the Apple adapter needs a Mac to test on |
| 3 | `runtimes`/`install` + TLS | 1 day |
| 4 | Docs, threat model rows | ½ day |

Total: about **5 days**. Phase 1 alone gives you "clone a vault, `sgit serve`, edit it in the
browser".

## 7. Decisions for you

1. **Image tag:** default to `latest` (always current, as you suggested) and record the
   digest in use, or pin per sgit release for reproducibility? My suggestion: `latest`, plus
   `--tag` and a recorded digest.
2. **Installing runtimes:** print the command only, or run it after confirmation?
3. **Apple `container` vs Podman** as the macOS recommendation: Apple's needs macOS 26 on
   Apple silicon; Podman runs everywhere.
4. **`--static` naming:** keep `sgit vault serve` as an alias, or move it fully?
5. Should I send the §5 asks to the SG/Send team as a brief?

# `sgit serve`: running a vault locally — research and plan, cli.sgit.ai

> How to run a vault locally: the vault server's API inventory, the browser modes, when TLS is and is not needed, and how much plumbing sgit would need.

*Source: <https://cli.sgit.ai/research/sgit-serve-running-a-vault-locally.html> · generated from the same content as the page, so the two cannot drift. Published from <https://github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__CLI/blob/182cfc16578fc599b151edb62e221722946c4a22/team/humans/dinis_cruz/claude-code-web/10/12/research__sgit-serve-local-vault-server.md>.*
